nodes.description: Source A documents three shellcode transformation methods: AES encryption via CNG (preferred over deprecated CryptoAPI), XOR with a key (same routine for encrypt/decrypt), and Base64 encoding via CryptStringToBinaryA/CryptBinaryToStringA or certutil.exe -encode. The material distinguishes encoding (no key) from encryption (requires key) and notes XOR is technically encryption because it uses a key. Raw shellcode in a binary is flagged by AV/EDR solutions.

nodes.label: IAT (Import Address Table) Hooking
nodes.description: IAT hooking overwrites the function pointer entries in the PE import data directory (one of 16 DataDirectory entries) so that calls to an imported function route to an attacker- or EDR-controlled handler. The IAT is normally read-only and the loader resolves it at load time; hooking requires VirtualProtect to flip the page to PAGE_READWRITE, overwriting the pointer, then restoring prior protections. Unlike inline hooking, IAT hooks only intercept calls routed through the import table, not calls resolved dynamically via GetProcAddress or PEB walking.

nodes.label: Inline (Prologue) Hooking
nodes.description: Inline hooking patches the first bytes of a target function with a jump instruction to a handler, redirecting execution before the original prologue runs. On 32-bit the patch uses a 5-byte JMP rel32 (E9 xx xx xx xx) preceded by a 2-byte short JMP (EB F9) over the MOV EDI, EDI hot-patch slot. On 64-bit a MOV RAX, imm64 followed by JMP RAX pattern is used because a single JMP cannot encode a 64-bit absolute target. Detours and EasyHook are the canonical implementations. EDRs use this on ntdll syscall stubs to inspect arguments before the syscall executes.

nodes.label: Hook Trampoline
nodes.description: A trampoline is a small code stub that contains the original bytes displaced by an inline hook, followed by a jump back to the byte immediately after the hook location in the original function. When the hook handler needs to invoke the real function it calls the trampoline, which executes the displaced prologue and returns control to the original function body past the patched region. Without a trampoline, calling the hooked function from inside the hook handler recurses infinitely because the hook JMP fires again. The number of bytes the trampoline must preserve depends on the length of the patched instructions, not a fixed count, because x86 instructions are variable-length.

nodes.label: EDR Userland Hooking Surface
nodes.description: EDRs inject a DLL into monitored processes that installs inline or IAT hooks on high-value ntdll syscall stubs (NtAllocateVirtualMemory, NtMapViewOfSection, NtWriteVirtualMemory, NtCreateThreadEx, NtProtectVirtualMemory, etc.). The hook handler inspects arguments and call order before deciding whether to pass, modify, or block the call. Userland hooks are the cheapest interception layer for the EDR but are entirely bypassable from the process itself because the hook code and the hooked bytes both live in user-mode memory the process can read, write, and avoid.

nodes.label: Hell's Gate SSN Resolution
nodes.description: Hell's Gate dynamically resolves syscall service numbers (SSNs) at runtime by walking the PEB to find ntdll, locating the target Nt* export, and reading the SSN out of the stub's mov eax, imm32 instruction. The technique is position-independent and does not rely on hardcoded syscall IDs, which would break across Windows versions. The check `(*(PBYTE)TargetFunction + 3) == 0xB8` validates that the stub's fourth byte is the mov opcode, confirming the SSN follows. Hell's Gate fails if the stub is already inline-hooked because the 0xB8 byte is no longer at offset +3.

nodes.label: Halo's Gate Hook-Aware SSN Resolution
nodes.description: Halo's Gate extends Hell's Gate to handle hooked stubs. Because SSNs in ntdll are stored in numerical order across consecutive stubs, if the target stub's 0xB8 byte is missing (hooked), the technique walks neighboring stubs forward or backward, reads their SSNs, and infers the target SSN by positional arithmetic. The instruction sequence is captured in the off_hooked pattern: repeatedly call off_hooked on near_syscall neighbors until a valid SSN region is found, then offset to the target. This avoids the need to unhook the stub before resolving its SSN.

nodes.label: Heaven's Gate Wow64 Transition
nodes.description: Heaven's Gate is the mechanism by which a 32-bit (Wow64) process on a 64-bit Windows system transitions to 64-bit code to issue native syscalls. The 32-bit code jumps to ntdll.Wow64Transition, which redirects via a far jmp (0x33 selector) to wow64cpu.dll in 64-bit mode, where the syscall is issued directly. Because 32-bit ntdll is mapped alongside 64-bit ntdll in Wow64 processes, a 32-bit implant can use this transition to invoke 64-bit syscall stubs that bypass any 32-bit-mode hooks. EDRs that only hook the 32-bit ntdll have no visibility into calls routed through the 64-bit stub via Heaven's Gate.

nodes.label: Wow64 Function Prologue Hot-Patch Slot
nodes.description: 32-bit Windows functions conventionally begin with MOV EDI, EDI, a 2-byte NOP that serves as a hot-patch slot. An inline hook replaces this with a 2-byte short JMP (EB F9, jump −5) that lands in the 5 bytes of padding preceding the function, where the E9 rel32 jump to the hook handler is installed. The pattern nop nop nop nop nop / mov edi, edi / push ebp / mov ebp, esp appears in non-hooked functions; the hooked variant shows jmp rel32 (E9 xx xx xx xx) preceded by jmp 0xFB (−5) (EB F9). Scanning for these byte patterns in ntdll identifies inline-hooked stubs.

nodes.label: Fresh Copy NTDLL.text Restoration
nodes.description: The Fresh Copy unhook obtains a pristine ntdll from C:\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll on disk and copies its entire.text section over the in-memory ntdll.text, displacing any EDR-installed inline hooks. The API sequence is CreateFileA → CreateFileMapping → MapViewOfFile → locate NT headers via the DOS stub and PE header → locate.text section via SectionHeader → memcpy the section bytes over the live ntdll.text. The on-disk copy is considered trustworthy because EDRs typically hook the in-memory stubs, not the on-disk file, although an operator could in theory patch on-disk ntdll to defeat this validation source.

nodes.label: Suspended Copy NTDLL Syscall Table Restoration
nodes.description: The Suspended Copy unhook spawns a new process via CreateProcess with CREATE_SUSPENDED. Because the new process has just been initialized by the loader but not yet had EDR DLLs injected (or even if injected, the ntdll.text is pristine at the suspend point), the operator locates the ntdll.text section in the suspended process, extracts the syscall table, and copies it into the hooked process. The suspended process is then either discarded or used as the injection target. This avoids disk I/O on ntdll.dll that the Fresh Copy method incurs.

nodes.label: PE DataDirectory and Import Address Table
nodes.description: The PE header's optional header contains an array of 16 DataDirectory entries. Index 1 (IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT) points to the import descriptor; the IAT itself is a parallel array of function pointers that the loader fixes up at load time. Each IAT entry holds the resolved address of an imported function after load. Modifying an IAT entry redirects all calls routed through that import without modifying the target function's body, which is why IAT hooking is less invasive but also less comprehensive than inline hooking.

nodes.label: x64 Syscall Stub Byte Pattern
nodes.description: 64-bit ntdll syscall stubs follow the pattern mov r10, rcx; mov eax, SSN; test byte ptr [...], 01; jne...; syscall; ret. The mov eax, imm32 instruction encodes the SSN at offset +3 in the stub (opcode 0xB8 followed by the 4-byte SSN). Hell's Gate checks for the 0xB8 byte at this offset to validate the SSN is readable. Inline hooks overwrite this region — commonly with mov rax, imm64; jmp rax — destroying the SSN's discoverable position and triggering the Halo's Gate fallback path.

nodes.label: AV Detection Engine Types
nodes.description: Antivirus products decompose detection into three engine types. The static engine performs signature matching against files and in-memory buffers without executing the sample. The dynamic engine executes samples in a virtualized container (sandbox) and observes behavior including API call sequence, file and registry modifications, and network activity. The scan engine provides on-demand or on-access scanning against a signature database. EDRs extend this with kernel-mode telemetry and behavioral analytics layered on top of the AV engines. Evasion techniques must defeat multiple engines simultaneously because no single bypass covers static signatures, dynamic sandbox heuristics, and kernel callbacks.

nodes.label: Syswhispers3 SSN Stub Generator
nodes.description: Syswhispers3 is a tool that generates header, source, and MASM assembly files implementing syscall stubs with multiple bypass modes: WoW64 stubs, egg-hunter SSN resolution (searching ntdll for an 0xB8-byte egg pattern), direct syscall jumps in both WoW64 and x64 modes, and direct syscall jumps to random syscall numbers as a jitter against per-SSN detection. Visual Studio projects must enable MASM build support to compile the generated.asm files. Syswhispers1, 2, and 3 represent progressive generations adding more evasion modes over the original direct-syscall implementation.

nodes.label: Kernel Callback Resilience to Userland Unhooking
nodes.description: Source A unit 18-20 explicitly teaches that unhooking userland ntdll hooks does not fully blind a security product because a kernel module may still be watching. Kernel-mode callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks, PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine, CmRegisterCallback) operate at PASSIVE_LEVEL inside the kernel and observe the same NT operations the userland hooks were intercepting, completely independent of ntdll's.text section state.

nodes.label: Import Address Table Hooking
nodes.description: IAT hooking (a.k.a. function-pointer hooking) modifies the array of imported-function addresses in a PE's IAT. Source A unit 27 documents the sequence: parse PE headers to find the import table, locate the module that implements the hooked function, change page protections on the IAT from read-only to PAGE_READWRITE (saving old permissions), overwrite the function pointer, then restore prior protections. EDRs use this to redirect API calls through introspection stubs.

nodes.label: AV Detection Engine: Static vs Dynamic Analysis
nodes.description: Source A unit 1 frames AV solutions as composed of static and dynamic detection engines. Static uses signature matching (YARA-like rules) against the file before runtime; dynamic executes samples in a virtualized container to observe malicious behavior. Bypass strategies differ per engine: static signatures are bypassed by changing code bases (encryption, polymorphism), while dynamic analysis is bypassed by delaying execution or encrypting payload until sandbox exit.

nodes.label: AMSI In-Process Patching of amsi.dll
nodes.description: Source A Lab 5.4 'AMSI No More' has the operator patch a PowerShell process that already has amsi.dll loaded, first observing how data is passed in for analysis, then exploring various methods to patch amsi.dll so AmsiScanBuffer returns clean without triggering. The lab emphasizes that the patch must be applied after amsi.dll is loaded and that the patch site is the buffer-submission function inside the loaded amsi.dll instance.

nodes.label: AppInit_DLLs Persistence for User32-linked Processes
nodes.description: Source A unit 14 names AppInit as the technique to use for processes linked against User32.dll. AppInit_DLLs is loaded into every process that loads User32.dll via the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs registry value, making it a broad-spectrum persistence and injection vector that piggybacks on the User32 import graph.

nodes.label: PE-sieve Memory Scanner
nodes.description: Source A units 12 and 23 reference PE-sieve as a representative defensive tool that scans a running process for the effects of offensive techniques — specifically detecting manually mapped / injected / hollowed modules by comparing in-memory PE headers and section contents against their on-disk originals and flagging memory regions whose backing image cannot be reconciled with a file path.

nodes.label: Parent-Child Process Relationship Heuristic
nodes.description: Source A unit 2 describes the defender heuristic of alerting when a process that should never spawn children (browsers, Office applications, PowerShell, cmd) produces unexpected child processes. Conversely, explorer.exe spawning many child processes is treated as benign. This heuristic is what T-015's PPID spoofing directly counters by re-attributing the implant's parent to explorer.exe.

nodes.label: AV/EDR Cloud Sample Submission Risk
nodes.description: Source A unit 7 lists sample submission to the cloud engine as the principal con of operating a custom bypass: if the implant is not properly cut off from internet, an unfamiliar sample is uploaded for cloud analysis, where reverse engineering can produce and distribute a new signature invalidating the bypass. This makes network egress filtering a prerequisite for operating custom evasion code.

nodes.label: WSASocket AF_INET SOCK_STREAM IPPROTO_TCP
nodes.description: Source A unit 10 documents WSASocket as the API used to create the C2 socket before callback to the listening post. The parameters af=AF_INET, type=SOCK_STREAM, protocol=IPPROTO_TCP produce a TCP socket with SOCKET return type. WSASocket is preferred over socket() for C2 implants because it accepts a WSAPROTOCOL_INFO structure allowing explicit provider selection and overlaps cleanly with subsequent bind/connect calls.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot for Process Enumeration
nodes.description: The CreateToolhelp32Snapshot API creates a snapshot handle enumerating processes, threads, heaps, or modules on the local system. The dwFlags parameter (with TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS being most relevant for process enumeration) controls what data is captured. The snapshot is a static view taken at the time of the call — subsequent process changes are not reflected. Iteration is performed via Process32First followed by Process32Next using PROCESSENTRY32 structures, defined in TlHelp32.h.

nodes.label: EnumProcesses API
nodes.description: EnumProcesses is a Win32 API for retrieving process IDs on the local system. It accepts a DWORD pointer (lpidProcess), a buffer size in bytes (cb), and a pointer to receive bytes needed (lpcbNeeded), returning only PIDs without detailed information. The function returns BOOL and is suitable when detailed process metadata is not required.

nodes.label: WTSEnumerateProcesses via Terminal Services
nodes.description: WTSEnumerateProcesses is a Windows Terminal Service API that provides an alternative enumeration path to CreateToolhelp32Snapshot and EnumProcesses. Source A highlights it as a documented method with potential to query remote systems when paired with a server handle, providing per-process information including SID data that the simpler EnumProcesses API does not surface.

nodes.label: NtQuerySystemInformation for Process Enumeration
nodes.description: NtQuerySystemInformation with SystemProcessInformation is an undocumented NT API that Source A lists alongside EnumProcesses and WTSEnumerateProcessesEx as a process enumeration method. It bypasses the Win32 API layer and returns kernel-maintained process lists directly, useful when Win32 APIs are hooked or filtered by EDR.

nodes.label: NetLocalGroupEnum for Local Group Enumeration
nodes.description: NetLocalGroupEnum enumerates local or remote system groups, returning LOCALGROUP_INFO_0 or LOCALGROUP_INFO_1 structures depending on the level parameter. It returns NET_API_STATUS and supports a resumehandle for paged enumeration of large group lists. Related APIs in the lmaccess.h header include NetUserEnum, NetLocalGroupGetMembers, NetUserGetInfo, and NetGetGroupUsers.

nodes.label: Service Control Manager Database Enumeration
nodes.description: The Service Control Manager (SCM) maintains the database of installed services. EnumServicesStatusEx enumerates entries in this database, requiring an SC_HANDLE with at least SC_MANAGER_ENUMERATE_SERVICE access. The InfoLevel parameter only accepts SC_ENUM_PROCESS_INFO. dwServiceType filters by SERVICE_WIN32 etc., dwServiceState filters active/inactive services, and pszGroupName can filter by service group or be NULL to enumerate all groups. QueryServiceStatusEx with SC_STATUS_PROCESS_INFO then retrieves per-service details including the hosting PID.

nodes.label: ITaskScheduler COM Interface for Task Enumeration
nodes.description: Scheduled task enumeration on Windows requires COM — the ITaskScheduler interface's Enum method returns an IEnumWorkItems enumerator object, whose Next method retrieves task names as LPWSTR strings. The sequence requires CoInitialize and CoCreateInstance before invoking these methods. This is the v1.0 Task Scheduler API surface; the v2.0 surface uses ITaskService and XML-based definitions.

nodes.label: GetAdaptersAddresses Network Interface Enumeration
nodes.description: GetAdaptersAddresses is the API Source A identifies as including logical interfaces in its results, distinguishing it from GetNumberOfInterfaces (which counts only physical interfaces) and GetIpStatistics (which returns IP-layer counters). The function returns unicast, anycast, and multicast addresses along with adapter metadata, making it the preferred enumeration primitive for full network topology discovery.

nodes.label: Snapshot Static View Semantics
nodes.description: Snapshots returned by CreateToolhelp32Snapshot are static views captured at the moment of the API call — subsequent process creation, termination, or state changes are not reflected in the snapshot handle. Operators enumerating dynamic targets (e.g., short-lived injection processes) must either re-snapshot or pair the snapshot with a live query such as QueryServiceStatusEx or OpenProcess followed by QueryInformationProcess for current state.

nodes.label: PE Inspection Toolchain
nodes.description: Source A enumerates a set of static analysis tools for inspecting PE/DLL contents: Dumpbin (Microsoft utility for exports/imports), PEview, PE-bear, and CFF Explorer. These tools surface the import/export tables, section layout, and header fields that an operator must understand when developing PE-parsing logic for injection (T-007) or evasion primitives that target PE structures.

nodes.label: ITaskScheduler COM Enumeration
nodes.description: The ITaskScheduler COM interface exposes the Enum method, which returns an IEnumWorkItems enumerator that allows iteration over registered scheduled tasks by name. The enumerator's Next method retrieves an array of LPWSTR task names. Source A presents this as the canonical COM-based approach to enumerating scheduled tasks on a Windows system.

nodes.label: Win32 Process Enumeration API Family
nodes.description: Source A covers four Win32/NT APIs for enumerating processes on a Windows system: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot (toolhelp snapshot), EnumProcesses/K32EnumProcesses (PSAPI), WTSEnumerateProcesses (Terminal Services), and NtQuerySystemInformation (NT direct). Each returns process information at a different abstraction level; Source A's lab sequence treats them as interchangeable alternatives with different EDR visibility profiles.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration
nodes.description: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with the TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS flag produces a snapshot handle that can be iterated with Process32First and Process32Next using a PROCESSENTRY32 structure. The same API also captures heap and thread snapshots via TH32CS_SNAPHEAPLIST and TH32CS_SNAPTHREAD. Source A frames this as the standard toolhelp API for process enumeration in implant development.

nodes.label: K32EnumProcesses (EnumProcesses)
nodes.description: K32EnumProcesses (exported as EnumProcesses in psapi.dll) returns an array of DWORD process IDs for every process on the system. Source A covers it as the simplest enumeration API — it returns only PIDs without additional context, requiring a follow-up call such as OpenProcess and GetModuleBaseName to retrieve names. The material flags it as 'undocumented' alongside WTSEnumerateProcessesEx and NtQuerySystemInformation in a unit review question.

nodes.label: NetUserEnum and USER_INFO Levels
nodes.description: NetUserEnum (netapi32.dll, declared in lmaccess.h) returns user account information at a level selected by the dwLevel parameter, with USER_INFO_0 through USER_INFO_20 providing progressively more detail (name only, then password metadata, then full account properties). The function returns a buffer that must be freed with NetApiBufferFree. Source A positions it as the Win32 enumeration primitive for surveying local or remote system users.

nodes.label: NetGroupGetUsers / NetLocalGroupGetMembers
nodes.description: The lmaccess.h header exposes a family of Net* APIs including NetGroupGetUsers (members of a global group), NetLocalGroupGetMembers (members of a local group), NetUseEnum (active use connections), and NetUseGetInfo. Source A lists these as additional survey APIs beyond NetUserEnum, useful for mapping group memberships and active SMB sessions during recon.

nodes.label: EnumServicesStatusEx SCM Enumeration
nodes.description: EnumServicesStatusEx enumerates services in the Service Control Manager database when supplied an SC_HANDLE with SC_MANAGER_ENUMERATE_SERVICE access. The InfoLevel parameter accepts only SC_ENUM_PROCESS_INFO. The dwServiceType filter (typically SERVICE_WIN32) and dwServiceState filter scope the result set, while pszGroupName filters by service group (NULL means enumerate all groups). The function requires a pcbBytesNeeded value to size the output buffer correctly.

nodes.label: FindFirstFile / FindNextFile Directory Enumeration
nodes.description: Source A frames directory listing as a non-malicious native Windows behavior also performed by legitimate binaries, and points to standard MSDN examples using FindFirstFile/FindNextFile pattern matching. The material notes that Meterpreter's ls command implements the same primitive, and that directory enumeration is a baseline recon capability expected of any implant.

nodes.label: __stdcall Calling Convention for Windows APIs
nodes.description: Unit 32 documents that __stdcall is used heavily for Windows APIs because they have a fixed number of arguments, allowing the callee to handle stack cleanup. For x86, arguments are pushed right-to-left onto the stack. For x64, the first four integer/pointer arguments are passed in RCX, RDX, R8, R9 and floating-point in XMM0-XMM3, with the stack used for additional arguments. The WINAPI, APIENTRY, and CALLBACK macros (Unit 28) all expand to __stdcall. Understanding this convention is prerequisite for interpreting ntdll syscall stubs and constructing FFI bindings.

nodes.label: __fastcall Calling Convention (x86 Only)
nodes.description: Unit 2/34 documents that __fastcall is x86-only and passes the first two DWORD-sized-or-smaller arguments in ECX and EDX respectively, with additional arguments pushed right-to-left on the stack. It is identified in assembly by the '@' symbol and trailing number (e.g., _Func@8). It does not appear in x86_64 code. Relevant when reading legacy 32-bit shellcode or analyzing older Windows binaries.

nodes.label: __thiscall Calling Convention for x86 C++ Member Functions
nodes.description: Unit 35 documents that __thiscall is a Microsoft-specific convention for x86 C++ class member functions. Arguments are pushed right-to-left on the stack, and the ECX register holds the 'this' pointer to the object instance. The 'this' pointer indexes a virtual function table for the member function being called. Not applicable to x64, which uses a unified calling convention. Relevant when reverse-engineering COM interface vtables for hijack or hook operations.

nodes.label: SAL Annotations on Windows API Declarations
nodes.description: Units 3, 4, 36, 37, and 38 document Microsoft's Source Annotation Language (SAL) used in Windows SDK header files to express parameter contracts: _In_, _Out_, _In_opt_, _Out_opt_, _Ret_z_, _Success_(expr), _When_(expr, anno-list), _Ret_writes_to_(s, c), and intermediate annotations like _Out_writes_bytes_all_(size). The _Success_ annotation defines the return-value expression indicating success; _When_ conditionally applies an annotation based on a runtime expression. Unit 38 notes that Select-String in PowerShell can search the Windows Kits headers (e.g., C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits) for annotation usage examples. These annotations document the intended contract of NT API parameters that the vault's wrappers.rs FFI declarations must honor.

nodes.label: HRESULT Return Value Layout
nodes.description: Units 5 and 21 document that HRESULT is a 32-bit value whose structure encodes severity (bit 31), facility code (bits 16-30), and the actual error code (bits 0-15). The SUCCEEDED and FAILED macros from winerror.h test whether the value is >= 0 or < 0 respectively. Unit 22 documents FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM, FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_HMODULE, and FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_STRING flags for converting HRESULTs and GetLastError codes to human-readable strings. Relevant for proper error handling in NT API wrappers.

nodes.label: NtCreateThreadEx / PspCreateThread Thread Creation Path
nodes.description: Unit 10 documents the kernel-side thread creation path: parameters are converted to flags, a Client ID and TEB address are added to an attribute list, the system determines local vs. remote process context, then NtCreateThreadEx initializes the user-mode thread context and calls PspCreateThread. The thread is created initially suspended and later resumed so it can begin executing its quantum. This path is triggered by both CreateThread and CreateRemoteThreadEx, and is the kernel surface that thread-based injection techniques (classic remote thread, APC, Early Bird) ultimately invoke.

nodes.label: Position-Independent Shellcode Build Settings (Visual Studio)
nodes.description: Unit 17 documents the Visual Studio build configuration for producing position-independent shellcode from C: linker flags /NOENTRY (no entry point for DLLs), /OPT:NOREF (don't strip unreferenced symbols), /NODEFAULTLIB (no CRT), /MAP (generate map file), /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE; C/C++ flags /GS- (no stack canary), /MT (static CRT or none with /NODEFAULTLIB), no C++ exceptions, /SDL- (no SDL checks), no debug info, no hotpatching. An explicit entry point (e.g., MyEntryPoint) replaces main. This configuration is the baseline for compiling C shellcode payloads the vault's loaders execute.

nodes.label: Reflective Loading (Memory-Only PE Execution)
nodes.description: Unit 25 describes reflective loading as 'commonly used to describe this method of manually loading something in memory,' enabling execution of a PE without writing it to disk. The unit frames the decision of when to use a custom loader as 'sometimes, all the time, or never' depending on operational context. This maps to the PE Loader entry in the vault's T-013 remaining injection methods and is the conceptual basis for module-overloading and self-injection patterns.

nodes.label: STARTUPINFOA Standard Handle Redirection for Reverse Shell
nodes.description: Unit 14 documents the pattern of populating STARTUPINFOA's hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError fields with a socket HANDLE, setting dwFlags to STARTF_USESTDHANDLES, and passing bInheritHandles=TRUE to CreateProcessA launching 'cmd.exe' so the spawned process inherits the socket as its standard I/O. This produces a reverse shell without modifying cmd.exe itself. Paired with WSAStartup (Unit 15) initializing Winsock 2.2 via MAKEWORD(2,2), this is the canonical Winsock reverse shell primitive.

nodes.label: Less-Common API Use for Signature Evasion
nodes.description: Units 39 and 40 argue that tool development is 'greatly limited by your creativity and/or your knowledge of operating system internals' and that using less common APIs to perform standard tasks in non-traditional ways 'can assist with making your tool different from others; signature-wise.' The units explicitly cite x86matthew as a reference for creative Windows internals exploration. This is the philosophical basis for the vault's approach of bypassing ntdll hooks with direct/indirect syscalls and using NT APIs (NtCreateUserProcess, NT sockets via AFD) instead of their Win32 wrappers.

nodes.label: dumpbin /exports for Library and DLL Symbol Inspection
nodes.description: Unit 13 documents using dumpbin /exports and dumpbin /all on.lib files to inspect exported symbol names, ordinals, hints, and the dependent DLLs of an import library. The example shows _PrintHello as a cdecl-decorated name with hint 0 and name 'PrintHello' in hello.lib dependent on hello.dll and KERNEL32.dll. This technique is used during tool development to verify symbol decoration, calling convention, and DLL dependencies before linking — relevant to the vault's manual API resolution and proxy DLL work.

nodes.label: Portable Executable File Structure
nodes.description: PE files begin with a DOS stub (legacy MS-DOS marker that prints 'cannot run in DOS mode'), followed by the PE signature (PE\0\0), the COFF header containing machine type, section count, timestamp, symbol table pointer, optional header size, and characteristics flags (e.g. IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE 0x0002), then the Optional Header and Section Headers. Understanding this layout is required for reflective loading because the custom loader must parse headers, map sections at their RVAs, resolve imports, and apply relocations manually.

nodes.label: Implicit vs Explicit DLL Linking
nodes.description: Implicit linking relies on the OS loader to resolve imports at load time via the import address table. Explicit linking uses LoadLibraryEx to load a DLL at runtime, GetProcAddress to resolve function addresses by name, and FreeLibrary to decrement the reference count and unload. The presence of LoadLibraryEx, GetProcAddress, and FreeLibrary calls is a definitive indicator of explicit linking. RDI replaces this entire model with manual mapping.

nodes.label: DLL Relocation and ASLR
nodes.description: DLLs specify a preferred base address in their Optional Header. When the loader maps a DLL and the preferred address is already occupied, it relocates the image by applying RVA-based fixups from the base relocation table to code and data references. ASLR randomizes module base addresses across system boots, making relocation the common case rather than the exception. Custom loaders must implement relocation processing themselves because they bypass the system loader.

nodes.label: In-Memory vs On-Disk Binary Patching
nodes.description: In-memory patching modifies a binary's loaded image in RAM — the change is temporary, affects only the current process, and is lost on process exit. On-disk patching modifies the file on the filesystem — the change is permanent, survives reboots, and can have cascading effects on all processes that load the modified binary. Patching critical system DLLs like ntdll.dll on disk risks system instability and increases detection probability through file integrity monitoring. The material recommends avoiding on-disk patches of critical system files unless absolutely necessary.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL)
nodes.description: SDDL is a string format for representing security descriptors. An SDDL string contains Owner (O:), Group (G:), DACL (D:), and SACL (S:) sections. DACL entries follow the format (AceType;;AccessMask;;ObjectGUID;;InheritedObjectGUID;;SID). Access mask abbreviations include RP (ADS_RIGHT_DS_READ_PROP), WP (ADS_RIGHT_DS_WRITE_PROP), CC (ADS_RIGHT_DS_CREATE_CHILD), GA (GENERIC_ALL). The NULL well-known SID S-1-0-0 appears in example ACLs. Understanding SDDL enables inspection and modification of ACLs on services, registry keys, files, and other securable objects.

nodes.label: GetNamedSecurityInfoA API
nodes.description: GetNamedSecurityInfoA retrieves the security descriptor of a named object. Parameters include the object name (LPCSTR), object type (SE_OBJECT_TYPE — covering NTFS files, services, registry keys, shares, file-mapping objects), and SECURITY_INFORMATION flags specifying which fields to retrieve (owner SID, group SID, DACL, SACL). The returned PSECURITY_DESCRIPTOR must be freed via LocalFree. This API enables red team tools to inspect ACLs before attempting modification for persistence or privilege escalation.

nodes.label: Port Monitor DLL Persistence via AddMonitor
nodes.description: The AddMonitor API registers a custom DLL as a port monitor. When the print spooler service starts, it loads all registered port monitor DLLs into its process. An attacker crafts a malicious DLL, registers it as a port monitor via AddMonitor, and achieves persistence with execution in the spooler service context. The registration persists across reboots because it is stored in the registry under the print monitors key.

nodes.label: AppInit_DLLs Registry Key
nodes.description: The AppInit_DLLs registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows specifies DLLs that are loaded into every process that loads user32.dll. Setting this key with a malicious DLL path causes the DLL to be injected into a wide range of user-mode processes. A known hazard is that the DLL may enter an infinite loading loop if it itself loads user32.dll during DllMain initialization, requiring careful payload construction to avoid this condition.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options + SilentProcessExit Persistence
nodes.description: IFEO persistence sets the GlobalFlag registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>\ to 512 (FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT). Combined with SilentProcessExit registry settings under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\<target>\ (ReportingMode=1, MonitorProcess=<implant_path>), when the target process exits the system launches the specified monitor process. Implementation can use reg.exe or the Win32 Registry APIs RegOpenKeyExA, RegCreateKeyExA, and RegSetValueEx.

nodes.label: WIN32_FIND_DATA File Enumeration Pattern
nodes.description: FindFirstFile and FindNextFile populate WIN32_FIND_DATA structures containing file metadata including attributes, timestamps, file size, and long/short filename. The UACMe project's FusionScanDirectory and FusionScanFiles functions use these APIs with HeapAlloc and HeapFree to recursively enumerate directories and catalog EXE files, storing results in the process heap for subsequent analysis by FusionCheckFile. This enumeration pattern supports UAC bypass research by identifying candidate binaries for hijacking.

nodes.label: KUSER_SHARED_DATA Syscall Dispatch Flag (0x7FFE0308)
nodes.description: The byte at fixed user-mode address 0x7FFE0308 (within the KUSER_SHARED_DATA page mapped read-only at 0x7FFE0000 in every process) is the SystemCall flag. The ntdll syscall stub tests this flag with 'test byte ptr [7FFE0308h],1' to choose between the modern 'syscall' instruction and the legacy 'int 2Eh' interrupt-based dispatch. The flag is set by the kernel at boot based on whether SYSCALL/SYSRET is available on the CPU.

nodes.label: Windows Syscall Number Version Variance
nodes.description: Unlike Linux where syscall numbers are stable across kernel versions, Windows syscall numbers (SSNs) are not guaranteed sequential or consistent across Windows versions. The j00ru (Mateusz Jurcsyk) syscall table documents SSNs from Windows XP SP1 through Windows 11 and shows the same syscall index (e.g., 0x00) resolves to NtAccessCheck on Windows 10/11 but a different function on older versions. Source A explicitly advises against hardcoding syscall numbers or kernel offsets in shellcode; dynamic SSN resolution is required for portability.

nodes.label: Native vs GUI Syscall Routing (ntdll vs win32u.dll)
nodes.description: All threads terminate in the kernel, but GUI threads route certain syscalls through win32u.dll into win32k.sys (the kernel-mode GUI subsystem driver) while native syscalls route through ntdll into the kernel/executive. Functions like NtUserOpenClipboard and NtUserCloseClipboard are dispatched via win32u.dll and land in win32k.sys; functions like NtOpenProcess and NtCreateProcess dispatch via ntdll into the executive. The split exists to keep GUI-related syscall surface in a separate kernel module. EDR products may hook both the ntdll and win32u.dll stub sets.

nodes.label: Inline (Prologue) Hooking
nodes.description: Inline hooking patches the first 5+ bytes of a target function with a jmp instruction to redirect execution to a controlled function. The implementation sequence is: obtain the function's memory address (typically via GetProcAddress), read and save the original 5+ bytes, patch the jmp in place, execute the hook logic, restore the saved bytes, and execute the original function (re-patching if needed for subsequent interception). EDR products use inline hooks on ntdll syscall stubs to intercept and inspect syscall arguments. Libraries implementing this pattern include Microsoft Detours and EasyHook.

nodes.label: Shellcode Reflective DLL Injection (sRDI)
nodes.description: sRDI converts the reflective loader into position-independent shellcode, allowing a DLL to be reflectively loaded without the DLL being compiled with RDI support. The sRDI payload is a complete PE loader in shellcode form, supporting section permissions and TLS callbacks. The shellcode exposes custom helper functions such as GetProcAddressR for resolving exports from the loaded DLL. Components include the bootstrap, the RDI logic itself, the existing DLL bytes, and a user-data region.

nodes.label: Manual PE Loader Implementation
nodes.description: A manual PE loader performs the Windows loader's work in-process: validate file format (Offset 0x00 == 'MZ') and architecture (FileHeader.Machine == x64), parse PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER, PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS64, PIMAGE_FILE_*, PIMAGE_OPTIONAL_*, PIMAGE_SECTION_* and PIMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY structures, process all data directories, build the IAT and EAT, apply base relocations against the actual load address, and jump to OptionalHeader.AddressOfEntryPoint. The implementation distinguishes DLL entry points (DllMain) from EXE entry points (WinMain/main) by entry-point signature analysis.

nodes.label: Native Application Entry Point (NtProcessStartup)
nodes.description: Native Windows applications (subsystem NATIVE, image linked with /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE) use the entry-point signature NTSTATUS NtProcessStartup(PPEB peb), distinct from the standard INT main(int argc, const char* argv[]) used by Win32 console applications. Native applications execute before the Win32 subsystem is initialized and are passed the PEB directly. They are used by tools like autochk and are relevant to loader-level offensive techniques that bypass the Win32 subsystem.

nodes.label: Implicit (Static) DLL Linking
nodes.description: Implicit linking binds an executable to a DLL at compile time via an import library (.lib). Requirements are: a header file (.h) declaring the function signatures, the actual DLL file at runtime, and an import library (.lib) linked into the EXE. Linking is configured either through Visual Studio project settings (Configuration Properties | Linker | Input | Additional Dependencies) or via the #pragma comment(lib, "name.lib") directive in source. The resulting EXE stores dependency module names in its import table; dumpbin /dependents reveals these dependencies and dumpbin /all reveals symbols imported from each.lib.

nodes.label: Inline Function Hooking (EDR)
nodes.description: EDR products insert a jmp instruction at the start of a hooked function (typically in ntdll syscall stubs) to redirect execution into the EDR's user-mode DLL. On x64 the hook uses mov rax, <addr>; jmp rax because relative jmp cannot address the full 64-bit space. The first 5+ bytes of the original prologue are overwritten, breaking the original syscall stub's mov r10, rcx; mov eax, SSN sequence.

nodes.label: Trampoline for Inline Hooks
nodes.description: A trampoline is a small executable stub that contains the original overwritten prologue bytes of a hooked function followed by a jump into the function body past the hook. Without a trampoline, calling the original function re-enters the hook and creates an infinite loop (e.g., hooking NtQuerySystemInformation and then calling NtQuerySystemInformation from within the hook recurses forever). The trampoline executes the saved prologue then jumps past the patched region.

nodes.label: Heaven's Gate (Wow64 32-to-64 Transition)
nodes.description: 32-bit processes on 64-bit Windows (Wow64) transition to 64-bit mode to issue syscalls via a segment-selector far jump, historically dubbed Heaven's Gate. ntdll.dll in a Wow64 process contains both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of syscall stubs; the 32-bit stub transitions to the 64-bit stub which then issues the syscall. Hooking in a Wow64 process must account for both code paths or the hook is bypassed by direct 64-bit stub invocation.

nodes.label: Fresh NTDLL Copy Mapping for Unhooking
nodes.description: CreateFile on \Device\HarddiskVolume\Windows\System32\ntdll.dll, CreateFileMapping to create a section object, MapViewOfFile to map it into the process, locate the.text section via PE header walking, then memcpy the clean.text over the in-memory hooked.text. This restores original syscall stub bytes without needing to read them from a suspended process or restore from a known-good copy embedded in the implant.

nodes.label: Hell's Gate Opcode Inspection Pattern
nodes.description: Hell's Gate resolves SSNs by reading the bytes of ntdll syscall stubs and checking for the pattern mov r10, rcx (4C 8B D1) followed by mov eax, <SSN> (B8 XX XX 00 00). The byte at offset +3 from the stub start is checked for 0xB8; if present, the four bytes following 0xB8 are the SSN. If the stub is hooked (no 0xB8 at +3 because the prologue was overwritten with a jmp), the resolution fails and fallbacks (Halo's Gate, Tartarus Gate) are required.

nodes.label: Syswhispers3 Syscall Stub Generator
nodes.description: Syswhispers3 is a Python tool that generates C header, source, and MASM assembly files for direct syscall invocation. It supports WoW64 stubs, egg-hunter patterns (search memory for a sentinel pattern to locate a syscall instruction), direct syscall jumps in both WoW64 and x64, and random-syscall jumps. Requires enabling MASM in Visual Studio project build customization. Does not produce MEM_IMAGE-backed stubs; generated stubs live in the implant's own.text section.

nodes.label: Explicit DLL Linking and Import Hiding
nodes.description: Explicit linking uses LoadLibraryExW + GetProcAddress to resolve function pointers at runtime, omitting the target DLL from the IAT. dumpbin /dependents on the resulting binary does not list the DLL and dumpbin /imports does not show its exported functions. This hides the dependency from static import-table analysis. LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress are commonly monitored by EDR, motivating PEB-walker-based manual resolution as a substitute.

nodes.label: DLL Export Declaration Methods
nodes.description: Four methods export functions from a DLL: __declspec(dllexport) per-function annotation, EXPORTS statement in a.def module definition file, linker /EXPORT option, and #pragma comment(linker, "/export:..."). The.def file approach scales better when exporting hundreds of functions because it avoids per-function source annotation. Exported functions appear in the DLL's export address table; internal functions do not. Proxy DLLs and export-hijack injection depend on accurately replicating the target DLL's export table.

nodes.label: WinINet API Family (InternetOpen/InternetConnect)
nodes.description: WinINet is the Win32 API family for HTTP and FTP client access. InternetOpenA creates a session handle (HINTERNET) with parameters for user-agent (lpszAgent), access type (direct vs proxy), proxy configuration, and flags for asynchronous behavior and cache bypass. InternetConnectA opens a per-server session for HTTP or FTP using the HINTERNET from InternetOpen. WinINet is user-mode and uses higher-level semantics than WinHTTP; both are commonly monitored by EDR for C2 traffic.

nodes.label: Winsock Initialization and WSASocket
nodes.description: Windows sockets require WSAStartup to load the Winsock DLL (version 2.2) and populate a WSADATA structure before any socket operation. WSASocketA(af, type, protocol,...) creates a SOCKET handle; AF_INET/SOCK_STREAM/IPPROTO_TCP produces a TCP socket. INVALID_SOCKET indicates failure with WSAGetLastError for details. The socket() function is a thin wrapper around WSASocket. Winsock is used for raw TCP C2 channels; WSASocket is the function monitored by EDRs for implant beacon socket creation.

nodes.label: STARTUPINFO Socket Handle Inheritance
nodes.description: The STARTUPINFO structure's hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError fields accept socket handles. When CreateProcessA is called with these fields populated from a connected WSASocket, the spawned cmd.exe inherits the socket as its standard I/O, producing a reverse shell without named pipes or additional I/O plumbing. This is the classic reverse-shell construction covered in Source A implant modules.

nodes.label: WinHTTP C2 API Call Sequence
nodes.description: Source A documents a five-call sequence for HTTP C2: WinHttpOpen creates the session handle, WinHttpConnect specifies the target server and port, WinHttpOpenRequest constructs the request handle with verb and flags, WinHttpSendRequest transmits, and WinHttpReceiveResults collects the response. Each step returns an HINTERNET handle that the next call consumes. WinHTTP is preferred over WinINet for non-GUI implants because it supports service execution, impersonation, IPv6, automatic redirects, and AutoProxy without prompting for credentials.

nodes.label: Certificate Pinning for C2 Transports
nodes.description: Source A describes certificate pinning to prevent TLS interception of C2 traffic. The sequence is: InternetQueryOption with INTERNET_OPTION_SERVER_CERT_CHAIN_CONTEXT retrieves the server's certificate chain, CertGetNameString with CERT_NAME_SIMPLE_DISPLAY_TYPE extracts the common name, and CertGetCertificateContextProperty with CERT_HASH_PROP_ID retrieves the certificate hash for comparison against a pinned value. The hash is converted to hex via std::stringstream for string comparison. Windows, Apple, and Android platforms all perform pinning natively.

nodes.label: CNG AES-GCM/CTR Encryption for Payload Protection
nodes.description: Source A recommends the Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) APIs (bcrypt.h) for encrypting implant-to-C2 traffic to evade SSL-intercepting proxies. The sequence is BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider with BCRYPT_AES_ALGORITHM, BCryptSetProperty with BCRYPT_CHAIN_MODE_GCM (or CTR), BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey to create the key, then BCryptEncrypt/BCryptDecrypt. Older Windows versions may require the wincrypt (Legacy) APIs instead. The material explicitly notes CNG ensures no plaintext malware payload is on the implant.

nodes.label: Legacy CryptoAPI AES Shellcode Decryption
nodes.description: Source A documents a deprecated AES decryption sequence using CryptAcquireContextA with PROV_RSA_AES, CryptCreateHash, CryptHashData, CryptDeriveKey, CryptDecrypt, then CryptReleaseContext/CryptDestroyHash/CryptDestroyKey. The material explicitly marks these as deprecated and recommends CNG APIs instead. This sequence derives the AES key from a hashed password rather than supplying a raw key, which is weaker than direct CNG key specification.

nodes.label: Visual Studio PIC Shellcode Build Configuration
nodes.description: Source A specifies linker and compiler settings required to produce position-independent shellcode from C: linker sets /NOENTRY (DLL) or custom Entry Point, /OPT:NOREF, /NODEFAULTLIB, no debug info, /MAP enabled, /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE; C/C++ sets /GS- (no stack cookies), /MT runtime, no C++ exceptions, /SDL-, no debug info format. These settings remove the security mitigations and CRT dependencies that would otherwise produce non-relocatable or externally linked code.

nodes.label: Compiler Intrinsics for CRT-Free Shellcode
nodes.description: Source A documents using #pragma intrinsic to direct MSVC to emit inline code for CRT functions like memset, strcmp, memcmp, memcpy, strcpy, and __movsb instead of generating external calls. The intrin.h header is required. This is necessary because shellcode built with /NODEFAULTLIB cannot link against the CRT, so any memory or string operation must be inlined. The example shows __movsb being used to copy decrypted shellcode bytes into a destination buffer.

nodes.label: Jittered C2 Check-in Loop
nodes.description: Source A describes the implant main loop as while(alive) { try { response = CheckIn(); CheckTasks(response); } catch() {}; sleep(jitter); }. The jittered sleep interval avoids fixed-period beaconing patterns that network behavioral detection can fingerprint. The try/catch wrapper ensures transient network failures do not terminate the implant. CheckTasks parses the JSON response for tasked actions identified by UUID/GUID task IDs.

nodes.label: Module-Definition (.def) Files for DLL Exports
nodes.description: Source A documents.def files as the linker-directive mechanism for controlling DLL exports. The EXPORTS statement marks functions for export with optional ordinals; LIBRARY names the DLL and triggers import library generation; VERSION sets the image version; NONAME exports by ordinal only (hiding the name); PRIVATE prevents an entry in the import library. The /DLL linker option must be set in project configuration. This mechanism is relevant to proxy DLL development where precise export matching is required.

nodes.label: IDAPro Strings Subview and.rdata Storage
nodes.description: Source A demonstrates that IDAPro's strings subview lists every string literal in a binary alongside its address, length, and type. By default, MSVC places string literals in the read-only data (.rdata) section. The strings subview directly reveals program purpose, printf format strings, error messages, and any hardcoded indicators. Reverse engineers use this as a first-pass analysis step, making string obfuscation a baseline requirement for implant tradecraft.

nodes.label: Endianness-Aware Network Serialization
nodes.description: Source A documents the use of _byteswap_ushort (16-bit), _byteswap_ulong (32-bit), and _byteswap_uint64 (64-bit) intrinsics to convert between host and network byte order before serializing structs into byte vectors. The alpaca library provides serialize/deserialize, and C++20 std::bit_cast enables type-punned unpacking. The material recommends intrinsic functions first, then std:: functions, then libraries, then manual implementation.

nodes.label: WinINet/WinHTTP Self-Signed Certificate Handling
nodes.description: Source A documents TLS enablement via INTERNET_FLAG_SECURE in HttpOpenRequest, combined with InternetSetOption flags INTERNET_FLAG_IGNORE_CERT_CN_INVALID and SECURITY_FLAG_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_CA to accept self-signed certificates. This permits C2 servers using self-signed PKI to function without installing a trusted root CA on the target. Both WinINet and WinHTTP offer similar capabilities for this pattern.

nodes.label: Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) BCrypt* API Family
nodes.description: Microsoft's CNG API family provides modern symmetric and asymmetric cryptography through functions including BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider, BCryptGetProperty, BCryptSetProperty, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey, and BCryptDecrypt. The training material presents CNG as the recommended replacement for the deprecated CryptoAPI (Crypt*) family for AES shellcode encryption, describing it as more advanced and extensible.

nodes.label: Legacy CryptoAPI (Crypt*) Family
nodes.description: The deprecated CryptoAPI family includes CryptAcquireContextA, CryptCreateHash, CryptHashData, CryptDeriveKey, CryptDecrypt, CryptReleaseContext, CryptDestroyHash, and CryptDestroyKey. The training material notes these are deprecated but remain functional due to Windows backwards compatibility, and presents a typical AES decrypt flow chaining these functions.

nodes.label: XOR Symmetric Shellcode Cipher
nodes.description: XOR with a single-byte key applied byte-by-byte across a shellcode buffer uses the same routine for encryption and decryption. The training material discusses the semantic debate over whether XOR constitutes encoding or encryption, noting that the presence of a key supports classifying it as encryption rather than encoding.

nodes.label: Base64 Shellcode Encoding via CryptStringToBinaryA
nodes.description: The Windows API pair CryptBinaryToStringA and CryptStringToBinaryA encode and decode shellcode to and from Base64. The training material also references certutil.exe -encode as a native OS utility for the same transformation, framing it as a transport obfuscation layer rather than cryptographic protection.

nodes.label: PEB Access via FS/GS Segment Register Offsets
nodes.description: On 32-bit Windows the Process Environment Block address is read from the Thread Environment Block via __readfsdword(0x30); on 64-bit Windows it is read via __readgsqword(0x60). The TEB itself is located through the FS segment register (32-bit) or GS segment register (64-bit). These offsets are the entry point for PEB walking and manual module resolution without calling LoadLibrary.

nodes.label: Windows-Specific Data Type System
nodes.description: Windows defines its own type aliases (DWORD, BOOL, BOOLEAN, WORD, QWORD, PVOID, LPVOID, HANDLE, HINSTANCE) layered over CRT types to insulate source code from architecture changes. BOOL is a 32-bit int while BOOLEAN is a single unsigned char (BYTE), a distinction that affects memory layout. The training material traces the type chain through WinDef.h and WinNt.h headers back to CRT root types such as int and unsigned char.

nodes.label: Explicit Linking (Runtime DLL Resolution)
nodes.description: Explicit linking is the practice of loading DLLs at runtime via Windows APIs rather than at compile time through import libraries. The training material contrasts this with compile-time linking and preprocessor-based linking. This is the operational model for dynamic API resolution techniques that avoid static import table entries.

nodes.label: DLL Function Export Methods
nodes.description: Functions can be exported from a DLL via __declspec(dllexport), a.def definition file, or EXTERN_C declarations. The training material presents __declspec() as the preferred method. DLLs that export functions are noted as beneficial for process injection because they can be loaded into a target process and their exports invoked.

nodes.label: Win32 API __stdcall Calling Convention
nodes.description: The __stdcall calling convention is the default for Win32 API functions. Arguments are pushed right-to-left and the callee cleans the stack before returning, which requires a fixed argument count. The WINAPI, APIENTRY, and CALLBACK macros all expand to __stdcall. Win32 imports declared with WINADVAPI use __declspec(import) and __stdcall together, which is how ntdll-exported syscall stubs are invoked from higher-level API layers and how IDA Pro represents Win32 function prologues.

nodes.label: Windows HANDLE as PVOID Equivalence
nodes.description: HANDLE, HKEY, HMODULE, and HINSTANCE all typedef to PVOID (void*) in winnt.h. HMODULE and HINSTANCE are functionally equivalent — both represent the base address of a loaded module. User applications cannot directly access system objects; they retrieve handles from an internal handle table and use those handles to modify objects. This equivalence is what allows the PEB walker to treat LDR module list entries as base addresses for in-memory PE parsing rather than opaque references.

nodes.label: __cdecl Calling Convention for Variadic Functions
nodes.description: __cdecl is the default for CRT functions and variadic functions such as printf. The caller cleans the stack after return, which permits a variable number of arguments. __cdecl remains in use on Windows even though __stdcall is the Win32 API default. The caller-cleans semantics make __cdecl slower per-call than __stdcall but enable VARARG support that __stdcall cannot accommodate.

nodes.label: Advanced Implant Capability Escalation Triggers
nodes.description: Source A frames advanced implant capabilities — manual image loading, API hook reimplementation, C2 callbacks, and shellcode execution — as last-resort options deployed when four triggers fire: the operator has met their match, the defender is tech-savvy, stealth is required, or basic techniques have failed. These capabilities carry significant development cost and should not be the first choice; they exist to overcome defensive postures that simpler techniques cannot. The framing positions basic API usage as the baseline and the advanced capabilities as parallel escalation paths rather than a sequential pipeline.

nodes.label: Create* API Family and Kernel Object Creation
nodes.description: The Create* family of Win32 APIs (96+ documented) does not create objects in user space — the kernel object manager creates the actual executive object (EPROCESS, ETHREAD, section, event, mutex, etc.) in kernel pool, and the API returns a user-space handle that is an index into the calling process's handle table. CreateProcess is anomalous in returning BOOL rather than a handle, with the handles delivered via the PROCESS_INFORMATION output structure. This handle/object split is why NtCreateUserProcess and direct syscall variants exist.

nodes.label: WldpQueryDynamicCodeTrust and Device Guard Code Integrity
nodes.description: WldpQueryDynamicCodeTrust queries the Device Guard / WDAC policy engine to determine whether in-memory dynamic code (a base address + size, or a file handle) is trusted to execute. The API's _When_ annotations encode mutual exclusivity: if a file handle is provided, the base image pointer must be NULL and vice versa. This is the programmatic query surface behind the WDAC/ACG dynamic code restrictions that T-016 must bypass to run shellcode loaders in protected processes.

nodes.label: PROCESS_INFORMATION Structure
nodes.description: PROCESS_INFORMATION returns hProcess, hThread, dwProcessId, and dwThreadId from CreateProcess. Both handles are kernel-object handles granted with the access mask specified in the SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES or the API's defaults. Both must be closed via CloseHandle to avoid handle leaks; the IDs are not stable across reboots and are reusable. The structure is the canonical way to verify a process was actually created — BOOL TRUE from CreateProcess does not guarantee the process image initialized.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration
nodes.description: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS captures a point-in-time snapshot of all processes; Process32First/Process32Next walk PROCESSENTRY32 records yielding szExeFile and th32ProcessID. The snapshot is a kernel-owned copy with its own handle. It is the standard Win32 process-enumeration API but is observable via ETW and avoids the PEB-walker approach used by stealthier loaders.

nodes.label: HRESULT 32-bit Layout
nodes.description: HRESULT is a 32-bit value with fields: Severity bit S (0 = success, 1 = fail), reserved R/C/N bits, Facility code (7 bits identifying the source — FACILITY_NULL, FACILITY_RPC, FACILITY_WIN32, etc.), and Code (16-bit). The SUCCEEDED and FAILED macros check only the severity bit. NT status values are mapped to HRESULTs via the N bit. LSTATUS (LONG) return values from registry APIs are a separate success/failure convention, distinct from HRESULT.

nodes.label: FormatMessage Error-to-String Lookup
nodes.description: FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM | FORMAT_MESSAGE_ALLOCATE_BUFFER converts a dwMessageId (typically from GetLastError) into a localized human-readable string allocated by the system. FORMAT_MESSAGE_IGNORE_INSERTS avoids consuming %1..%N insertion placeholders from the message resource. The function is the canonical Win32 error-lookup routine used for diagnostic logging and is relevant when instrumenting loader-stage failure paths.

nodes.label: Windows Executive Object Types (Process, Thread, Section, Token, Mutex, Key, Desktop)
nodes.description: Object manager types include Process (virtual address space controlling thread execution), Thread (executable portion of a process), Section (shared memory/file-mapping), Token (security profile for threads/processes), Mutex (serialization primitive), Key (registry reference), and Desktop (window-station contained object). The full list is enumerable via WinObj; each type has type-specific access masks and object-body layouts. Handles to these objects are the currency of process-injection and persistence techniques.

nodes.label: Portable Executable (PE) File Format
nodes.description: PE files begin with a DOS stub (legacy MS-DOS marker), followed by the PE\0\0 signature, the COFF header (machine type, section count, timestamp, symbol table pointer, optional header size, characteristics flags such as IMAGE_FILE_EXECUTABLE_IMAGE 0x0002), the Optional Header, and section headers. The Optional Header's Data Directory entries (Export Directory, Debug Directory) reside in the.rdata section, verifiable by comparing their RVAs against section bounds. Both EXEs and DLLs share this format.

nodes.label: Explicit (Runtime) DLL Linking
nodes.description: Explicit linking loads a DLL at runtime via LoadLibraryExW, resolves exported function addresses via GetProcAddress, casts the result to a matching function pointer signature, and unloads with FreeLibrary. The DLL and its functions do not appear in the importing module's IAT — dumpbin /dependents shows only the implicit dependencies (typically KERNEL32.dll for the loader APIs themselves). The material states these APIs are commonly monitored by security products.

nodes.label: Implicit (Load-Time) DLL Linking
nodes.description: Implicit linking requires a header file declaring the function, the actual DLL, and an import library (.lib) linked via Visual Studio's Additional Dependencies or #pragma comment(lib, "name.lib"). The loader resolves the dependency at process startup, populates the IAT, and the process will fail to load if the DLL is absent. dumpbin /dependents on the resulting EXE lists every implicitly linked module.

nodes.label: Import Address Table (IAT)
nodes.description: The IAT is the data structure populated by the loader for implicitly linked DLLs; it holds resolved function pointers that calls via the import library dispatch through. dumpbin /imports enumerates the IAT to reveal every imported symbol. Explicitly linked functions are absent from the IAT because no import thunk exists — the call dispatches through a runtime-resolved function pointer instead.

nodes.label: dumpbin PE Inspection Utility
nodes.description: dumpbin is the Visual Studio PE analysis tool used to inspect a binary's structure. dumpbin /exports lists exported symbols and ordinals from a.lib or.dll. dumpbin /dependents lists modules the binary implicitly depends on. dumpbin /all dumps the full header, section, symbol, and export table. The material uses dumpbin to verify that explicitly linked DLLs do not appear in the dependency list.

nodes.label: Windows HANDLE as PVOID (void*) Abstraction
nodes.description: WinNt.h typedefs HANDLE as PVOID, which is itself void*. All H-prefixed handle types (HKEY, HMODULE, HINSTANCE, HRSRC) build on this base typedef. HMODULE and HINSTANCE are functionally equivalent — both are simply the base address of a module — and can be interchanged. Source A Units 22-24 document this, noting that while PVOID cannot participate in pointer arithmetic, the handle-to-void* equivalence is what permits passing HMODULE values where HINSTANCE is declared.

nodes.label: COM Initialization Pattern (CoInitialize → CoCreateInstance)
nodes.description: Before any COM interface can be instantiated, the calling thread must call CoInitialize (or CoInitializeEx) to initialize the COM library. Only after initialization succeeds can CoCreateInstance instantiate a COM class by CLSID and yield an interface pointer. Source A Units 25 and 31 demonstrate this with the WUA IUpdateSession object — the I prefix on interface names reflects COM convention. Any COM-dependent capability (COM hijack persistence, WMI execution, browser automation) follows this prerequisite sequence.

nodes.label: Registry Two-Call Query Pattern (Open → Query Size → Allocate → Query Data)
nodes.description: Reading a registry value safely requires opening the key with RegOpenKeyExW, then calling RegQueryValueExW twice — first with a NULL buffer to receive the required size in the lpcbData parameter, then allocating a buffer of that size and calling again to receive the data. Source A Unit 26 demonstrates this pattern with std::make_unique<BYTE[]> for the buffer. Skipping the first call produces a buffer-overrun risk or an empty result.

nodes.label: PE Format: MZ Header to IMAGE_NT_HEADERS
nodes.description: A Windows PE file begins with the MS-DOS 2.0 EXE header marked with 'MZ' (Mark Zbikowski's initials). The DOS header contains an offset to the PE header proper, which begins with the 'PE\0\0' signature. IMAGE_NT_HEADERS32 and IMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 differ only in the OptionalHeader field (IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 vs IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64). The _WIN64 preprocessor symbol selects the active typedef. Source A Units 33 and 38 document this layout, which is the parsing foundation for any reflective loader, module stomper, or PE-header-stomp evasion routine.

nodes.label: Anonymous Pipes for Inter-Process Communication
nodes.description: CreatePipe returns two handles — one read-only, one write-only — that form a unidirectional channel between processes. Child processes inherit pipe handles via the bInheritHandle flag in SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES, or handles are shared via DuplicateHandle. Source A Unit 35 documents the BOOL CreatePipe signature. Anonymous pipes are the basis for redirecting stdin/stdout/stderr of spawned child processes (used by command-shell C2 channels and custom-implant command dispatch).

nodes.label: Windows Service Process Architecture (SCM, Handler, Service Thread)
nodes.description: A Windows service requires a main thread that calls StartServiceCtrlDispatcher, a service thread that performs the service work, and a service control handler registered via RegisterServiceCtrlHandler. The SCM (Service Control Manager) communicates with the service through the handler, which must process control requests (STOP, PAUSE, INTERROGATE). Source A Unit 34 diagrams this three-component architecture, which underlies service-based persistence and service-hijack techniques.

nodes.label: DLL Function Export Mechanics (__declspec,.def, EXTERN_C)
nodes.description: Functions can be exported from a DLL via __declspec(dllexport), a.def definition file, or EXTERN_C linkage. Source A Units 5-7 identify __declspec() as the preferred export method. Explicit (runtime) linking loads the DLL via LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress rather than at compile time via import library. This distinction is the basis for proxy DLL attacks (where exports must match the original DLL's export table) and for exported-function callback execution in T-013's callback injection methods.

nodes.label: Windows Data Type Portability (DWORD, BOOL, PVOID)
nodes.description: Windows-specific data types (DWORD, BOOL, PVOID, HANDLE, HINSTANCE) were introduced to abstract away compiler-dependent sizing of standard C types across 16-bit, 32-bit, and 64-bit Windows migrations. Using DWORD instead of int allowed code to survive the 16→32-bit transition without per-line edits. Source A Unit 11 documents this history and the recommended practice of using Windows types and macros wherever possible so code adjusts automatically if the underlying typedefs change. This is why implant source uses DWORD/QWORD rather than int/long.

nodes.label: IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY and Export Table Resolution
nodes.description: The IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY structure (40 bytes) contains NumberOfFunctions, NumberOfNames, AddressOfFunctions, AddressOfNames, and AddressOfNameOrdinals arrays. Resolving a function by name requires walking the AddressOfNames array to find a matching string, using the array index as a position into AddressOfNameOrdinals to get the ordinal, then indexing AddressOfFunctions with that ordinal to get the RVA. Functions exported by ordinal only do not appear in the AddressOfNames array. This is the mechanism behind manual GetProcAddress implementations used in PEB walking and shellcode API resolution.

nodes.label: IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR and ILT/IAT Mechanics
nodes.description: The IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR array (DataDirectory index 1) contains OriginalFirstThunk (Import Lookup Table / ILT), TimeDateStamp (0 = unbound, -1 = bound), ForwarderChain, Name (RVA to DLL name string), and FirstThunk (Import Address Table / IAT). During loader initialization, the ILT provides function name/ordinal references that the loader resolves to actual addresses, writing them into the IAT. After loading, the IAT contains the resolved function pointers. Bound imports (TimeDateStamp = -1) skip resolution. This structure is central to IAT camouflage and import table manipulation techniques.

nodes.label: CONTEXT Structure and Thread Context Hijacking
nodes.description: The CONTEXT structure stores the complete register state of a thread, including DWORD64 Rip (instruction pointer) on x64. GetThreadContext retrieves this structure for a thread handle with THREAD_GET_CONTEXT access. An attacker can modify the Rip field to redirect execution to injected shellcode, then call SetThreadContext to apply the change. This is typically performed on a suspended thread. Debuggers use the same mechanism to implement breakpoints. Thread context manipulation is the foundation of thread hijacking injection methods including WaitingThread hijack.

nodes.label: PE Injection (Additional Image, Non-Hollowing)
nodes.description: PE Injection loads an additional PE image into a target process's address space without removing or hollowing the original image. The target process holds two PE images simultaneously. The technique uses CreateToolhelp32Snapshot for process enumeration, OpenProcess for handle acquisition, VirtualAllocEx for memory allocation in the target, WriteProcessMemory for PE image transfer, and CreateRemoteThread for execution. Debug privileges (SeDebugPrivilege) must be enabled via OpenProcessToken, LookupPrivilegeValue, and AdjustTokenPrivileges before opening system processes. This method is distinct from process hollowing, which replaces the original image.

nodes.label: Reflective DLL Injection Walkthrough
nodes.description: Reflective DLL Injection manually replicates the system loader: allocate a heap buffer of OptionalHeader.SizeOfImage, copy all PE headers and sections from raw bytes, apply base relocation fixups using the relocation table, resolve and fix up the IAT (import address table), process the EAT (export address table) if the DLL exports functions, then call DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH. The result is a loaded DLL in the target process memory without using LoadLibrary, evading loader-based detection such as module list enumeration and image load events.

nodes.label: Position-Independent Code Requirements in C
nodes.description: Position-independent shellcode written in C must satisfy three constraints: no external references or dependencies (no calls to external libraries), no references to data sections (no initialized string literals stored in.rdata), and all memory operations performed via manually resolved API pointers. Compiler intrinsics replace CRT function calls. Stack alignment to 16 bytes or 32 bytes is required before Win32 API calls on x64 to avoid crashes from SSE/AVX instructions used by API implementations. The result is self-contained shellcode that can execute at any memory address.

nodes.label: Compiler Intrinsics for CRT-Free Shellcode
nodes.description: Compiler intrinsics declared via #pragma intrinsic(memset), #pragma intrinsic(__movsb), or comma-separated lists replace CRT function calls with direct CPU instructions emitted by the compiler. The intrin.h header provides access to intrinsic functions. This allows shellcode to perform memory operations (memset, memcpy, strcmp, memcmp, strcpy, __movsb) without linking the C runtime library, which is mandatory for position-independent code that cannot reference external DLLs. Intrinsics are the bridge between C-level productivity and assembly-level self-containment.

nodes.label: Visual Studio Build Settings for Shellcode Generation
nodes.description: Position-independent shellcode from C requires specific Visual Studio linker and compiler settings. Linker: /NOENTRY (no default entry point, for DLLs), custom Entry Point, /OPT:NOREF (prevent unused function removal), /NODEFAULTLIB (no CRT), no debug info, /MAP (generate map file), /SUBSYSTEM:NATIVE. C/C++: /GS- (no stack cookies), /MT (static CRT if used at all), no C++ exceptions, /SDL- (no SDL checks), no debug info format, no hotpatching. These settings produce a self-contained binary with no external dependencies and no security cookie instrumentation that would introduce CRT references.

nodes.label: CNG API AES Encryption for Shellcode
nodes.description: The Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) API provides AES encryption via BCrypt* functions (BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider, BCryptSetProperty, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey, BCryptEncrypt, BCryptDecrypt). The algorithm and its properties (chain mode, padding) must be explicitly specified. CNG is the modern Windows-native crypto API replacing CryptoAPI. For shellcode encryption, the decrypt function can be compiled as position-independent code and the CNG provider resolved dynamically. The approach is extensible to other algorithms (AES-GCM, ChaCha20) by changing the algorithm provider string.

nodes.label: String Storage in Read-Only Data Section
nodes.description: By default, the C compiler stores string literals in the.rdata (read-only data) section of the PE. These strings are visible in the IDAPro Strings subview, which lists address, length, type, and content. A reverse engineer can read printf format strings, API names, error messages, and configuration values directly from this view without disassembling code. String obfuscation or encryption is required to prevent this — strings must be constructed at runtime via stack buffers or decrypted from encrypted blobs, never stored as plaintext literals in.rdata.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Manipulation via GetNamedSecurityInfoA/SetNamedSecurityInfoA
nodes.description: GetNamedSecurityInfoA retrieves the security descriptor (owner SID, group SID, DACL, SACL) of a named object — including NTFS files, services, registry keys, shares, and file-mapping objects. SetNamedSecurityInfoA applies a modified security descriptor. The EXPLICIT_ACCESS_A structure defines access control entries for a trustee (user, group, or program). An attacker can modify the DACL of a persistent service to deny SERVICE_STOP to all principals except the attacker, preventing defenders from stopping the service. This enhances persistence resilience by restricting remediation actions.

nodes.label: SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS for Service Resilience
nodes.description: The SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS structure configures actions taken when a service fails: SC_ACTION_RESTART (restart the service), SC_ACTION_REBOOT (reboot the system), or SC_ACTION_RUN_COMMAND (run a command). The ChangeServiceConfig2 API applies these actions with a failure count reset period. An attacker configuring a persistent service with SC_ACTION_RESTART and a short reset period ensures the service automatically restarts after defender termination, crash, or reboot. This is the service-level equivalent of the PhantomPersist resilience monitor in T-017.

nodes.label: Network Serialization and Endianness Handling
nodes.description: Data transmitted over network connections must be serialized with consistent byte ordering. Windows is little-endian; network protocols often use big-endian (network byte order). The _byteswap_ushort (16-bit), _byteswap_ulong (32-bit), and _byteswap_uint64 (64-bit) intrinsics reverse byte order. The alpaca C++ library provides serialize/deserialize to byte vectors. C++20 std::bit_cast reinterprets raw bytes as typed data. For implant C2, data must be packed in the correct order before transmission and unpacked on receipt, with endianness conversion applied to multi-byte integer fields.

nodes.label: PE OptionalHeader.SizeOfImage for Memory Allocation
nodes.description: The SizeOfImage field in the IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER specifies the total virtual size of the PE image when loaded into memory (all headers and sections rounded up to SectionAlignment). This value is used by the system loader to reserve a contiguous virtual memory region. In manual PE loading (RDI, PE injection), SizeOfImage determines the allocation size. The on-disk file size (SizeOfHeaders + sum of SizeOfRawData) may differ from SizeOfImage because sections can have larger VirtualSize than SizeOfRawData, with the difference zero-filled at runtime.

nodes.label: Syscall Index Version Dependence
nodes.description: Each Windows syscall is indexed by a number into a kernel dispatch table, but these indices change across Windows versions and builds. Hardcoding a syscall number is unreliable because the kernel function bound to that index on one build may differ on another. This version-dependence is the fundamental motivation for runtime SSN resolution techniques.

nodes.label: sRDI Bootstrap Stage
nodes.description: Shellcode Reflective DLL Injection (sRDI) is described by Source A as RDI 'with a few twists', composed of a Bootstrap stage, the RDI loader itself, an Existing DLL, and User-Data. The Bootstrap is a small position-independent stub whose role is to locate the larger RDI payload and the DLL to load, then transfer control. This two-stage construction lets the operator deliver RDI as pure shellcode without a host PE.

nodes.label: Manual x64 PE Parsing and Loading
nodes.description: Source A specifies the implementation requirements for a custom x64 PE loader: validate MZ signature at offset 0x00, validate FileHeader.Machine equals x64, traverse PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER → PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS64 → PIMAGE_FILE_HEADER → PIMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER → PIMAGE_SECTION_HEADER, process PIMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY entries to build IAT and EAT, apply base relocations, and jump to OptionalHeader.AddressOfEntryPoint. Both DLL and EXE entry points are supported.

nodes.label: WSAStartup WinSock Prerequisite
nodes.description: Source A highlights that Windows sockets differ from Linux sockets primarily because Win32 APIs require an explicit WSAStartup initialization call before any socket operation.
