The reverse-TCP socket structures resemble their Linux counterparts, but the WinSock initialization handshake is mandatory and is a distinguishing artifact of Windows-side C2 transport setup.

nodes.label: WinINet HTTP Session API Sequence
nodes.description: Source A documents the WinINet HTTP session sequence: InternetConnect opens a session handle (HINTERNET) for an HTTP or FTP site, then HttpOpenRequest creates an HTTP request handle from that session. Both APIs return HINTERNET handles that are passed to subsequent WinINet calls. This is the conventional WinINet-based HTTP C2 transport pattern.

nodes.label: Implant Interactive Shell Dispatch Loop
nodes.description: Source A specifies the canonical implant shell pattern: an infinite while(TRUE) loop that displays a prompt (e.g., printf("RAT670 $> ")), calls ReadCommandLine(), calls ProcessArgs(), and calls ExecuteArgs(). The loop persists until the process is terminated or a graceful-exit command is issued. Basic commands include directory listing, cd, file upload/download, and arbitrary command execution.

nodes.label: Shellcode Development in C — Pitfalls
nodes.description: Source A review material identifies three elements to avoid when writing shellcode in C: bugs, external references, and the heap. External references break position independence because they require resolution at load time, and heap allocation introduces runtime state and dependencies that complicate shellcode portability across processes and architectures.

nodes.label: WINAPI / __stdcall Calling Convention
nodes.description: Source A establishes that the WINAPI, APIENTRY, and CALLBACK macros all expand to __stdcall. Win32 API function declarations use these decorations in header files to enforce the stdcall calling convention, where the callee cleans the stack rather than the caller. This convention governs every Windows API an implant invokes.

nodes.label: Microsoft Source-Code Annotation Language (SAL)
nodes.description: SAL is Microsoft's source-code annotation language defined in sal.h, used to describe how function parameters are used (input, output, read, written, element count, byte count). Intermediate annotations include _In_reads_(s), _Out_writes_(s), _Out_writes_bytes_all_(s), _Ret_maybenull_. Advanced annotations include _Inout_updates_(s), _Check_return_, _Must_inspect_result_, _Use_decl_annotations_. Microsoft applies SAL pervasively across the Windows SDK headers.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration
nodes.description: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot captures a snapshot of running processes and threads. The caller walks the snapshot with Process32First/Process32Next, retrieving PROCESSENTRY32 structures containing the process name and PID. The API provides limited information per entry — process name and PID only — but the caller can open a handle to each returned PID with PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION (or more restricted access) to gather additional metadata. This is the standard Win32 approach to process discovery from user mode.

nodes.label: PE Export Address Table (EAT)
nodes.description: The Export Address Table is the IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY structure within a PE's.edata section that maps an exported function name (via the Name Pointer Table and ordinal) to an RVA of the function's first instruction. dumpbin /exports enumerates this table by name and ordinal. The EAT is the structure that export-hijack injection (Threadless) overwrites with a trampoline, and that PEB-walker-style API resolution (DJB2 hash → name → RVA) traverses to resolve function pointers without calling GetProcAddress.

nodes.label: x64 CONTEXT Structure
nodes.description: The CONTEXT structure (defined via IMAGE_AMD64_CONTEXT) on x64 Windows contains the full CPU register state for a thread: Rax through R15, Rip, segments, debug registers, and floating-point/SIMD state. The PCONTEXT handle is passed to GetThreadContext/SetThreadContext and is the mechanism by which thread-hijack injection mutates a suspended thread's Rip to redirect execution to shellcode. The LastExceptionToRip/LastExceptionFromRip fields are Windows-specific additions used by the kernel to track software exception transitions.

nodes.label: User-Mode APC Queuing Primitive
nodes.description: QueueUserAPC (and the underlying NtQueueApcThread) queues a user-mode APC to a target thread; the APC function pointer and argument are pushed to the thread's APC queue and execute when the thread enters an alertable wait state. The Source A APCInjection lab (Lab 3.3) is the introductory form: open a thread in a target process, queue an APC that points to allocated shellcode. This primitive is the foundation for Early Bird (T-013) and Early Cascade (T-012) refinements that target specific thread-init windows to avoid alertable-wait dependency.

nodes.label: Print Spooler Port Monitor DLL Persistence
nodes.description: A Port Monitor is a DLL loaded by the print spooler service (spoolsv.exe) into the SYSTEM context. Installation requires registry keys under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors and the DLL placed in a path the spooler loads. Because the spooler restarts on the next print operation or service restart, a malicious Port Monitor DLL achieves SYSTEM-level persistence. The Source A course reviews Port Monitor source code as a persistence tradecraft module.

nodes.label: WSASocket Redirected Socket Handles
nodes.description: WSASocket (versus the simpler socket API) accepts socket handles that can be redirected — i.e., the underlying SOCKET_DESCRIPTOR can be passed across process boundaries via duplicate handle or inherited as a_stdin/stdout/stderr-style socket for cmd.exe redirection. The Source A review question establishes that WSASocket supports handle redirection while socket() does not, which is the property that makes WSASocket the standard choice for bind-shell and reverse-shell socket redirection in implants.

nodes.label: SetNamedSecurityInfo and DACL/SACL Modification
nodes.description: SetNamedSecurityInfoA (advapi32) applies OWNER, GROUP, DACL, and SACL fields to a named kernel object (file, service, registry key, etc.) via the SECURITY_INFORMATION bitmask. An operator uses this API to grant a low-privileged principal write access to a protected resource — for example, modifying a service binary's DACL so that a payload can overwrite it. The pDacl parameter accepts a discretionary ACL that supersedes the existing one; the SACL controls audit logging behavior.

nodes.label: Windows Calling Conventions (__stdcall, __cdecl, __fastcall)
nodes.description: Source A documents that WINAPI, APIENTRY, and CALLBACK are macros defined in WinDef.h that all expand to __stdcall. The __cdecl convention (used by CRT functions like printf) requires the caller to clean the stack, visible in disassembly as an 'add esp, N' after the call. The __fastcall convention passes the first two parameters in ECX/RCX and EDX/RDX. ntdll syscall stubs and Win32 API entry points use __stdcall, which is relevant to indirect syscall dispatch and to stack-spoofing techniques that must reconstruct valid __stdcall frames.

nodes.label: PE32 / PE32+ DLL File Format
nodes.description: Dynamic-linked Libraries on Windows use the PE32 format for 32-bit binaries and PE32+ format for 64-bit binaries. The dumpbin /headers command reveals the PE signature, file type (DLL vs EXE), and FILE HEADER VALUES including the time date stamp. DLLs are designed to be shared across processes and use extensions such as.lib (import library) and.dll (the loaded module). Understanding this format is a prerequisite for module overloading, module stomping, function stomping, and reflective PE loading.

nodes.label: Windows Data Type to CRT Type Mapping
nodes.description: Win32 types are typedefs layered on top of other Win32 types that ultimately resolve to C-runtime types. Multiple Win32 types can map to the same CRT type: UCHAR, BYTE, and BOOLEAN all resolve to unsigned char (one byte). INT and BOOL map to int (32-bit signed). UINT maps to unsigned int (32-bit unsigned). PVOID, LPVOID, and LPCVOID are all void pointers; on modern systems there is no difference between LPVOID and PVOID because the long-pointer vs near-pointer distinction from 16-bit Windows no longer applies.

nodes.label: Explicit DLL Linking via Windows APIs
nodes.description: Source A defines explicit linking as linking to DLLs at runtime via Windows APIs (LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress), in contrast to compile-time linking via import libraries. Explicit linking is the mechanism by which an implant resolves API functions dynamically to avoid static IAT entries that signature scanners and EDR static analysis rely on. This is the conceptual basis for PEB walking (T-004), proxy DLL loading (T-016), and dynamic resolver templates in the framework runtime.

nodes.label: Windows API Wrappers over CRT Functions
nodes.description: Windows provides API wrappers for standard C runtime functions, e.g., RtlCopyMemory behaves identically to memcpy. Source A recommends using Windows-specific APIs and macros rather than CRT equivalents for nearly every type of functionality in an implant, because if Windows changes underlying behavior the macros adjust automatically and because CRT linkage can introduce unwanted static dependencies. This principle underlies why the dark_crystal wrappers.rs module binds NT APIs via windows_targets::link! rather than relying on the C runtime.

nodes.label: Thread Context, States, and CONTEXT Structure
nodes.description: Each thread maintains a CONTEXT structure capturing register state (RIP, RSP, segment registers) sampled when the thread enters its quantum. Source A's thread module enumerates thread states and notes that 'what state we need a thread to be in for a certain injection method' varies — hijacking requires suspending the thread, capturing its context via GetThreadContext, modifying RIP to redirect execution, then restoring via SetThreadContext. Without understanding thread states, injection methods that depend on alertable waits or suspended states silently fail.

nodes.label: Port Monitor DLL Persistence via Print Spooler
nodes.description: A Port Monitor is a DLL registered with the print spooler service (spoolsv.exe) that the spooler loads at service start. Source A dedicates a source code review module (Unit 25) to walking through Port Monitor implementation. Because spoolsv runs as SYSTEM and restarts on failure, a Port Monitor DLL yields elevated, reboot-persistent code execution. The technique historically shares lineage with Stuxnet's persistence model and is constrained by the print spooler service running as a distinct process.

nodes.label: Binary Patching as an Evasion Primitive
nodes.description: Binary patching is the modification of bytes in a compiled module on disk or in memory to alter runtime behavior. Source A introduces it as a distinct module (Unit 24) with objectives to 'Define binary patching' and 'Discuss benefits of binary patching,' situating it as a foundational evasion technique whose targets include the.text section of ntdll (unhooking) and amsi.dll (AMSI bypass via patched AmsiScanBuffer prologue).

nodes.label: Position-Independent Code from C/C++ with Compiler Flag Control
nodes.description: Source A's shellcode-creation module (Units 28–30) teaches generating position-independent shellcode by writing specific functions in C/C++ and using compiler/linker flags to suppress unwanted emissions (CRT initializers, relocations, imports). The module warns that 'the compiler will almost always do something we do not want so we need to override certain items' — making compiler flag mastery a prerequisite for producing shellcode that survives injection into foreign processes.

nodes.label: Win32 Data Type typedef Cascade to CRT
nodes.description: Win32 type names (BOOL, INT, DWORD, PVOID, HINSTANCE, HANDLE) are typedefs that ultimately resolve to CRT primitives (int, unsigned long, void*). Source A Units 6 and 8 document that several Win32 types map to the same CRT type — UCHAR, BYTE, and BOOLEAN all collapse to unsigned char. Understanding the typedef cascade is necessary when reading windows-sys bindings in Rust or hand-declaring FFI signatures, because mismatched Win32 aliases cause silent truncation or alignment errors in syscall stubs.

nodes.label: Heaven's Gate WoW64 32-to-64-bit Syscall Transition
nodes.description: Heaven's Gate is the mechanism by which 32-bit (x86) processes on 64-bit Windows reach native 64-bit syscalls. A 32-bit process issues 'call ntdll.Wow64Transition', which jumps through 'jmp 033:wow64cpu+offset' to switch the code segment to 64-bit (the 0x33 selector), then executes 'mov r10, rcx; mov eax, INT; syscall' in ntdll.dll's 64-bit stub. The transition involves ntdll.dll, wow64cpu.dll, and the segment-selector jump. EDRs that hook only the 32-bit ntdll do not see the syscall because the actual syscall instruction executes in the 64-bit stub.

nodes.label: InitializeProcThreadAttributeList Process Creation API
nodes.description: InitializeProcThreadAttributeList creates a PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST used to pass extended attributes to CreateProcess and CreateProcessAsUser. The API requires a two-pass pattern: call once with NULL to retrieve size, allocate, then call again with the buffer. UpdateProcThreadAttribute inserts entries such as PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PID (PPID spoofing), PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_MITIGATION_POLICY (Block-DLL, ACG, CIG), and PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST (restricted handle inheritance). DeleteProcThreadAttributeList must free the list. This single API is the foundation for most attribute-driven process-creation tradecraft.

nodes.label: Windows Service Hiding via SDDL DACL Modification
nodes.description: A Windows service's visibility in 'sc query' and SCM enumeration is governed by its Security Descriptor (SDDL). The DACL can be modified programmatically via SetSecurityDescriptorControl and SetNamedSecurityInfo (headers securitybaseapi.h, aclapi.h) to deny SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS and SERVICE_QUERY_CONFIG to principals other than the service account. A service with a restrictive DACL does not appear in standard enumeration by unprivileged or even admin contexts unless the caller has the matching access rights. The technique avoids leaving manual SDDL strings on disk because the modification is applied via the Win32 security APIs.

nodes.label: Native Subsystem Application Entry Signature
nodes.description: Native Windows applications (IMAGE_SUBSYSTEM_NATIVE) receive entry parameters via 'NTSTATUS NtProcessStartup(PPEB peb)' rather than the CRT 'int main(int argc, char* argv[])'. The PEB pointer is passed directly by the kernel's native process loader, exposing the loaded module list, process parameters, heap, and TEB-related structures without requiring module-walk APIs. This entry signature is distinct from standard subsystem (Win32) applications and is used by minimalist implants that want to avoid the CRT and standard loader behavior.

nodes.label: Crypto Next Gen (BCrypt) AES APIs
nodes.description: The Crypto Next Gen (CNG) APIs exposed via bcrypt.h (BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey, BCryptEncrypt, BCryptDecrypt) are the supported AES primitive on modern Windows. The older Wincrypt (CryptAcquireContext, CryptEncrypt with CALG_AES_*) AES variants are deprecated. CNG supports AES-GCM, AES-CBC, and other modes via BCryptSetProperty on the algorithm handle. Implants that encrypt shellcode, beaconing payloads, or staged DLLs should use CNG to avoid loading deprecated API surfaces that defenders can monitor.

nodes.label: STARTUPINFO Socket Handle Redirection
nodes.description: Setting STARTUPINFOA.hStdInput, hStdOutput, and hStdError to a SOCKET HANDLE with dwFlags = STARTF_USESTDHANDLES causes CreateProcessA to bind the spawned process's standard I/O to the socket. CreateProcessA must be called with bInheritHandles = TRUE so the handle is inherited. The pattern is the canonical reverse-shell primitive: a network socket is created via WSASocket/WSAStartup/connect, then cmd.exe is spawned with its I/O redirected to that socket, producing an interactive shell over the C2 channel. The pattern is detected by inspecting handle inheritance patterns in process-creation telemetry.

nodes.label: WinINet vs WinHTTP API Family Distinction
nodes.description: WinINet (InternetOpenA/InternetConnectA/HttpOpenRequestA) is the higher-level HTTP API family originally designed for user-facing applications; it inherits Internet Explorer proxy and cache settings, supports interactive authentication, and is generally discouraged for implant use because it pulls state from the user profile. WinHTTP (WinHttpOpen/WinHttpConnect/WinHttpOpenRequest) is the programmatic/server-side variant, supports explicit proxy configuration, has no cache dependency, and is the preferred API for C2 transports. WinHttpOpenRequest creates a request handle without sending data — the verb (GET/POST), object name, version, referrer, and accept-types are configured before the request is dispatched.

nodes.label: WSAStartup/WSASocket Winsock Initialization Pattern
nodes.description: Winsock initialization requires calling WSAStartup with MAKEWORD(2,2) for Winsock 2.2 before any socket API is used; WSAGetLastError retrieves error codes. WSASocketA(af=AF_INET, type=SOCK_STREAM, protocol=IPPROTO_TCP) creates a SOCKET handle. WSASocket differs from the CRT 'socket()' function in that WSASocket allows explicit specification of a WSAPROTOCOL_INFO structure and supports overlapped I/O flags — the Source A material explicitly notes that WSASocket allows for redirected handles. WSAStartup/WSACleanup must be balanced per process.

nodes.label: CNG AES Decryption Sequence for Shellcode
nodes.description: Microsoft's Cryptography Next Generation (CNG) API family provides AES decryption via a fixed call sequence: BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider opens an AES algorithm provider, BCryptGetProperty/BCryptSetProperty configure chaining mode and key length, BCryptGenerateSymmetricKey derives the symmetric key handle, and BCryptDecrypt performs the actual decryption. The legacy CryptoAPI equivalents are deprecated but still callable for backwards compatibility. CNG is the modern Microsoft-blessed path and appears as legitimate system API usage to behavioral monitors, which is why it is preferred over hand-rolled AES in implants.

nodes.label: CreateProcess to Executive Object Flow
nodes.description: When a user-mode application calls CreateProcess, the API internally invokes NtCreateFile-equivalent object services that cause the kernel to allocate a system-space executive object, link it into the kernel's process linked list, and return a handle to the caller. The kernel, not the user-mode caller, performs the system-level work of object construction and thread injection. This is the path bypassed by T-014 NtCreateUserProcess, which calls the underlying NT system service directly.

nodes.label: _EPROCESS and _KPROCESS Kernel Process Objects
nodes.description: The kernel represents every running process with an _EPROCESS executive structure wrapping a _KPROCESS dispatcher structure. The kernel maintains all process objects in a doubly-linked list (the ActiveProcessLinks list) that tools like Process Explorer and EDRs walk to enumerate processes. Operations that unlink a process from this list produce a hidden process; operations that hijack fields in these structures are the basis of DKOM-style process hiding and process-hollowing relocation.

nodes.label: QueueUserApc and THREAD_SET_CONTEXT Access
nodes.description: QueueUserApc (processthreadsapi.h) takes PAPCFUNC pfnAPC, HANDLE hThread, ULONG_PTR dwData and queues an APC object to the target thread's APC queue. The caller must hold THREAD_SET_CONTEXT access on hThread. The queued APC executes only when the thread enters an alertable wait state. This primitive is the substrate for Early Bird injection (T-013) and Early Cascade (T-012), where the target thread is freshly created and not yet executing user-mode code, so the APC drains at the next alertable wait during thread initialization.

nodes.label: AddMonitor Port Monitor Persistence
nodes.description: AddMonitor (winspool API) installs a local port monitor backed by an attacker-supplied DLL described in MONITOR_INFO_2's pDLLName field. The pEnvironment member must match the target architecture (e.g. 'Windows x64' on a 64-bit system) or the call fails. Because print spooler loads the monitor DLL into spoolsv.exe on service start and on every print spooler restart, this yields reboot-survivable code execution in a SYSTEM-context process. It is a persistence primitive distinct from schtask, COM hijack, and NTFS EA layers.

nodes.label: IMAGE_FILE_HEADER for PE Parsing and Loaders
nodes.description: The IMAGE_FILE_HEADER (defined in winnt.h) carries WORD Machine, WORD NumberOfSections, DWORD TimeDateStamp, DWORD PointerToSymbolTable, DWORD NumberOfSymbols, WORD SizeOfOptionalHeader, and WORD Characteristics. NumberOfSections drives the loop that iterates each IMAGE_SECTION_HEADER, and SizeOfOptionalHeader tells the parser where the section table begins. These two fields are the minimal metadata a custom loader needs to walk the section table and copy sections into allocated memory.

nodes.label: Manual LoadLibrary Mimicry for Reflective DLL Injection
nodes.description: Reflective DLL injection is implemented by reproducing what the system loader does inside LoadLibrary: open the DLL on disk with CreateFileA, read raw bytes with ReadFile, allocate memory with VirtualAlloc, parse PE headers, map each section to its VirtualAddress, apply base relocations against the new base address, resolve imports via the IAT, and finally call DllMain with DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH. Because no LoadLibrary call is made, the loaded image does not appear in the PEB Loader list — which is both the evasion benefit and the reason scanners use unbacked-RWX heuristics against it.

nodes.label: Executive Object Creation and Handle Return
nodes.description: When CreateFile invokes NtCreateFile, the kernel constructs an executive file object in system space and inserts a handle pointing to it in the calling process's handle table; that handle is what user mode receives. The same construct-object-then-return-handle pattern applies to process, thread, section, and token objects. Understanding this two-step is prerequisite to grasp why handle-blocking defenses (T-016) are effective: an attacker cannot obtain a handle without triggering ObRegisterCallbacks and the object's security descriptor check.

nodes.label: Winsock Reverse TCP Socket Pattern
nodes.description: Windows sockets resemble Linux sockets in structure (sockaddr_in, socket descriptor semantics) but require the Win32-specific Winsock.dll initialization sequence: WSAStartup with a WSADATA structure before any socket API call, then socket/connect/send/recv. Source A teaches reverse TCP shellcode that calls WSAStartup then connects back to an attacker listener. This is the userland API surface that the T-022 TCP transport wraps, and it is the historical pattern EDRs hunt for in beacon callbacks.

nodes.label: SAL Annotations and API Parameter Contracts
nodes.description: The Microsoft Source Annotation Language (SAL), defined in sal.h and used pervasively in Windows SDK headers, annotates how function parameters are used: _In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _In_opt_, _deref_out_, etc. The full set of annotations lives in C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Include. Source A recommends using PowerShell's Select-String cmdlet to grep the SDK headers for annotation usage examples. SAL informs how an implant author reads MSDN signatures when hand-binding NT APIs (relevant to T-004 PEB Walker and T-002 SSN resolution signatures), because the annotation tells you whether a pointer is consumed, produced, or optional.

nodes.label: x86 Windows Calling Conventions (__stdcall, __cdecl, __fastcall, __thiscall)
nodes.description: Source A documents four x86 calling conventions. __stdcall is the default for Win32 APIs: callee cleans the stack, arguments pushed right-to-left, fixed argument count. __cdecl is the CRT default (printf), caller cleans the stack, supports variadic arguments. __fastcall passes the first two arguments in ECX/RCX and EDX/RDX. __thiscall is used by C++ class member functions and passes 'this' in ECX. All conventions use the stack for arguments beyond the register-passed ones. x64 collapses these into a single Microsoft x64 ABI (RCX/RDX/R8/R9 + shadow space) but the named macros persist in headers for source compatibility.

nodes.label: WinDef.h Calling-Convention Macros (WINPI, APIENTRY, CALLBACK)
nodes.description: WINAPI, APIENTRY, and CALLBACK are macros defined in WinDef.h that all expand to __stdcall on x86. WINAPI marks Win32 API entry points. APIENTRY appears on functions in winreg.h and similar headers, often combined with WINADVAPI (DECLSPEC_IMPORT) to indicate an imported __stdcall function. CALLBACK marks function-pointer types for callback registrations (window procs, enumeration callbacks, PROPSHEETPAGE). On x64 all three resolve to the empty string because the Microsoft x64 ABI is the only convention.

nodes.label: Microsoft Source-Code Annotation Language (SAL)
nodes.description: SAL is Microsoft's annotation language for function parameters, defined in sal.h. Basic annotations include _In_ (read-only input validated for non-null), _Out_ (output written to caller-provided buffer), _Inout_ (read-write), _In_opt_ (input pointer that may be NULL), _Out_opt_ (output that may be skipped), and _Ret_z_ (function returns a null-terminated string). Visual Studio performs static analysis against these annotations at compile time. SAL pervades Windows SDK headers and disambiguates pointer directionality, buffer ownership, and nullability that the C type system cannot express — essential for correct manual binding of NT APIs from Rust FFI.

nodes.label: Windows Data Type Aliases (HINSTANCE/HMODULE, LPVOID/PVOID, DWORD/ULONG)
nodes.description: Windows headers define many interchangeable type aliases. HINSTANCE and HMODULE are the same type on modern systems (both wrap a module base address). LPVOID and PVOID are identical on flat-memory systems — the 'L' (long) prefix is a 16-bit Windows relic with no semantic difference today. DWORD aliases ULONG (unsigned long), WORD aliases unsigned short. Source A stresses familiarity with these aliases because the same underlying type appears under different names across the Win32 API surface, and misreading an alias as semantically distinct produces incorrect FFI bindings.

nodes.label: Basic Technique Failure Escalation Trigger
nodes.description: Source A frames advanced implant capabilities — manual image loading into memory, re-implementing API hooks, C2 callbacks, and shellcode execution — as last-resort options invoked only when basic techniques fail, when facing a tech-savvy administrator, or when stealth is required. The escalation is operational, not technical: development cost is high (months of effort) and these capabilities should be reserved rather than deployed eagerly.

nodes.label: SAL (Standard Annotation Language) for Windows APIs
nodes.description: Microsoft annotates Windows API function declarations with SAL annotations (_In_, _Out_, _Inout_, _In_opt_, _In_reads_(s), _Out_writes_bytes_all_(s), _Success_(expr), _When_(expr, anno-list), _Must_inspect_result_, _Check_return_, _Ret_maybenull_) that describe parameter mutability, optionality, buffer sizes, success conditions, and conditional behavior. The annotations are parsed by Visual Studio's static code analyzer but their primary value to an operator is documentary: they specify the contract between caller and callee for every Win32/NT API the vault wraps.

nodes.label: Windows Kernel Object and Handle Model
nodes.description: Create* APIs do not create objects in user space — the kernel creates the actual object (process, thread, file, token, etc.) in kernel space and returns a user-space handle that represents the object. The handle lives in the calling process's handle table; all subsequent operations on the object are made through that handle rather than through direct kernel-memory access. CreateProcess is the exception in the Create* family: it returns BOOL rather than a handle, with the actual process and thread handles returned via the PROCESS_INFORMATION output structure.

nodes.label: CreateProcess Executable Search Order
nodes.description: When lpApplicationName is NULL, CreateProcess searches for the executable in a fixed order: (1) directory of the calling executable, (2) current directory of the process, (3) system directory (GetSystemDirectory), (4) Windows directory (GetWindowsDirectory), (5) %PATH%. The lpCommandLine buffer must be writable (LPWSTR, not LPCWSTR) because CreateProcess may modify it during path resolution. Operators must account for this search order when staging payloads and for the writability requirement when passing const string literals.

nodes.label: InitializeProcThreadAttributeList and STARTUPINFOEX
nodes.description: InitializeProcThreadAttributeList initializes a PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST used with STARTUPINFOEX (the extended startup info struct) to attach attributes to a new process or thread at creation time. The API's SAL annotations show that the lpAttributeList pointer is treated as _Out_ when NULL is passed (used for size probing) and as _Inout_ when non-NULL (used for actual initialization). The attribute list is the mechanism through which PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS is appended for PPID spoofing, and through which handle-restriction policies such as PROCESS_MITIGATION_* are applied.

nodes.label: CREATE_SUSPENDED Process Creation Flag
nodes.description: CREATE_SUSPENDED causes CreateProcess to suspend the new process's primary thread before it begins executing LdrInitializeThunk. This is the foundational primitive for process hollowing, Early Bird APC injection, Early Cascade injection, and module stomping — all of which require the loader to be paused so the operator can write to the process address space, queue an APC, or replace image contents before execution begins. The flag is observable in process-creation telemetry as a suspended initial thread state.

nodes.label: WldpQueryDynamicCodeTrust and Device Guard Dynamic Code Policy
nodes.description: WldpQueryDynamicCodeTrust queries whether a given in-memory code region (specified either by fileHandle or baseImage, with the two parameters being mutually exclusive per the API's _When_ annotations) is trusted by Device Guard / Windows Defender Application Control policy. The function is the user-mode query path into the kernel's code-integrity decision logic; code that is not file-backed and not signed cannot pass this trust check under a strict WDAC policy. This is the policy mechanism that blocks the 'execute newly allocated RWX memory' pattern and motivates the MEM_IMAGE-backed stub approach used in T-006 (Phantom Stubs) and the module-stomping variants in T-013.

nodes.label: Position-Independent Code and XREF Removal
nodes.description: Position-independent shellcode must avoid external references (XREFs) — imports, fixups, and absolute addresses that the loader normally resolves at load time. The Source A material identifies XREF removal as a manual post-compilation discipline: the operator inspects disassembly to confirm that the binary contains no fixup entries the loader would apply, since a fixup indicates non-position-independent code that cannot be relocated arbitrarily in memory. Strings are flagged in the same pass because they are identifiable in static analysis; the recommendation is to obfuscate or encrypt strings before embedding in shellcode.

nodes.label: Windows Kernel Executive Object Taxonomy
nodes.description: The Windows object manager exposes typed kernel objects including Process, Thread, Section, Token, Mutex, Key, Desktop, Event, and File. Each object has a standardized header with type-specific sub-headers; generic services (CloseHandle, DuplicateHandle, WaitForSingleObject, query/set security) operate uniformly across types while create/open/query services are type-specific. The WinObj utility enumerates all live object types and instances.

nodes.label: Executive File Object and Handle Table Model
nodes.description: CreateFile transitions through Kernelbase.dll into the NtCreateFile system call, which constructs an executive file object in kernel space and returns a process-relative handle. The handle table maps small integer handles to kernel object pointers, enabling cross-process handle duplication and the object-centric access control model that injection and handle-blocking techniques operate against.

nodes.label: EPROCESS and KPROCESS Process Objects
nodes.description: CreateProcess triggers kernel-side creation of process objects in system space, represented by EPROCESS (executive process) wrapping KPROCESS (kernel process) structures. The kernel maintains all process objects on a doubly-linked list, which is the same list queried by WTSEnumerateProcessesEx, EnumProcesses, and the kernel's PsActiveProcessHead walker used by rootkits and detection tools.

nodes.label: Cross-Session Process Injection via WTSEnumerateProcessesEx
nodes.description: WTSEnumerateProcessesEx returns per-process WTS_PROCESS_INFO structures including SessionId, PID, and process image name. Unlike EnumProcesses which yields only PIDs, this API lets an implant enumerate processes across terminal-service sessions and select targets outside its own session, enabling cross-session injection paths that bypass session-scoped defensive controls.

nodes.label: COM-Based Windows Update Agent API Pattern
nodes.description: The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API is entirely COM-based. Threads must call CoInitialize before instantiating COM objects; the IUpdateSession interface is obtained via CoCreateInstance against the CLSID and supports search/download/install/uninstall operations. This pattern exemplifies how COM classes are registered, instantiated, and dispatched via the registry-resolved class store — the same mechanism COM hijack persistence abuses by re-registering CLSID to a malicious in-proc server.

nodes.label: Windows API Error Return Value Taxonomy
nodes.description: Win32 API functions signal failure through inconsistent return types: BOOL returns FALSE, LSTATUS returns non-zero (ERROR_SUCCESS is 0), HRESULT encodes severity/facility/code in a 32-bit bitfield checked via SUCCEEDED/FAILED macros, and HANDLE returns NULL or INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE. GetLastError retrieves the per-thread last-error code and must be captured immediately before any intervening call overwrites it. FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM resolves numeric codes to human-readable strings.

nodes.label: FindFirstFile/FindNextFile Recursive Directory Walk
nodes.description: Directory enumeration begins with FindFirstFileA returning a search HANDLE and populating a WIN32_FIND_DATA structure; FindNextFile continues enumeration and FindClose releases the handle. lpFileName supports wildcards (* and ?) for pattern matching. Recursive directory walks combine FindFirstFile with depth-first traversal using. and.. filter exclusion, enabling an implant to enumerate filesystems for files of interest such as credentials, documents, or staged payloads.

nodes.label: HRESULT 32-bit Severity/Facility/Code Layout
nodes.description: HRESULT is a 32-bit value laid out as S|R|C|N|r|Facility|Code, where bit 31 (S) is severity (0=success, 1=failure), R/C/N/r are reserved facility-code bits including an NT-mapped-status indicator, the Facility field identifies the originating subsystem (FACILITY_NULL, FACILITY_RPC, FACILITY_DISPATCH, FACILITY_WIN32, etc.), and the Code field holds the actual error number. SUCCEEDED(hr) tests (hr >= 0); FAILED(hr) tests (hr < 0).

nodes.label: PE Format as Architecture-Agnostic Container
nodes.description: The Portable Executable format, defined in winnt.h, is architecture-agnostic: the same container layout (DOS header → NT headers → section table → sections) describes both PE32 (32-bit, Magic 0x10B) and PE32+ (64-bit, Magic 0x20B) images. The format covers executable images (EXE, DLL) and object files (COFF). The internal structure is complex, with multiple layered structures a parser must traverse in order.

nodes.label: IMAGE_FILE_HEADER Structure
nodes.description: The IMAGE_FILE_HEADER sits inside the NT headers and contains Machine, NumberOfSections, TimeDateStamp, PointerToSymbolTable, NumberOfSymbols, SizeOfOptionalHeader, and Characteristics. NumberOfSections drives the loop that walks the section table, and SizeOfOptionalHeader tells the parser how far to skip to reach the section table. These two fields are essential for any custom PE parser or loader.

nodes.label: IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 (PE32+)
nodes.description: The 64-bit optional header begins with Magic (0x20B for PE32+), followed by linker version, SizeOfCode/InitializedData/UninitializedData, AddressOfEntryPoint, ImageBase, SectionAlignment, FileAlignment, DllCharacteristics (CFG, ASLR, DEP flags), SizeOfStackReserve/Commit, SizeOfHeapReserve/Commit, and a DataDirectory array of IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES entries. The DataDirectory entries for IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT and IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT are the bridge to resolving named exports and imports.

nodes.label: IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY and RVA-Based Export Resolution
nodes.description: The IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY (40 bytes) contains NumberOfFunctions, NumberOfNames, AddressOfFunctions (RVA to function pointer array), AddressOfNames (RVA to name pointer array), and AddressOfNameOrdinals (RVA to ordinal array). NumberOfFunctions may exceed NumberOfNames because some functions are exported only by ordinal. To resolve a named export: binary search AddressOfNames for the target name, use the index into AddressOfNameOrdinals to get an ordinal, then use that ordinal as the index into AddressOfFunctions to get the function RVA. This is the mechanism a manual GetProcAddress implementation replicates.

nodes.label: Manual GetProcAddress via Export Directory Walk
nodes.description: Instead of calling GetProcAddress — which is itself hooked by EDRs and leaves static call traces — an operator parses the export directory of an already-resolved module (typically ntdll, kernel32, kernelbase) and walks AddressOfNames → AddressOfNameOrdinals → AddressOfFunctions to locate the target function's RVA. This produces a function pointer without invoking the loader's API surface and is the basis for PEB-walker-style dynamic API resolution used to bootstrap syscall stubs and NT API bindings.

nodes.label: Filesystem Enumeration Triplet (FindFirstFile/FindNextFile/FindClose)
nodes.description: Directory enumeration on Windows uses three Find* APIs: FindFirstFileW opens a search handle and returns the first match, FindNextFileW iterates subsequent matches in a do/while loop checking its BOOL return, and FindClose releases the search handle. The WIN32_FIND_DATAW structure returned per entry contains file attributes, timestamps, size, and long/short names. This pattern is the primitive for host-survey file discovery, exfil targeting, and persistence-target location.

nodes.label: Registry Access API Pattern
nodes.description: Registry operations follow a fixed sequence: RegOpenKeyExW returns an HKEY with KEY_READ/KEY_WRITE/KEY_SET_VALUE access (returns LSTATUS, errors resolved via FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM), RegQueryInfoKey retrieves subkey count and max-name sizes for buffer allocation, RegEnumKeyEx iterates subkeys (loop ends on ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS), RegQueryValueExW queries named values using a two-call pattern (size query then value read), and RegCloseKey releases the handle. This pattern is the primitive for registry-based persistence target discovery and host-fingerprint collection.

nodes.label: IPHLPAPI Network Reconnaissance Primitives
nodes.description: GetIpStatistics fills a MIB_IPSTATS structure with dwDefaultTTL, dwInReceives, dwInHdrErrors, dwInAddrErrors, dwForwDatagrams, dwOutRequests, dwOutDiscards, dwOutNoRoutes, and routing/fragment counters — the data netstat surfaces. GetAdaptersAddresses accepts Family (AF_INET/AF_INET6/AF_UNSPEC), Flags, Reserved, AdapterAddresses, and SizePointer, returning an IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES linked list covering both IPv4 and IPv6. These IPHLPAPI calls are the documented primitives for replicating ipconfig/arp/netstat without spawning those binaries.

nodes.label: Language Diversity for Signature Avoidance
nodes.description: The material explicitly recommends varying implementation language (C, C++, Rust, C#, Go) and even compiler choices across a toolset to produce diverse static signatures, reducing the value of static signature coverage against any single toolchain. Rust is called out as increasingly used for offensive tools and shellcode. The operational principle: a toolset built entirely in one language/compiler produces a coherent signature surface that one detection rule can collapse.

nodes.label: PE DataDirectory Array
nodes.description: The IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 contains a 16-entry DataDirectory array. Each entry is an IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY with VirtualAddress (DWORD RVA) and Size (DWORD) fields. Index 1 is the Import Directory. The RVAs are relative to the image base and must be added to the loaded module base to yield an absolute virtual address at runtime. WinDbg's dx command can dump the entire array and individual entries for inspection.

nodes.label: IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR Structure
nodes.description: Each imported DLL is described by an IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR with OriginalFirstThunk (RVA to Import Lookup Table / INT), TimeDateStamp (0 = not bound, -1 = bound), ForwarderChain (-1 = no forwarders), Name (RVA to DLL name string), and FirstThunk (RVA to Import Address Table / IAT). The loader walks this structure during process initialization to resolve and patch imported function addresses into the IAT, which is the same structure a PEB walker parses to locate function pointers in a loaded module.

nodes.label: CONTEXT Structure and Context Switching
nodes.description: Each thread has a CONTEXT structure holding its saved register state — including R11 through R15, Rip, and the LastExceptionToRip/LastExceptionFromRip fields — captured when its quantum ends or it is preempted by a higher-priority thread. The processor swaps these contexts to schedule threads. CR3 (page-table base) governs per-process address space and swaps as part of the broader scheduling state. GetThreadContext and SetThreadContext expose CONTEXT to user mode and are the primitives used to suspend a thread, modify Rip to redirect execution to shellcode, and resume — the material frames this as the malicious use of thread context.

nodes.label: Windows Service Control Manager Programming Model
nodes.description: A Windows service binary must implement a service entry point, a ServiceMain function, and a ServiceControlHandler. The process connects to the SCM via StartServiceControlDispatcher, registers its handler via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx, and reports state transitions through SetServiceStatus using a SERVICE_STATUS struct (dwServiceType, dwServiceSpecificExitCode, dwWaitHint). SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS indicates the service runs in its own address space rather than sharing a host (svchost). The handler must respond to SCM control requests. This contract is the surface an implant binary implements to masquerade as a legitimate service and receive SCM-launched execution at boot.

nodes.label: CreateService Parameter Semantics
nodes.description: CreateService parameters control the service's runtime identity: lpBinaryPathName is the full executable path and may include trailing command-line arguments; lpLoadOrderGroup is optional (NULL acceptable); lpdwTagId is only meaningful for kernel driver services; lpDependencies is an optional list of dependent service names; lpServiceStartName is the logon account under which the service executes; lpPassword is the account password. These parameters determine how the SCM loads and authenticates the service at boot, which determines the privilege context and persistence characteristics of an implant deployed as a service.

nodes.label: Anonymous Pipes (CreatePipe) for IPC
nodes.description: Anonymous pipes are created with CreatePipe, which returns separate read and write handles, each access-restricted to its respective operation. They are local-only (cannot traverse the network), one-way (cannot read and write at the same end), and restricted to related processes (parent/child). Handle inheritance or DuplicateHandle propagates pipe ends to child processes, typically via stdin/stdout redirection. They carry lower overhead than named pipes, which is the tradeoff for the restricted flexibility.

nodes.label: Named Pipes for IPC
nodes.description: Named pipes support duplex (bidirectional) communication and can traverse the network, unlike anonymous pipes. They are accessible to unrelated processes — not just parent/child — and are created with CreateNamedPipe. The additional flexibility carries higher overhead than anonymous pipes, which is the tradeoff operators evaluate when choosing between the two IPC mechanisms for staged payload communication or implant-to-host channels.

nodes.label: AppInit_DLLs Registry Key
nodes.description: The HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs registry value causes specified DLLs to be loaded into any process that loads user32.dll. Unit 1 (InitToWinit bootcamp challenge) frames AppInit_DLLs as a DLL execution foothold. Modern Windows restricts loading based on the RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs flag and architecture matching, but the mechanism remains a documented persistence and injection vector distinct from the techniques in T-017.

nodes.label: AddMonitor Port Monitor API
nodes.description: The AddMonitor API (winspool.drv) installs a port monitor under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors. Unit 35 explicitly distinguishes AddMonitor from plausible-but-wrong candidate names (CreateNewMonitor, AddNewMonitor) as the correct API for installing a new port monitor. Port monitor DLLs load into the spoolsv.exe service context at service startup and survive reboot, making this a recognized persistence vector not present in the vault's T-017.

nodes.label: SilentProcessExit Registry Key
nodes.description: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit can be configured to trigger actions when a process exits, including attaching a debugger or launching a monitoring process. Unit 36 lists SilentProcessExit and Debugger as registry keys usable to watch for process termination. Defenders use the key for forensic monitoring; attackers abuse the same key as a persistence trigger that fires when a sacrificial process exits.

nodes.label: PE-sieve Memory Scanner
nodes.description: PE-sieve is a defensive scanning tool that inspects running processes for malware artifacts and injection indicators. Unit 29 (Lab 1.1) positions PE-sieve as a 'hackerverse' GitHub project that catches injection methods. The scanner is used during payload development to verify which injection techniques leave detectable artifacts in process memory (unbacked executable regions, modified.text sections, replaced PE images).

nodes.label: MS-DOS Header Byte Layout
nodes.description: Unit 30 frames the byte following the MS-DOS header as 0x00 (the correct answer among 0x00, 0x90, 0x5A). This byte is the start of the MS-DOS stub program that follows the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER in a PE file. The stub is a minimal DOS program that typically prints 'This program cannot be run in DOS mode' and exits; its first byte is part of the stub's instruction sequence. The unit reinforces that PE parsing begins with recognizing the DOS header and stub before the e_lfanew pointer transitions to the NT headers.

nodes.label: ITaskScheduler COM Enumeration Interface
nodes.description: Unit 11 frames ITaskScheduler as the COM interface used to create enumeration objects for scheduled tasks (vs. IUnknown or 'IBelieve'). ITaskScheduler is the legacy COM interface exposed by the Windows Task Scheduler service; modern code uses ITaskService, but ITaskScheduler remains the documented interface for task enumeration on legacy Windows and is referenced in T-017's schtask persistence work.

nodes.label: Process Creation Pre-LdrInitializeThunk Window
nodes.description: Unit 22 frames a review question about process-creation states (Suspended, Terminated, Running) and the stage at which hooks are not yet implemented. In a CREATE_SUSPENDED process, the loader (LdrInitializeThunk) has not yet executed, so userland EDR hook DLLs have not been injected into the new process. This pre-LdrInitializeThunk window is the basis for T-012 Early Cascade APC injection and informs T-014 NtCreateUserProcess and T-015 PPID Spoofing tradecraft.

nodes.label: SAL Source Annotation Language
nodes.description: Unit 8 frames SAL as standing for 'Source-code annotation language' (vs. 'Structured annotation language' or 'Silent analysis language'). Unit 24 (Lab 1.5: Safer with SAL) notes that SAL annotations make code more understandable. SAL is Microsoft's annotation syntax for expressing buffer sizes, pointer validity, and call contracts on Windows API functions, used in headers like winnt.h to communicate contract expectations between callers and callees.

nodes.label: MS-DOS Header and DOS Stub
nodes.description: The MS-DOS header (MZ) at the start of every PE file is followed by the DOS stub. The unit review quiz identifies the byte following the MS-DOS header as 0x90, which corresponds to the first instruction of the DOS stub program that typically prints 'This program cannot be run in DOS mode.'

nodes.label: Thread Scheduling Quantum
nodes.description: The default thread scheduling quantum on Windows Server editions is the subject of an Source A/Source A unit review question with options of 2, 8, and 12 clock cycles. The quantum governs how long a thread runs before the scheduler preempts it, which is relevant to APC draining behavior, thread-hijack timing windows, and sleep-obfuscation frame windows.

nodes.label: Token Theft / Impersonation Lab
nodes.description: Source A Lab 3.5 'TokenThief' covers stealing and reusing Windows access tokens for privilege escalation and lateral movement. The vault currently has no dedicated technique card for token impersonation, theft, or MakeToken-equivalent tradecraft despite its central role in red team operations.

nodes.label: Windows Object Manager Handle/Object Model
nodes.description: Windows represents system resources (files, processes, threads, registry keys, sections, tokens, mutexes, desktops) as data structures in system address space. The kernel creates the object at the request of a user application and returns a handle to the caller; user space never touches the object directly. The Source A material notes over 4,000 executive object types, many not reachable through documented Win32 APIs. This separation is why cross-process operations require handle duplication and why object types such as Process and Section gate injection primitives.

nodes.label: Executive Object Types (Process, Thread, Section, Token, Mutex, Key, Desktop)
nodes.description: The Windows executive implements object types that gate operations relevant to offensive tradecraft: Process objects own a virtual address space controlling one or more Thread objects; Section objects back shared memory and file mappings used by mapping injection and module loaders; Token objects hold the security profile that governs what a thread/process can access; Mutex objects serialize access; Key objects reference registry data; Desktop objects bound window-station-scoped UI operations. The full type list is visible via the WinObj utility from Sysinternals.

nodes.label: CreateFile to NtCreateFile to Executive Object Flow
nodes.description: A Win32 API call such as CreateFile transitions to NtCreateFile, which causes the object manager to allocate an executive File object in system space and return a handle to the user-mode caller. The same flow applies to CreateThread, CreateEvent, CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, and the broader Create* family (nearly 100 functions). The transition crosses the user/system boundary via the NT syscall dispatcher, which is the layer EDRs hook and the layer indirect-syscall techniques (T-001, T-002, T-003) bypass.

nodes.label: Windows DLL Search Order
nodes.description: When a process resolves a DLL by name without a full path, Windows searches in a documented order: (1) the directory containing the configuration file, (2) the current directory of the process, (3) the system directory returned by GetSystemDirectory, (4) the Windows directory returned by GetWindowsDirectory, and (5) directories listed in %PATH%. The current-directory slot (2) is the basis for DLL search-order hijacking and is constrained by SafeDLLSearchMode and the DllCharacteristics IMAGE_DLLCHARACTERISTICS_DYNAMIC_BASE-equivalent flags. This order governs where a proxy or hijacked DLL must be placed to load in preference to the legitimate module.

nodes.label: FindFirstFile/FindNextFile Directory Enumeration
nodes.description: FindFirstFileA/W initializes a directory walk by returning a search handle and populating a WIN32_FIND_DATA structure with the first matching entry. The wildcard-capable lpFileName parameter accepts patterns such as C:\Windows\System32\*.dll. Subsequent FindNextFile calls drain the search until no more matches exist, at which point the handle must be closed with FindFindClose to avoid handle leaks. The ANSI variant should be avoided for non-English paths because it cannot represent characters outside the system code page.

nodes.label: HINSTANCE and HMODULE Handle Equivalence
nodes.description: In the Win32 API, HINSTANCE and HMODULE are interchangeable handle types that both reference a loaded module's base address. The equivalence exists for historical 16-bit Windows compatibility, where an instance handle and a module handle were distinct concepts. Modern 32-bit and 64-bit Windows treats GetModuleHandle and GetInstanceHandle results as the same value, which matters for PEB-walking code that resolves module bases via either API.

nodes.label: Securable Object ACL and Security Descriptor
nodes.description: Objects exposed to user mode are protected by access control lists (ACLs) and security descriptors. The Object Manager acts as a gatekeeper, checking ACLs before granting access to querying or manipulating processes. Kernel-internal objects not exposed to user mode do not require the same ACL protection. Process Explorer can enumerate and display handles to securable objects, making handle-based tradecraft visible to defenders who inspect open handles and their associated access masks.

nodes.label: _EPROCESS and _KPROCESS Structures
nodes.description: Process creation via CreateProcess triggers the kernel to construct a process object in system space. The _EPROCESS is the executive process object containing the PEB pointer, image filename, and security context. The _KPROCESS is the kernel process object (embedded within _EPROCESS) containing scheduler-related fields such as thread list and quantum. The kernel tracks all processes by linking _EPROCESS objects in a doubly-linked list, which is the mechanism underlying process enumeration and PEB-based module walking.

nodes.label: NtQuerySystemInformation with SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION
nodes.description: NtQuerySystemInformation is the NT-level API for enumerating system information. When called with the SystemProcessInformation class, it returns an NTSTATUS and populates a buffer of SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structures, each describing a process's image name, PID, thread count, handle count, and CPU time. This API underlies tools that perform process enumeration without relying on the Win32 Toolhelp API (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot) or WTS session enumeration (WTSEnumerateProcesses).

nodes.label: Windows Service Packs and Hotfix Bundling
nodes.description: Service packs bundle groups of hotfixes so that a user can apply all prior fixes in a single update without installing each one sequentially. Different service pack levels change the set of patched vulnerabilities on a target, which affects exploit compatibility — implant developers and LPE technique authors must account for the target OS version and service pack when selecting or adjusting exploits, including those sourced from frameworks like Metasploit.

nodes.label: Windows Update Agent (WUA) APIs for Patch Enumeration
nodes.description: The Windows Update Agent APIs provide a programmatic interface for querying installed patches and hotfixes. Red team tools can use WUA APIs to retrieve patch information during reconnaissance, determining which vulnerabilities remain unpatched on a target system and therefore which exploits or LPE techniques are viable.

nodes.label: Windows Dispatcher Thread Scheduling
nodes.description: Windows uses a preemptive, priority-based dispatcher. Threads are selected for execution but may never actually run because a higher-priority thread preempts them. Each thread runs for a quantum measured in clock cycles. When a high-priority thread leaves its waiting state and becomes ready, it preempts any currently-running lower-priority thread in its quantum. Server and endpoint configurations use different default quantum values.

nodes.label: APC Alertable Wait State
nodes.description: An Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) is a mechanism that allows an I/O operation to complete later, providing asynchronous execution. APC objects are placed into a thread's queue and execute only when the thread enters an alertable waiting state. A thread that never enters an alertable wait will not drain its user-mode APC queue, causing queued APCs (including injection payloads) to remain pending without error.

nodes.label: svchost.exe Shared vs Isolated Service Hosting
nodes.description: Windows services are special processes with no GUI and no direct user interaction. A shared service hosts multiple services sharing address space within a single svchost.exe process; if one crashes, they all crash. An isolated service is hosted in svchost.exe without sharing its address space with other services. The hosting model determines blast radius and affects which services can be safely targeted for process injection.

nodes.label: NTFS Directory Entry Table
nodes.description: NTFS tracks directories and child directories in a directory tree. Each directory has a table holding entries with the names of files contained in that directory. The directory entry table, combined with hard links, forms the structural basis for NTFS file system navigation. APIs include CreateDirectory, CreateDirectoryEx, and CreateDirectoryTransacted.

nodes.label: RegQueryInfoKey Registry Enumeration API
nodes.description: RegQueryInfoKey (declared in Winreg.h, returns LSTATUS) retrieves detailed information about a registry key: class string, number of subkeys (lpcSubKeys), number of values (lpcValues), max subkey name length (lpcbMaxSubKeyLen), max value name length (lpcbMaxValueNameLen), and max value data size (lpcbMaxValueLen). Used to enumerate registry structure before walking subkeys and values.

nodes.label: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue Registry Watchdog
nodes.description: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue (declared in Winreg.h, returns LSTATUS) is used to be notified when specific changes happen to a registry key. Parameters include hKey (must have REG_NOTIFY access mask), bWatchSubtree (Boolean for recursive watch), dwNotifyFilter (which change types trigger notification), hEvent (optional event handle), and fAsynchronous (Boolean for async vs sync notification). Functions as a sentry for registry persistence writes.

nodes.label: Process Initial Thread and AddressOfEntryPoint
nodes.description: A thread is an entity within a process that can be scheduled for execution — the smallest unit of execution tied to a process. Every process has at least one initial thread that kicks off image code execution at the image's AddressOfEntryPoint. This initial thread and its entry point form the foundation of process startup that injection techniques such as Early Cascade (T-012) intercept before LdrInitializeThunk.

nodes.label: Securable Objects and SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES
nodes.description: Windows securable objects — files, processes, threads, registry keys — carry a security descriptor that the SRM checks on every access request. The Create* Win32 API family (CreateProcess, CreateThread, CreateFile) accepts a SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure pointer to attach a descriptor at object creation. OpenProcess and similar handle-acquisition APIs trigger an access check against this descriptor, returning ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED when the caller lacks the requested access rights in the DACL.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL)
nodes.description: SDDL is a string format consumed by ConvertSecurityDescriptorToStringSecurityDescriptor and ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptor. The string encodes Owner (O:), Primary Group (G:), DACL (D:), and SACL (S:) sections, each with control flags. ACE strings follow the form (AceType;;AccessMask;;;Sid) — e.g. (A;;RPWPCCDCLCSWRCWDWOGA;;;S-1-0-0) is an ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE_TYPE granting READ_CONTROL|WRITE_DAC|WRITE_OWNER|GENERIC_ALL to the NULL SID.

nodes.label: Windows Port Monitors (spoolsv.exe to Kernel Bridge)
nodes.description: Windows print monitors come in two types: language monitors and port monitors. A port monitor bridges user-mode spoolsv.exe (the Windows Print Spooler service) to a kernel-mode port driver. Port monitors are implemented as DLLs loaded by spoolsv.exe and registered through the Win32 AddPrinter API. Because spoolsv.exe loads these DLLs at service start, registering a malicious port monitor DLL achieves persistence with SYSTEM-equivalent privileges in the spooler process.

nodes.label: Common Information Model (CIM) and WMI Schemas
nodes.description: CIM is an industry-standard object-oriented model WMI uses to represent systems, processes, devices, and applications. CIM defines three class levels: Core (general managed objects), Common (system, application, network extensions), and Extended (technology-specific). Classes are grouped into schemas: the CIM Schema contains classes prefixed CIM_ (Core and Common definitions), and the Win32 Schema contains classes prefixed Win32_ (Extended CIM specific to the Win32 environment). Developers can author custom classes in either schema.

nodes.label: NTDLL Native vs WIN32K.SYS GUI Syscall Split
nodes.description: Windows exposes two syscall surfaces. NTDLL.DLL provides native syscalls (NtOpenProcess, NtCreateProcess) that enter the kernel and executive directly. WIN32.DLL (user32/gdi32) provides GUI syscalls (NtUserOpenClipboard, NtUserCloseClipboard) that route into WIN32K.SYS, a separate kernel-mode subsystem. A console/native thread makes only NTDLL syscalls; a GUI thread additionally issues WIN32K syscalls. Syscall dispatch techniques operating on ntdll gadgets do not cover the WIN32K syscall surface.

nodes.label: Win32 DLL Loading APIs (LoadLibrary / GetProcAddress)
nodes.description: Windows provides LoadLibrary/FreeLibrary for explicit DLL load and unload, and GetProcAddress for symbol address resolution. These are the Win32 parallels to Linux dlopen/dlclose/dlsym. Both PE (Windows) and ELF (Linux) export symbols that the loader resolves at runtime. Manual resolution techniques (PEB walking, export table parsing) reimplement GetProcAddress behavior without invoking the API directly, avoiding IAT-based detection of which functions a module imports.

nodes.label: Object Header and Object Body Schema
nodes.description: Every executive object has a standardized header containing type, name, directory, security descriptor, handle count and list, and optional subheaders; the object body is unique to the object type. This separation is what lets the Object Manager service any object with generic operations. The handle count and list in the header track every process handle table entry that currently references the object — relevant when a process object's handle count is inspected by EDR or when an injector relies on the handle list for duplication.

nodes.label: Handle Value Mechanics
nodes.description: Handle values are always a multiple of 4, never zero, with the first valid handle being 4. A handle is a per-process table index (scaled by 4 on use) into the process handle table, which is itself managed by the Object Manager. Source A notes handle values are 32-bit or 64-bit depending on architecture. The 'multiple of 4' property encodes the table slot index in the low bits and historically left room for inherit/protect/audit attributes in the low two bits — relevant when an operator inspects or forges handle values.

nodes.label: Securable Objects, ACLs, and Security Descriptors
nodes.description: Objects exposed to user mode must be protected. Each securable object carries its own access control list (ACL) and security descriptor that dictates what actions a querying process may perform. The system acts as gatekeeper, performing access checks on every Open*/NtOpen* call. Source A notes that internal kernel objects not exposed to user mode may not carry the same protections — a distinction operators rely on when reasoning about which objects an EDR's kernel callback can observe.

nodes.label: Generic vs. Type-Specific Object Services
nodes.description: All objects regardless of type support generic services (Close, Duplicate, Query/Set Security, WaitForSingleObject); each object type additionally exposes type-specific services (Create, Open, Query). CloseHandle works on file, process, thread, event, and key handles alike because the generic dispatch path reads the object header to find the type-specific close routine. This is why a single NtClose syscall retires any handle and why handle-blocking techniques must intercept at the generic layer to be effective.

nodes.label: HANDLE/HMODULE/HINSTANCE Typedef Lineage
nodes.description: Per WinNt.h, HANDLE is a typedef of PVOID (void*). Derived handle types (HKEY, HMODULE, HINSTANCE, HRSRC, LPHANDLE) are all built on this HANDLE base and are technically interchangeable — Source A demonstrates casting HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE directly to PVOID with no functional issue. The convention exists for code clarity, not type safety. HMODULE and HINSTANCE are explicitly interchangeable; this matters when an operator inspects a loader-returned HMODULE in PEB-walking code (T-004) and treats it as a raw pointer for arithmetic.

nodes.label: System DLL Hierarchy: Ntdll, Kernel32, Kernelbase, User32
nodes.description: Several system DLLs are mapped into nearly every process. Ntdll is the only one strictly required and is mapped by the OS. Ntdll exports functions acting as the gateway to kernel land. Kernel32 re-exports a large number of ntdll functions, with some exports consisting of nothing but jumps or forwarders to ntdll. User32 holds GUI component functions. The material notes that user-mode hooks placed in these DLLs can be bypassed by unloading the system DLLs.

nodes.label: Windows Thread States: Ready, Running, Waiting
nodes.description: Windows tracks threads in three primary states: Ready (eligible to run but not currently dispatched), Running (currently executing on a logical processor), and Waiting (blocked on a dispatcher object such as an event, semaphore, or alertable wait). Thread-state-dependent injection techniques select threads in Waiting state because their context is stable and their resume semantics are predictable.

nodes.label: Preemptive Priority-Based Thread Scheduling
nodes.description: The Windows dispatcher selects threads for execution under a preemptive, priority-based scheduling model. Higher-priority threads preempt lower-priority ones. This affects injection timing because a hijacked or APC-targeted thread's quantum arrival depends on its priority and the dispatcher's selection, not on a deterministic call from the implant.

nodes.label: Thread Creation Internal Flow: NtCreateThreadEx → PspCreateThread
nodes.description: Thread creation converts parameters into flags, adds the client ID and TEB address to an attribute list, determines whether the thread is local or remote, then calls NtCreateThreadEx which initializes user-mode thread context and invokes PspCreateThread. The thread is created initially suspended and later resumed so the dispatcher can schedule it. This suspended initial state is the window during which APC injection payloads are queued before the thread runs.

nodes.label: APC Queue as Routine Dispatch Mechanism
nodes.description: Threads process routines queued to their APC queue when they enter their quantum. The APC queue is the mechanism that allows kernel and user-mode code to schedule routine execution on a target thread without direct invocation. APC injection techniques exploit this by queuing payload-bearing APCs to threads that will drain the queue during an upcoming quantum or alertable wait.

nodes.label: Securable Objects and SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES
nodes.description: Securable objects in Windows carry a corresponding security descriptor. The Create* family of Win32 APIs (CreateProcess, CreateThread, CreateFile, CreateRegistryKey, etc.) accept a pointer to a SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure that controls access. Handles returned from these APIs are gated by the security descriptor and the handle table. Process injection and handle-blocking evasion techniques interact with this model when opening remote process handles or denying external handle access.

nodes.label: Anonymous and Named Pipes for IPC
nodes.description: Pipes are one of several interprocess communication methods on Windows. Anonymous pipes are local only, one-way, and have less overhead than named pipes. Named pipes support bidirectional and cross-host communication. Implant tradecraft uses pipes for C2 channel multiplexing, localhost relay between staged components, and impersonation token theft via named pipe security descriptors.

nodes.label: Common Information Model (CIM) Class Hierarchy
nodes.description: WMI uses the industry-standard Common Information Model to represent managed objects in an object-oriented schema. CIM defines three tiers: Core (universal, technology-agnostic primitives), Common (commonly applicable system, process, and device abstractions like Win32_Process), and Extended (vendor- or technology-specific extensions). Understanding the tier hierarchy clarifies which WMI classes are guaranteed across Windows versions and which are vendor-specific.

nodes.label: WQL Data, Event, and Schema Queries
nodes.description: Windows Query Language supports three query classes. Data queries (e.g., SELECT * FROM Win32_NTLogEvent WHERE logfile='System' AND EventCode='4625') retrieve instances. Event queries subscribe to instance lifecycle changes via __InstanceCreationEvent / __InstanceDeletionEvent with a WITHIN polling interval. Schema queries (SELECT * FROM meta_class WHERE __this ISA 'Win32_Process') enumerate class definitions rather than instances. Intrinsic events require explicit polling intervals while extrinsic events fire from provider callbacks.

nodes.label: WMI Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Event Model
nodes.description: Intrinsic WMI events are synthesized by the WMI infrastructure from instance changes (creation, modification, deletion) in a CIM repository and must be polled at a defined WITHIN interval — the consumer does not receive them unless it actively queries. Extrinsic events are raised by event providers directly (e.g., Win32_ProcessStartTrace), require no polling interval, and deliver near-real-time. Persistence consumers using intrinsic events incur polling overhead and a maximum delay equal to the WITHIN interval.

nodes.label: WMI Event Subscription Persistence
nodes.description: WMI permanent event subscriptions achieve persistence by binding an __EventFilter (a WQL trigger condition) to an __EventConsumer (typically CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer) via a __FilterToConsumerBinding instance. All three are stored in the CIM repository and survive reboots. The subscription fires asynchronously whenever the filter condition is satisfied, executing the consumer payload without an attacker-controlled process needing to remain resident.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Persistence
nodes.description: IFEO registry entries under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>.exe allow an attacker to register a Debugger value that is invoked in place of (or in addition to) the target executable. When the system launches the target binary, the debugger path is executed instead, providing a fileless, reboot-surviving persistence trigger tied to legitimate binary launches.

nodes.label: SDDL ACE Granting to NULL SID (S-1-0-0)
nodes.description: The SDDL string 'O:AOG:DAD:(A;;RPWPCCDCLCSWRCWDWOGA;;;S-1-0-0)' encodes a DACL with a single ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE_TYPE entry granting READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC | WRITE_OWNER | GENERIC_ALL to the NULL well-known SID (S-1-0-0). Granting rights to NULL SID effectively permits access to subjects with no authenticated identity — a known technique for loosening security descriptors on services, named pipes, or kernel objects to permit anonymous or low-privilege access.

nodes.label: Windows Update Agent (WUA) Hotfix Enumeration
nodes.description: The Windows Update Agent API family is the documented method for querying installed hotfixes, also known as Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) updates. Source A identifies WUA as the correct API family for hotfix enumeration (vs. LUA or FUA), used by offensive operators to enumerate patch level and identify missing security updates for vulnerability selection.

nodes.label: Process Enumeration API Triad
nodes.description: Three Win32/NT APIs provide process information from a PID: OpenProcess() returns a handle used for subsequent queries; WTSEnumerateProcessesEx() enumerates all processes in a session with extended info in a single call; NtQuerySystemInformation() with SystemProcessInformation returns a flat buffer of all EPROCESS-linked process records from the kernel. The trade-offs are handle-based access vs. snapshot enumeration vs. native NT buffer walk.

nodes.label: Windows Hotfix / Quick Fix Engineering Updates
nodes.description: Windows Hotfixes, also referred to as Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) updates, are Microsoft's mechanism for applying critical fixes to deployed software. They are enumerated via the WUA API family and appear in WMI as Win32_QuickFixEngineering instances. Operators enumerate QFE state to identify missing patches and select viable privilege-escalation or LPE primitives.

nodes.label: Thread Quantum Slice and Running State
nodes.description: A thread executing during its allocated quantum slice is in the Running state, distinct from Waiting (blocked on a dispatcher object) and Ready (eligible to run but not currently scheduled). The quantum is the time allowance the scheduler grants before preempting the thread for another Ready thread of equal priority. This state distinction matters for injection techniques that target suspended or waiting threads, because a thread in Running state has an actively executing context that cannot be safely modified without synchronization.

nodes.label: Anonymous Pipes (Windows IPC)
nodes.description: Anonymous pipes are a one-way, local-only interprocess communication mechanism with lower overhead than named pipes. Because they cannot span process boundaries on remote machines and lack the kernel namespace registration of named pipes, they are less observable via Sysmon Event ID 17/18 (PipeEvent) and are sometimes used for parent-child implant communication where stealth is preferred over flexibility. They require an inheritable handle to be passed to the child at creation time.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Persistence
nodes.description: Image File Execution Options is a registry-based persistence mechanism under HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target.exe> where setting the Debugger value to an attacker-controlled path causes any launch of target.exe to invoke the attacker binary instead with the original command line appended. Source A lists IFEO alongside registry keys, services, port monitors, and WMI Event Subscriptions as a Section 4 persistence topic. The technique is detectable via registry monitoring on the IFEO key tree and is privilege-gated to HKLM write access.

nodes.label: Extrinsic vs Intrinsic Event Polling
nodes.description: Extrinsic events are externally triggered and require the implant to poll at some interval to detect them — examples include file drops, registry changes, or external process creation. Intrinsic events are driven by the implant's own execution state and can be handled synchronously. Source A poses both as event classes that must be polled at some interval, which frames the operational trade-off: tighter polling improves responsiveness but increases the implant's CPU footprint and detection surface; looser polling reduces footprint but risks missing transient signals like short-lived child processes or rapidly deleted staging files.

nodes.label: Windows Dispatcher and Thread Quantum
nodes.description: The Windows dispatcher is a preemptive, priority-based scheduler. Threads are assigned priorities and run for a fixed number of clock cycles called a quantum. A higher-priority thread leaving its waiting state and becoming ready preempts any lower-priority thread currently in its quantum. Thread state transitions between Running, Ready, and Waiting govern when user-mode APCs can be delivered, since APCs require the target thread to enter an alertable wait state.

nodes.label: Thread Object Residency in System (Kernel) Space
nodes.description: Newly created thread objects reside in system (kernel) space, not user space or the process handle table. The ETHREAD/KTHREAD structures are kernel objects managed by the executive. User-mode code interacts with them only through opaque handles returned by NtCreateThreadEx. This residency underpins why thread hijacking, APC queuing, and thread-context manipulation all require NT syscalls and cannot be performed via Win32 userland APIs alone.

nodes.label: PE-sieve Memory Scanner
nodes.description: PE-sieve is an open-source memory scanner that detects injected implants by walking process memory and comparing in-memory module contents against their on-disk counterparts. It flags modified.text sections, unbacked executable regions, and replaced module content. The tool operates from user mode by default and is therefore subject to the same handle-access constraints as EDR userland scanners.

nodes.label: WMI Event Subscription Persistence
nodes.description: WMI Event Subscriptions are a persistence mechanism that combines an EventFilter (a query describing the triggering condition), an EventConsumer (an action to take — typically CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer), and a FilterToConsumerBinding linking them. The subscription executes asynchronously when the filter condition is met, with no requirement for an interactive logon. Source A lists this as a Section 4 persistence lab.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Persistence
