nodes.description: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) is a registry subtree under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options that supports a Debugger value. When a process matching the IFEO subkey name is launched, the debugger value is executed instead, allowing an attacker to redirect execution to a malicious payload on every invocation of the targeted binary. Source A documents this as Lab 4.3 'IFEOPersist'.

nodes.label: Port Monitor Persistence
nodes.description: Port Monitors are print spooler components registered under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors. A malicious DLL registered as a Port Monitor is loaded by the print spooler service (spoolsv.exe), which runs as SYSTEM, on service start. The technique persists across reboots and runs in a privileged context. Source A lists Port Monitors as a Section 4 persistence topic.

nodes.label: NTDLL Unhooking (Source A framing)
nodes.description: Source A's Section 5 lab 'UnhookTheHook' frames NTDLL unhooking as restoring the ntdll.dll.text section to a clean state to defeat userland API hooks placed by AV/EDR. The course positions this as a prerequisite evasion step before additional AV/EDR bypass techniques are layered on.

nodes.label: AMSI Bypass (Source A framing)
nodes.description: Source A's Section 5 lab 'AMSI No More' covers bypassing the Anti-Malware Scan Interface. AMSI is a Windows service interface that allows registered AV products to scan script content from PowerShell, VBA, and similar script engines. Bypass approaches typically target amsi.dll in the script host process.

nodes.label: Custom Loader Development
nodes.description: Source A's Section 5 opens with custom loader development (Lab 5.1: The Loader) as the foundation for staging shellcode, applying evasion, and establishing C2. The loader is positioned as the host component that integrates subsequent evasion modules (unhooking, AMSI bypass) before the implant calls home.

nodes.label: WTSEnumProcesses and CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Recon
nodes.description: WTSEnumProcesses enumerates processes on a WTS session (including other sessions on the same host) and returns per-process SID information. CreateToolhelp32Snapshot takes a snapshot of process, thread, heap, and module state. Source A Section 2 covers both as primary recon primitives for implant situational awareness — enumerating processes to identify targets for injection, defense-relevant processes, and adversary tooling already in the environment.

nodes.label: Windows Update Agent API for Patch Recon
nodes.description: The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API exposes interfaces (notably IWindowsUpdateAgent) that can enumerate installed hotfixes and service packs. Source A identifies WUA as the API family used to query hotfixes, used by implants to determine patch level and infer whether specific privilege-escalation or kernel-exploit paths are viable on a target.

nodes.label: AppInit_DLLs Registry Persistence
nodes.description: When LoadAppInit_DLLs (REG_DWORD) is set to 1 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows, every newly created user-mode process linked against User32.dll loads the comma-separated DLLs listed in AppInit_DLLs (REG_SZ). Requires administrative privileges. Documented as used by APT39, CherryPicker, and T9000. Operator must avoid infinite loops where the injected DLL spawns a process that re-triggers AppInit loading.

nodes.label: Silent Process Exit via GlobalFlag
nodes.description: Configured via Gflags.exe (Windows SDK, located at C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64) or directly via the GlobalFlag registry key. The 'Silent Process Exit' feature monitors an exiting process (the 'Image') and invokes a configured 'Monitor' process. Used as a persistence trigger fired on process termination rather than on system boot or process launch. GflagsX by Pavel Yosifovich provides a modern GUI for managing these flags.

nodes.label: Service ImagePath/binPath/FailureCommand Persistence
nodes.description: Existing or newly created Windows services can be modified for persistence by altering ImagePath (registry key holding the absolute path to the service binary), binPath (the command-line passed to the service binary), or FailureCommand (executed when the service fails to start or terminates unexpectedly). Modifications performed via sc.exe or the CreateService API. Service modification produces reboot-survivable execution via SCM.

nodes.label: Classic CreateRemoteThread DLL Injection
nodes.description: The legacy four-step DLL injection flow documented in Source A: (1) obtain a handle to the target process, (2) allocate memory in the target via VirtualAllocEx, (3) write the DLL path string to the allocated region via WriteProcessMemory, (4) spawn a remote thread via CreateRemoteThread with start address pointing to LoadLibraryA/W. Requires the target process to expose LoadLibrary in its export table.

nodes.label: APC Queue and Thread Quantum Scheduling
nodes.description: Per the Source A review question, the APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when entering their quantum. User-mode APCs drain during alertable waits; kernel APCs drain at IRQL drop. Thread quantum entry provides a scheduling window where queued APCs dispatch — the same window Early Cascade (T-012) targets with pre-LdrInitializeThunk APCs.

nodes.label: WIN32_FIND_DATA Structure
nodes.description: User-mode structure that holds the attributes of a file returned by FindFirstFile/FindNextFile. Distinguished from KUSER_SHARED_DATA (shared user/kernel page containing system time and tick count) and FILE_OBJECT (the kernel-mode structure representing an open file instance). The Source A review answer identifies WIN32_FIND_DATA as the user-mode file-attribute structure.

nodes.label: MS-DOS / PE Header Layout
nodes.description: PE files begin with an MS-DOS stub. The Source A review question asks what byte typically follows the MS-DOS header — establishing that the operator must recognize the MS-DOS header boundary to navigate to the PE header (e_lfanew field at offset 0x3C points to 'PE\0\0'). Required knowledge for manual PE parsing in injection and module-stomping techniques.

nodes.label: SDDL Security Descriptor Definition Language
nodes.description: Security Descriptor Definition Language is the language used to describe the security of a Windows object descriptor. The Source A review question confirms SDDL (not ACL or DACL, which are components within a security descriptor) is the descriptive language. sc.exe is the command-line utility for viewing an object's security descriptor.

nodes.label: ITaskScheduler COM Interface
nodes.description: COM interface used to create enumeration objects for scheduled tasks. Source A review question identifies ITaskScheduler (not IUnknown) as the interface called to create a task enumeration object. Relevant to scheduled-task persistence enumeration and creation via COM rather than the schtasks.exe command-line.

nodes.label: KUSER_SHARED_DATA
nodes.description: User-readable shared page (fixed virtual address 0x7FFE0000 on x86, 0x7FFE0000 on x64) mapped read-only into every process. Contains system time, tick count, CPU information, and other low-overhead globally-shared values. Distinguished from WIN32_FIND_DATA and FILE_OBJECT in the Source A review question. Useful for system-time queries without syscalls.

nodes.label: Thread Object Residency in System Space
nodes.description: Per the Source A review question, when a new thread is created the thread object resides in system (kernel) space, not user space and not the process handle table. Thread objects are kernel structures (ETHREAD/KTHREAD) accessible from user mode only through handles. Establishes why thread manipulation requires object-handle access patterns.

nodes.label: APC Queue and Thread Quantum Dispatch
nodes.description: APC queues allow routines to be queued for execution when a thread enters its quantum or alertable wait. Source A identifies the APC queue as the mechanism that lets threads process routines during quantum entry. User-mode APCs require an alertable wait to drain; kernel APCs are not subject to that constraint. This is the scheduling primitive that Early Bird, Early Cascade, and other APC-based injection techniques depend on.

nodes.label: Registry Run / RunOnce / RunOnceEx Autostart Keys
nodes.description: Run, RunOnce, and RunOnceEx under HKCU and HKLM Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion are the most-used persistence keys across APTs (Source A cites APT28 and Emotet as examples). HKCU keys require no elevation; HKLM keys require Administrator. HKLM variants execute as the receiving context (e.g., SYSTEM for machine-wide Run, Admin for user-targeted HKLM Run). The method is not novel but remains effective because of implementation simplicity and visibility fatigue.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Debugger Value
nodes.description: IFEO is a registry key under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options intended for tracing or debugging a process at startup. Setting the Debugger value on a target subkey causes the specified debugger path to launch instead of the original executable. Source A recommends targeting early-boot processes such as userinit.exe for reliable trigger frequency. The mechanism persists across reboots without modifying the original binary.

nodes.label: SDDL-Based Service Hiding
nodes.description: Services can be hidden from detection by manipulating the Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL) on the service object to deny read or enumerate access to non-privileged queries. Source A documents manual service hiding via SDDL as the closing lab of its services-persistence module, preventing listing tools from surfacing the malicious service entry.

nodes.label: WMI Permanent Event Subscription Persistence
nodes.description: WMI permanent subscriptions combine an event filter (__EventFilter), a consumer (typically ActiveScriptEventConsumer or CommandLineEventConsumer), and a binding (__FilterToConsumerBinding) stored in the CIM repository. They survive reboots and execute on configured triggers such as system uptime thresholds, process creation, or failed logon. Source A Lab 4.6 OhMyWMI builds a subscription keyed on system uptime to launch a persistence tool. The configuration persists in the WMI repository rather than on disk as a script file.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration
nodes.description: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS produces a snapshot handle; Process32First and Process32Next iterate PROCESSENTRY32 records exposing process name, PID, parent PID, and thread count. Source A's example passes NULL as the third argument to capture all processes rather than a single one. The handle is checked against INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure. This is the canonical user-mode recon primitive for selecting injection or token-theft targets.

nodes.label: OpenProcessToken for Token Handle Acquisition
nodes.description: OpenProcessToken takes an OpenProcess handle and a desired access mask, returning a token handle used by subsequent token-manipulation APIs such as DuplicateTokenEx and SetThreadToken. Source A identifies OpenProcessToken() as the API for obtaining a process token handle, distinct from OpenProcess() (process handle) and the non-existent OpenToken().

nodes.label: Windows Sockets for C2 Callback
nodes.description: Source A explicitly names Windows Sockets (Winsock) as the transport for implant callbacks to a C2 listening post, checking in for pending tasks and returning results on subsequent connections. The callback module frames socket selection as one of multiple callback methods the operator chooses among rather than the only option.

nodes.label: Peer-to-Peer Listener Chaining (SMB/TCP)
nodes.description: Source B documents Cobalt Strike peer-to-peer listeners as a method for chaining Beacon communications over SMB or TCP when a compromised host cannot reach the Team Server over HTTP. Each Beacon becomes a relay, extending reach into network-segmented hosts. The listener name persists across lateral-movement Beacon commands, so descriptive naming is operationally important.

nodes.label: HKLM SAM and BCD Registry Hives
nodes.description: The HKLM hive contains the SAM subkey holding account password hashes and the BCD subkey holding boot configuration entries. Source A surfaces both as high-value registry targets during post-exploitation. SAM extraction requires either SYSTEM access or offline hive parsing; BCD modification can enable boot-time persistence.

nodes.label: In-Memory Execution and Fileless Malware
nodes.description: Source A's module summary defines in-memory execution as loading and running payload without touching disk, citing WannaCry and EternalBlue as high-profile examples. Advantages include reduced on-disk artifact footprint; disadvantages include volatility across reboots and exposure to memory-forensics techniques that scan for unbacked executable regions. Memory forensics is identified as the primary defensive counter.

nodes.label: Service Control Manager Attributes (Start Type, Service Type, Error Level)
nodes.description: Each Windows service carries Start Type (auto-start, on-demand, disabled), Service Type (own process vs shared svchost grouping), and Error Level (severity and recovery action on failure). Source A emphasizes SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS for malicious services because shared-process hosting causes cascading crashes if a sibling service faults; failure actions can be configured to auto-restart.

nodes.label: SCM Five-Step Service Startup
nodes.description: When SCM starts a service it executes five housekeeping steps including image load, process creation, ServiceMain dispatch via StartServiceCtrlDispatcher, RegisterServiceCtrlHandler registration, and SetServiceStatus reporting. A service binary must implement ServiceMain, the control handler, and status reporting or SCM will treat the service as failed.

nodes.label: CreateService / ChangeServiceConfig API Surface
nodes.description: CreateService is the underlying API for service installation used by sc.exe and PowerShell service cmdlets. ChangeServiceConfig and ChangeServiceConfig2 modify existing services, including lpBinaryPathName and trigger configuration. SERVICE_NO_CHANGE preserves a parameter during partial config edits. Unquoted binary paths in lpBinaryPathName are an explicit privilege escalation vector.

nodes.label: Anonymous vs Named Pipe IPC Distinction
nodes.description: Anonymous pipes are local-only, one-way, and restricted to parent-child process pairs. Named pipes support duplex communication, can be accessed between unrelated processes, and — with the Server service running — become accessible over the network via \\ComputerName\pipe\PipeName. Named pipes are created with CreateNamedPipe and connected via CreateFile or CallNamedPipe.

nodes.label: Windows Thread State Machine (Ready/Running/Waiting)
nodes.description: Windows tracks at least nine thread states; Source A focuses on Ready (scheduled, awaiting quantum), Running (executing on a CPU during its quantum), and Waiting (blocked on a synchronization event). Only Ready threads are picked up by the dispatcher. Thread state must be modified during thread hijacking operations.

nodes.label: APC Queue Dispatch at Quantum Entry
nodes.description: The APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when entering their quantum. User-mode APCs require the target thread to be in an alertable wait state to drain; the dispatcher drains the APC queue as the thread transitions back to Running. This dispatch path is what APC injection techniques queue into.

nodes.label: Primary vs Impersonation Access Token
nodes.description: After successful logon, each process receives a primary token containing SID, Logon SID, default DACL, privileges, and a primary/impersonation flag. The security descriptor of the token is checked on access to securable objects. Impersonation tokens are tied to a thread for client-impersonation scenarios. TOKEN_PRIVILEGES (winnt.h) enumerates enabled/disabled privilege state.

nodes.label: Medium-IL Privilege Auto-Enablement Without Elevation
nodes.description: Source A demonstrates that SeTimeZonePrivilege transitions from Disabled to Enabled when SystemSettings.exe changes the time zone, with no UAC prompt — SystemSettings.exe runs at Medium-IL. This illustrates that privilege enablement is distinct from privilege presence; a token may hold a privilege without it being enabled, and Medium-IL processes can enable certain privileges autonomously.

nodes.label: WMI Architecture (Providers, Infrastructure, Consumers)
nodes.description: WMI is structured into Providers and Objects (data sources, e.g. the Win32 provider enumerating processes), WMI Infrastructure (the WMI Repository and WMI Query Language — WQL), and WMI Consumers (C++, PowerShell, or COM-based clients that query or subscribe to events). Data flows from providers into the repository and onward to consumers.

nodes.label: WMI Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Events
nodes.description: Intrinsic WMI events fire on changes to the standard WMI model — e.g. __InstanceCreationEvent when an object is added to the repository. Extrinsic events fire on external conditions not directly tied to model changes — e.g. RegistryKeyChangeEvent. Both event classes are subscribable via WQL filters.

nodes.label: SCM Handle Types (SCManager, Service, Database Lock)
nodes.description: Interacting with the SCM requires distinct handle types: SCManager handles for top-level database access, Service handles for per-service operations, and Database lock handles for serialized modification. Handles are required to query (QueryServiceStatusEx, QueryServiceConfig), modify (ChangeServiceConfig), delete, or create (CreateService) service objects.

nodes.label: WMI Permanent Event Subscription (FilterToConsumerBinding)
nodes.description: WMI permanent subscriptions combine three classes: __EventFilter (the trigger query, e.g. filtering for notepad.exe process creation or system uptime thresholds), __EventConsumer (the action — typically CommandLineEventConsumer for executing a binary), and the FilterToConsumerBinding class that links the two. Permanent subscriptions survive reboot because they are stored in the WMI repository rather than running only in the WMI provider host process.

nodes.label: AppCert DLLs Registry Loading Mechanism
nodes.description: The AppCert registry key is queried when CreateProcess, CreateProcessAsUser, CreateProcessWithLogon, CreateProcessWithToken, or WinExec is called. Windows examines the key for a list of DLLs that must be loaded into the newly created process. Requires administrative privileges and a system reboot to take effect, and is easily enumerated by Sysinternals AutoRuns.

nodes.label: Run / RunOnce / RunOnceEx Registry Keys
nodes.description: The Run key is identified by Source A as 'the most used key for persistence by several APTs' under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM\...\Run. RunOnce and RunOnceEx execute the process once and delete the registry entry, useful for artifact minimization but inadequate for long-term persistence. HKLM variants require Administrator privileges and execute as SYSTEM; HKCU variants are usable by standard users as an initial downloader stage.

nodes.label: Service Control Manager Failure Contract
nodes.description: The SCM considers a service to have failed when the service terminates without reporting SERVICE_STOPPED status to the SCM, or when the Win32ExitCode member of SERVICE_STATUS does not indicate ERROR_SUCCESS. Services must answer to the SCM and are promptly terminated if they do not. This contract defines the trigger surface for SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS-based persistence.

nodes.label: SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS Structure
nodes.description: SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONSA defines what takes place after a service failure as determined by SCM. Members include dwResetPeriod (failure count reset window), lpRebootMsg, lpCommand (command executed on failure), cActions, and lpsaActions (array of SC_ACTION structures specifying actions like SC_ACTION_RESTART with delays). Set via ChangeServiceConfig2, this structure can be abused to execute a persistence binary when an attacker-controlled service 'fails' on demand.

nodes.label: Memory Forensics Scanner Suite (Volatility, PE-sieve, Moneta)
nodes.description: Three memory forensics tools are identified by Source A as the detection surface for in-memory fileless implants: Volatility (full-process memory analysis framework), PE-sieve (scans for PE modules in memory that do not match on-disk images — detects hollowed, injected, and unmapped PE payloads), and Moneta (scans for unbacked executable memory and anomalies). These tools specifically target the memory-resident techniques the dark_crystal framework relies on for execution without disk artifacts.

nodes.label: On-Disk Patching of System Binaries
nodes.description: Patching binaries on the file system rather than their memory-mapped images enables survival across reboots but introduces cascading risks. Source A flags that patching system files like Ntdll.dll could render the system unstable, that changes are harder to undo than in-memory patches, and that on-disk modifications are detected faster by file integrity monitoring. The technique has a legitimate use case of patching signature-scanning binaries to disable AV capability persistently.

nodes.label: Strategic Disk Placement Tradecraft
nodes.description: When a memory-resident implant must drop to disk to survive reboot, placement follows blending rules: candidate directories include Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Temp, AppData, Program Files, SysWOW64, System32, and OneDrive. Operational rules specify not being the first or last file in a folder (which attracts analyst attention), choosing less-browsed directories, and using a limited-feature binary for the disk-resident component to minimize exposure if the binary is captured and reverse-engineered.

nodes.label: Sysinternals AutoRuns Enumeration Surface
nodes.description: AutoRuns enumerates the Run/RunOnce/RunOnceEx keys, AppInit_DLLs, AppCert DLLs, scheduled tasks, services, and dozens of other autostart extensibility points (ASEPs) in a single consolidated view. Source A explicitly notes that all registry-based persistence methods discussed — Run, RunOnce, AppInit, AppCert — 'should be easily detected using SysInternals AutoRuns,' flagging it as the canonical hunter tool for these vectors.

nodes.label: Fileless Reboot Flush Limitation
nodes.description: Memory-resident implants are flushed from RAM on system reboot (power loss, Windows update restart, scheduled maintenance). The limitation is framed by Source A as 'arguably the biggest disadvantage when it comes to fileless malware' — the operational consequence is that pure in-memory execution cannot maintain access across reboots, forcing operators to maintain multiple persistence methods to regain initial access after a power cycle.

nodes.label: Implant DRM for Capture Resistance
nodes.description: Source A references the PoC Skrull as an example of 'DRMing' an implant to protect it from analysis if captured on disk. The technique applies creative anti-analysis measures to the dropped binary itself so that even if the disk artifact is captured by defenders, reverse engineering the implant is hindered. This complements but is distinct from the operational goal of avoiding detection in the first place.

nodes.label: Custom Windows Service Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence via OpenSCManager + CreateService to install a malicious service that runs under SYSTEM via the Service Control Manager. Source A frames this as the 'perfect action' once admin or SYSTEM privileges are obtained, because services execute at boot under SYSTEM authority and survive reboots.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL)
nodes.description: Microsoft's string format for security descriptors consumed by ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptor and ConvertSecurityDescriptorToStringSecurityDescriptor. SDDL encodes Owner (O:), Group (G:), DACL (D:), and SACL (S:) with control flags (SDDL_PROTECTED, SDDL_AUTO_INHERITED). ACE strings include ace_type (A/D/OA/OD/AU/AL), ace_flags (CI/OI/NP/IO/ID), and rights tokens (GA/GR/GW/GX, RC/SD/WD/WO, KA/KR/KW, etc.).

nodes.label: spoolsv.exe (Print Spooler Service)
nodes.description: User-mode Windows service (Spooler) that bridges user-mode printer queue management to kernel-mode port drivers. Source A identifies spoolsv.exe as the host process for port monitors — abusing port monitor registration causes spoolsv.exe to load attacker-controlled DLLs at service startup.

nodes.label: IFEO and SilentProcessExit Registry Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence via HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options. The Debugger value substitutes a target executable's launch with an attacker payload; SilentProcessExit uses GlobalFlag=512 (FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT) plus SilentProcessExit\ReportingMode=1 and MonitorProcess pointing to the attacker payload, triggering execution on target process exit. Source A explicitly notes Admin or SYSTEM is required.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Registry Key
nodes.description: Registry path HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options contains per-executable subkeys. Originally designed for debug/trace hooks (Debugger value swaps the executable launch path), IFEO is also abused for persistence and process redirection. SilentProcessExit subkey triggers process-exit monitoring via the Windows Error Reporting (WER) subsystem.

nodes.label: Silent Process Exit Monitoring Mechanism
nodes.description: Windows mechanism that triggers user-configured actions when a process exits after IFEO GlobalFlag is set. Configured under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit with ReportingMode (1 = launch monitor process, 2 = notify, 4 = dump) and MonitorProcess (path to executable). Implementation routes through RtlReportSilentProcessExit and the Windows Error Reporting service.

nodes.label: GlobalFlag Registry Value (FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT)
nodes.description: The GlobalFlag DWORD value under IFEO\<ProcessName> configures system-wide debug/trace flags for a process. Flag 0x200 (512, FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT) enables the Silent Process Exit monitoring hook — when the target process exits, Windows Error Reporting invokes the configured MonitorProcess. Source A instructs setting GlobalFlag=512 as the IFEO persistence precursor.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Control APIs
nodes.description: Windows APIs in securitybaseapi.h and aclapi.h that programmatically manipulate service/object security descriptors: SetSecurityDescriptorControl, SetNamedSecurityInfo, SetServiceObjectSecurity. Source A contrasts these with manual sc.exe sdset SDDL string authoring, framing the API path as more reliable for automated service-hiding workflows.

nodes.label: Admin / SYSTEM Privilege Gate
nodes.description: Access control boundary that prevents non-admin users from writing HKLM\...\Image File Execution Options, HKLM\...\SilentProcessExit, the Services SCM namespace, and the Print Monitors registry path. Source A explicitly lists Admin and SYSTEM as the only effective privilege levels for IFEO persistence — basic users receive ACCESS_DENIED.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Debugger Key
nodes.description: The Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry key (under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options) allows associating a debugger with a target executable. Source A identifies IFEO as a registry key used to watch for process creation — when the target executable is launched, the configured debugger process is invoked instead, enabling both persistence and process creation monitoring.

nodes.label: NtQuerySystemInformation for Process Enumeration
nodes.description: Source A identifies NtQuerySystemInformation as an undocumented API that can be used to enumerate processes. When called with the SystemProcessInformation class, it returns an array of SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structures describing every process on the system. Unlike the documented Win32 enumeration APIs, this NT-level function bypasses userland wrappers and provides direct kernel-level process data.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot and Its Snapshot Timing Limitation
nodes.description: Source A describes CreateToolhelp32Snapshot as a popular method for enumerating processes, threads, and modules. It takes a snapshot of the system state at a point in time. The material explicitly identifies the major downside: newly created processes after the snapshot is taken will be missed. This timing gap is a fundamental limitation of snapshot-based enumeration compared to continuous monitoring approaches.

nodes.label: Windows Update Agent (WUA) API
nodes.description: Source A identifies WUA (Windows Update Agent) as the update family of APIs used to query hotfixes. The UpdateSearcher object is used to find updates on a system, and UpdateSession creates the search context. This API family provides programmatic access to installed hotfix and patch information, which is useful for vulnerability assessment and recon. The PowerShell cmdlet Get-HotFix queries the Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) class as a higher-level wrapper around the same data.

nodes.label: Native Application Entry Point: NtProcessStartup
nodes.description: Source A identifies NTSTATUS NtProcessStartup(PPEB peb) as the function signature for a native Windows application. Native applications bypass the Win32 subsystem and receive a pointer to the Process Environment Block (PEB) directly. This entry point convention is relevant to direct NT process creation and minimal-footprint implants that avoid the Win32 initialization path.

nodes.label: Reflective DLL Loading from Memory
nodes.description: Source A identifies reflective loading as the preferred method for loading a DLL received over a socket — keeping the DLL in memory and loading it reflectively rather than writing it to disk and calling LoadLibrary. This avoids disk-based artifacts (file creation events, on-disk AV scans) and enables in-memory only execution. The technique requires a reflective loader stub that performs the work of LoadLibrary manually: mapping sections, resolving imports, fixing relocations, and calling DllMain.

nodes.label: C2 Check-In Loop with Jittered Sleep
nodes.description: Source A describes the C2 check-in loop as a while(alive) loop that performs a check-in to the C2 listening post, parses the response for tasks via JSON parsing, executes any tasked commands, stores results, and sleeps for a jittered interval before the next check-in. The check-in serves dual purposes: reporting implant liveness and retrieving pending tasks. Failure to check in at expected times signals compromise or failure. Results can be sent during check-in or independently, and a thread pool may handle encryption and encoding of results before HTTP POST transmission.

nodes.label: Userland Unhooking and Kernel Residual Monitoring
nodes.description: Source A establishes that unhooking userland hooks does not truly blind a security product because a kernel module may still be watching. This means that NTDLL unhooking removes userland introspection (ntdll hook-based detection) but does not affect kernel-level EDR components such as kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks), ETW-TI, or minifilter drivers. The residual kernel monitoring layer continues to receive telemetry regardless of userland hook state.

nodes.label: Windows Service Process Types (SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS)
nodes.description: SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS indicates a service that does not share its address space with other processes — each instance runs in its own process. The alternative, SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS, places multiple services in a single host process (svchost). OWN_PROCESS is selected when an operator needs the service binary to occupy a dedicated address space, which is required for in-memory execution or self-contained payload staging within the service host.

nodes.label: CreateService SCM Registration
nodes.description: CreateServiceA accepts hSCManager, lpServiceName, lpDisplayName, dwDesiredAccess, dwServiceType, dwStartType, dwErrorControl, lpBinaryPathName, and dependencies. It returns an SC_HANDLE to a newly registered service object added to the SCM database. An operator uses OpenSCManager first to obtain the hSCManager handle, then CreateService to register a binary, then StartService to launch it. dwStartType controls boot trigger (SERVICE_DEMAND_START, SERVICE_AUTO_START).

nodes.label: Windows Registry Five-Hive Structure
nodes.description: The Windows Registry is a collection of five hives (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_USERS, HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG), each exposing configuration data. The registry API family (RegOpenKeyEx, RegSetValueEx, RegQueryValueEx) is the canonical interface. HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run is the most commonly used persistence key per Source A, autoloaded at user logon.

nodes.label: Registry Run Key Persistence
nodes.description: The HKCU or HKLM Run key (SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) is the most commonly used registry key for persistence per Source A. Values written under this key are interpreted as executable paths and launched automatically by explorer.exe (HKCU) or winlogon.exe (HKLM) at logon. RunOnce executes once then deletes the value. The technique is noisy — registry modification telemetry and Sysmon E13 capture it directly.

nodes.label: Thread Dispatch States (Ready/Running/Waiting)
nodes.description: Windows threads occupy at least nine states; the three operational ones are Ready (queued for dispatch, not on a CPU), Running (executing instructions during its quantum slice), and Waiting (blocked on an event or object signal). Only Ready threads are dispatched by the scheduler. A thread is in the Running state specifically during its quantum slice. The Waiting state is the prerequisite for alertable APC delivery — a thread must transition through a Wait with ALERTABLE set before user-mode APCs drain from its queue.

nodes.label: Kernel-Resident Thread Object
nodes.description: When a new thread is created, the thread object resides in system (kernel) space, not user space or the process handle table. The ETHREAD/KTHREAD structures are kernel objects. User-mode code receives a handle to this kernel object via the process handle table, but cannot directly dereference the object — all access goes through NT syscalls. This placement constrains user-mode thread-context manipulation to the NtGetContextThread/NtSetContextThread syscall interface and prevents direct memory patching of thread state.

nodes.label: APC Queue In-Quantum Routine Dispatch
nodes.description: The APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when the thread enters its quantum. User-mode APCs are delivered when the thread transitions to an alertable wait (SleepEx with ALERTABLE, WaitForSingleObjectEx, etc.). Kernel APCs are delivered regardless of alertable state. Early Bird injection queues an APC before the thread begins executing its real entry point, causing the APC routine to run first. Context and Event objects do not provide this dispatch path.

nodes.label: Thread Context (Legitimate vs Malicious)
nodes.description: Thread context is the saved CPU register state (RIP, RSP, general-purpose registers, segment registers, FPU/XMM state) for a thread, accessed via GetThreadContext/SetThreadContext or the NT equivalents. Legitimate use includes debuggers suspending and inspecting threads, and fibers saving/restoring state across cooperative switches. Malicious use includes thread hijack injection: suspend target thread, overwrite RIP with payload address, resume — the thread begins executing injected code in its original process context with its original token.

nodes.label: Process Integrity Levels (System/High/Medium/Low)
nodes.description: Each process token carries a mandatory integrity level (System, High, Medium, Low, AppContainer). Process Explorer displays these levels: wm10gon.exe runs at System (kernel-equivalent trust), explorer.exe at Medium (standard user), procexp64.exe at High (elevated admin). Processes cannot write to higher-integrity objects. UAC splits Medium (filtered admin) from High (full admin) — the boundary UAC bypass techniques cross. Token theft (TokenThief) often targets a System-integrity token from a process like winlogon or lsass.

nodes.label: Windows Access Token Structure
nodes.description: An access token describes the security context of a process or thread — user SID, group SIDs, privileges (SeDebugPrivilege, SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege), integrity level, and logon session. Primary tokens are assignable to new processes; impersonation tokens can be attached to threads. Token theft duplicates a victim's token (via DuplicateTokenEx) and applies it with CreateProcessAsUser or SetThreadToken. SeDebugPrivilege permits opening any process for token extraction, including lsass and winlogon.

nodes.label: Process Monitor (ProcMon) Defensive Telemetry
nodes.description: Process Monitor captures real-time file, registry, process, thread, and network I/O activity with call stacks for every operation. Source A uses ProcMon in Lab 1.2 to demonstrate how defenders observe application behavior — the same telemetry defenders use to detect registry writes (persistence), file drops (dropper artifacts), and process spawns (service launch). ProcMon's filter highlights registry Run key writes, SCM service install calls, and suspicious file opens during token theft — the operations T-017 and T-021 techniques perform.

nodes.label: Fileless / In-Memory Execution
nodes.description: In-memory execution is code execution not backed by a file on disk — the payload resides entirely in process memory as MEM_PRIVATE or MEM_IMAGE-mapped shellcode or a reflective PE. Source A frames this as the operational counter to on-disk AV scanning. The trade-off is memory-resident detection: scanners like Moneta and PE-sieve specifically hunt for code regions that lack on-disk backing. Dropping to disk brings filesystem telemetry risk; staying in memory brings memory-scan risk.

nodes.label: Suspended Process Creation State Without Hooks
nodes.description: A process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED enters the suspended state before its initial thread executes, before ntdll's LdrInitializeThunk runs, and before any user-mode hooking layer (ntdll inline hooks installed by EDR) has been applied to the new process address space. Source A identifies this suspended stage as the window in which no hooks are implemented. Techniques that queue an APC for execution during the suspended state (Early Bird, Early Cascade) operate before EDR hooks land in the new process.

nodes.label: Risk of Dropping Capability to Disk
nodes.description: Source A frames dropping a capability (DLL, EXE, shellcode) to disk on a target with an unknown security product as risking both detection (AV signature scan) and loss of capability (quarantine/deletion). The 'all of the above' framing in the review answer indicates both outcomes are operationally equivalent failures. This risk drives the entire class of file-less execution techniques that keep payloads in memory or use delete-pending/section-mapped execution paths.

nodes.label: IFEO Debugger Key Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence via the Image File Execution Options registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>.exe with a Debugger value naming an attacker executable. When the target executable is launched, the OS transparently launches the attacker executable instead, passing the target's original command line as an argument. Source A Lab 4.3 (IFEOPersisto) covers this variant, distinct from the SilentProcessExit variant.

nodes.label: SilentProcessExit Monitoring Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence and process-monitoring via the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\<process>.exe registry key with ReportingMode and MonitorProcess values. When the monitored process exits, WerFault.exe launches the configured MonitorProcess executable. Source A identifies SilentProcessExit as a registry key that can watch for process termination and process creation, functioning as an event-driven persistence trigger activated by the exit of a specific process rather than a fixed schedule.

nodes.label: WMI Extrinsic vs Intrinsic Events
nodes.description: Intrinsic WMI events fire immediately when an instance of a WMI class is created, modified, or deleted (e.g., __InstanceCreationEvent). Extrinsic events are produced by an event provider on a specific occurrence (e.g., Win32_ProcessStartTrace) and must be polled at some interval because the provider raises them asynchronously. Source A review questions ask which event types must be polled, with extrinsic being the canonical answer; intrinsic events do not require polling because the CIM repository raises them in real time.

nodes.label: Egress vs Peer-to-Peer C2 Listeners
nodes.description: Source B distinguishes egress listeners (beacon reaches the team server across a network boundary, typically HTTP/S to the internet) from peer-to-peer listeners (beacon chains through another compromised host, e.g., SMB or TCP peer-to-peer). The HTTP egress listener is described as the majority-of-the-time listener, with peer-to-peer used for pivoting through segmented networks or when direct egress is blocked. Exposing port 50050 directly to the internet is identified as an OPSEC failure; VPN or SSH tunnel access is recommended for remote operators.

nodes.label: Security Descriptor Viewing via sc.exe
nodes.description: Source A review questions identify sc.exe as the command-line utility for viewing an object's security descriptor (via sc sdshow). A security descriptor encodes the owner SID, group SID, DACL (discretionary access control list), and SACL (system access control list) for a securable Windows object — service, file, registry key, etc. cmd.exe and tasklist.exe do not expose security descriptor content; sc.exe's sdshow/sdset subcommands are the canonical service-security-descriptor tool.

nodes.label: Service Control Manager Hidden Service
nodes.description: A Windows service can be hidden from typical enumeration by manipulating Service Control Manager database entries so that standard listing APIs do not return the record. Techniques include deleting the service registry entry while keeping the binary loaded, or modifying DisplayName, ImagePath, and Description to mimic legitimate services, evading sc query and Get-Service enumeration.

nodes.label: Suspended Process Pre-Initialization Window
nodes.description: A process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED begins life before its main thread has executed LdrInitializeThunk, before ntdll.dll has been hooked by EDR products, and before any DLLs in the IAT have been loaded. This pre-initialization window is the rationale for techniques such as process hollowing and Early Bird APC injection that queue work to the suspended thread so the payload runs before userland EDR hooks are in place.

nodes.label: Capability Staging Operational Security
nodes.description: Operational principle that capability DLLs and tools should not be written to disk on systems where the deployed security product is unknown. Dropping a capability to disk risks both losing the capability via quarantine or deletion and detection by static signature or behavioral monitoring. Reflective in-memory loading is the preferred alternative when transporting capability DLLs over sockets.

nodes.label: _EPROCESS Kernel Process Object
nodes.description: The _EPROCESS structure is the kernel object representing a process. Microsoft treats it as opaque to user mode. Notable members shown in the Source A WinDbg dump include Pcb (the embedded _KPROCESS at offset 0x0), ProcessLock at 0x438, UniqueProcessId at 0x440, ActiveProcessLinks (a LIST_ENTRY at 0x448), and RundownProtect at 0x458. The structure is approximately 0xa40 bytes on the build shown. Enumeration APIs and tools such as Get-Process and tasklist walk the ActiveProcessLinks list rather than querying a fixed table.

nodes.label: ActiveProcessLinks DKOM Process Hiding
nodes.description: Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) attacks unlink a target _EPROCESS from the doubly-linked ActiveProcessLinks list maintained by the kernel. Once unlinked, the process disappears from standard enumeration tools (Get-Process, tasklist, EnumProcesses, CreateToolhelp32Snapshot) because those tools walk the list rather than scanning kernel memory directly. The attack requires kernel-mode write access. The Source A material treats this as the canonical kernel-level counterpart to user-mode process hiding such as PEB unlink.

nodes.label: Process and Thread Access Rights
nodes.description: Process and thread handles carry access masks that gate what operations can be performed on the underlying object. The rights relevant to offensive tradecraft per the Source A material include PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (all possible process rights), THREAD_ALL_ACCESS (all possible thread rights), PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS (create a child process from this process), PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD (create a thread in the process — required for CreateRemoteThread), and PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE (duplicate a handle out of the process). GetCurrentProcess and GetCurrentThread return pseudo-handles for the calling process and thread, respectively.

nodes.label: Leaked Handle Exploitation
nodes.description: Handles are considered leaked when an application fails to close them after use. Source A shows that handles leaked to high-privilege objects such as a SYSTEM process with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS can be enumerated by an attacker using Process Explorer or Sysinternals handle.exe and then abused for shellcode injection via VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread against the leaked handle. The pattern is a privilege-escalation primitive that bypasses the need to call OpenProcess with the desired access.

nodes.label: Programmatic Service Hiding via DACL
nodes.description: Windows services can be hidden from standard service enumeration by modifying the discretionary access control list (DACL) on the service object so that the Service Control Manager and standard enumerators are denied read access. Source A contrasts a manual approach against a programmatic approach using Windows security APIs to alter the service object's permissions, hiding the service while retaining its ability to start and persist across reboots.

nodes.label: EnumProcesses Process Enumeration API
nodes.description: EnumProcesses is a documented Psapi function that returns an array of process identifiers on the system. The function signature takes an output DWORD buffer, a buffer size, and a pointer that receives the number of bytes returned. It is the simplest of the documented enumeration APIs but returns only PIDs — no process name, session, parent, or other metadata. Additional information must be obtained by opening a handle to each PID via OpenProcess and querying attributes individually.

nodes.label: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Enumeration API
nodes.description: CreateToolhelp32Snapshot produces a snapshot of processes, threads, heaps, and modules. The process enumeration variant is commonly used in malware because it returns more detailed information than EnumProcesses (PID, parent PID, process name, module list) in a single iteration via Process32First and Process32Next. Source A identifies it as 'perhaps one of the more common APIs used in malwarez for process enumeration.'

nodes.label: WTSEnumerateProcessesEx Cross-Session Enumeration
nodes.description: WTSEnumerateProcessesEx queries process information from the Terminal Services subsystem and returns a count plus detailed per-process information including the session identifier associated with each process. Unlike EnumProcesses, it can query remote systems and enumerate processes across multiple local sessions. The session field enables the operator to select injection targets in a different logon session, which Source A calls cross-session process injection.

nodes.label: Windows Update Agent UpdateSearcher Object
nodes.description: The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API exposes COM objects for querying installed patches and available updates. UpdateSession creates an UpdateSearcher, whose Search method returns a SearchResult containing the matching updates. The Source A material identifies UpdateSearcher as the WUA object used to find updates on a system, and Get-HotFix as the PowerShell cmdlet that queries the Win32_QuickFixEngineering WMI class for installed hotfixes. Together these support patch-gap analysis during post-exploitation reconnaissance.

nodes.label: Host Survey Tool Pattern
nodes.description: Source A frames the host survey tool as the developer's primary post-exploitation deliverable after initial access: a tool that gathers OS, process, patch, and security-product information to decide whether to continue operations. The pattern is the operational precursor to selection of injection targets, persistence placement, and C2 staging. The host survey output drives go/no-go decisions based on observed defensive controls.

nodes.label: NetUserEnum API and USER_INFO Levels
nodes.description: NetUserEnum (Netapi32.dll) retrieves information about all user accounts on a local or remote system. The level parameter selects the USER_INFO structure returned: level 0 returns account names only, level 10 returns name/comment/auth flags, level 20 returns extended info including last logon. The returned buffer must be freed with NetApiBufferFree. The function accepts a remote servername parameter enabling domain-wide enumeration.

nodes.label: GetUserNameA and Impersonation Token Behavior
nodes.description: GetUserNameA returns the username of the current thread or process token. When called from a thread impersonating a client, the function returns the impersonated user's name rather than the process owner. The lpBuffer and pcbBuffer parameters follow the standard pattern where the caller provides a buffer and a pointer to its size; if the buffer is too small the function fails and returns the required size in pcbBuffer.

nodes.label: Windows Service Process Archetypes
nodes.description: Windows defines three service hosting models: special process (no GUI, runs in background), shared service (multiple services share address space in a single svchost.exe — if one service crashes they all crash), and isolated service (hosted in its own svchost.exe without sharing address space). The SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS flag indicates a service that does not share its address space with other services; SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS indicates shared svchost hosting.

nodes.label: Task Scheduler COM Enumeration Interfaces
nodes.description: Scheduled task enumeration on legacy Task Scheduler v1.0 uses COM via CoInitialize followed by CoCreateInstance of the TaskScheduler CLSID. The ITaskScheduler::Enum method returns an IEnumWorkItems enumerator; IEnumWorkItems::Next then retrieves task name strings in batches. This COM path avoids spawning schtasks.exe or at.exe, leaving no process-creation telemetry for the enumeration step.

nodes.label: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE Subkey Hierarchy
nodes.description: HKLM is the root key holding systemwide configuration. Major subkeys: BCD00000000 (boot entries), COMPONENTS (Component-Based Servicing state), HARDWARE (enumerated hardware description), SAM (account password database — restricted access requiring SYSTEM), SECURITY (security policy and LSA secrets — restricted), SOFTWARE (non-boot-critical systemwide configuration and third-party app settings), SYSTEM (boot-critical configuration with a maintenance copy of the last known good control set).

nodes.label: HKLM\SAM Subkey (Security Accounts Manager)
nodes.description: The SAM subkey under HKLM stores the local account password database as hashed credentials. Direct access is restricted to the SYSTEM principal; even Administrators cannot read it in-flight without impersonating SYSTEM or extracting the hive offline. The material identifies this as the credential store targeted by tools that dump SAM via registry save or in-memory hash extraction.

nodes.label: HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA (HKPD) Programmatic-Only Access
nodes.description: HKPD is unique among registry root keys because it cannot be viewed via regedit.exe — it must be accessed programmatically via RegQueryValueEx. Performance counters from system components or server applications appear here, but the data is not actually stored in the registry; it is provided on demand by external perfmon providers. The material notes Pdh.dll functions are a preferred alternative for retrieving performance data.

nodes.label: Registry Value Types (REG_DWORD, REG_BINARY, REG_SZ)
nodes.description: Registry values can be one of 12 types but three dominate: REG_DWORD (32-bit number or boolean), REG_BINARY (raw data — used for values exceeding 32-bit or encrypted material), and REG_SZ (Unicode or ANSI string used for names, paths, file names, type identifiers). The type determines how the byte payload is interpreted when the value is read back via RegQueryValueEx or enumerated via RegEnumValue.

nodes.label: RegNotifyChangeKey Registry Watchdog
nodes.description: RegNotifyChangeKey signals a caller when a registry key or its values change. The material notes it only signals that a change occurred — it does not report what changed, requiring the caller to re-read the key to identify the delta. Implants use it as a watchdog to detect post-installation events such as antivirus product installation or tampering with the implant's own persistence keys. The material cautions against polling too frequently.

nodes.label: RegEnumValue Iteration Pattern
nodes.description: RegEnumValue retrieves one value under an open registry key per call, indexed by dwIndex. The standard pattern initializes dwIndex to 0, calls the function, increments, and repeats until ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS is returned. The lpValueName buffer receives the value name; lpcchValueName receives the character count on return. The function is declared in WinReg.h and returns LSTATUS.

nodes.label: HKLM\SYSTEM Last Known Good Control Set
nodes.description: The SYSTEM subkey under HKLM holds boot-critical configuration. Modifying it can render the system unbootable, so Windows maintains a maintenance copy known as the Last Known Good control set, selectable at boot. This allows administrators to revert to a working configuration if a change breaks the boot sequence. The control set structure is what persistence mechanisms that target boot-time drivers or services must respect.

nodes.label: FindFirstFile / FindNextFile Directory Walk
nodes.description: Directory enumeration in Win32 uses FindFirstFile to open a find handle against a path spec (typically with a wildcard) and FindNextFile to iterate subsequent matches. A recursive walk from the system root visits every file and directory reachable to the caller's permissions, yielding software inventory, document inventory, and operator-tooling discovery. The material notes a recursive walk from the root can take a while but can yield significant survey information.

nodes.label: Registry Virtualization (WoW64 Redirect)
nodes.description: 32-bit applications running under WoW64 on a 64-bit Windows system are transparently redirected from HKLM\Software to HKLM\Software\WOW6432Node for many writes. This redirection enables legacy 32-bit installers to persist settings without modification while the native 64-bit view remains clean. The material notes this affects registry survey tooling because a 32-bit survey tool sees a different registry view than a 64-bit tool querying the same logical paths.

nodes.label: APC Queue and Thread Quantum Processing
nodes.description: The APC queue is the mechanism Windows uses to schedule routines for execution when a thread enters its quantum. User-mode APCs require the target thread to be in an alertable wait state to drain; kernel APCs bypass this constraint. This is the dispatch primitive Early Bird, Early Cascade, and threadless APC injection variants all rely on — the difference is the timing and mechanism of queue insertion.

nodes.label: Thread Object Kernel-Space Residency
nodes.description: When a new thread is created, the thread object (ETHREAD/KTHREAD) resides in system (kernel) space — not user space, not the process handle table. The handle table holds references to kernel objects but the object body itself is in the kernel's paged/nonpaged pools. This means user-mode scanners cannot directly enumerate thread internals without handle-mediated access, which affects how injection techniques must locate thread state and APC delivery targets.

nodes.label: Integrity Levels and UAC Gating
nodes.description: Windows Mandatory Integrity Control assigns processes Low, Medium, or High integrity levels. Standard user processes run at Medium-IL with only SeChangeNotify enabled by default; an elevated process (right-click → Run as Administrator, consent via UAC prompt) runs at High-IL with a substantially larger disabled-but-present privilege set (SeDebug, SeImpersonate, SeTcb, etc.) that can be enabled on demand via AdjustTokenPrivileges. Process Explorer exposes integrity level per-process. The UAC prompt is the gate separating Medium from High-IL — bypassing it (T-021) is the prerequisite for accessing High-IL privilege sets.

nodes.label: OpenProcessToken API
nodes.description: OpenProcessToken takes a ProcessHandle, DesiredAccess mask, and outputs a TokenHandle. The desired access mask (TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, TOKEN_QUERY, TOKEN_DUPLICATE, TOKEN_ALL_ACCESS) determines what subsequent operations are permitted — AdjustTokenPrivileges requires TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, DuplicateTokenEx requires TOKEN_DUPLICATE. Has a BOOL return type; failure modes are silent unless GetLastError is consulted. This is the entry point for every token theft and privilege adjustment workflow.

nodes.label: SCM Service Startup Housekeeping
nodes.description: When the Service Control Manager starts a service, it performs five housekeeping steps: (1) check the service account information against LSASS, (2) load the user profile for the service account, (3) create the service process in suspended state (effectively a process-hollowing-like start), (4) map the service binary, (5) resume execution from the suspended state. This suspended-start sequencing is what allows service-based persistence to inject and aligns with how legitimate services bootstrap — operators creating malicious services must conform to this contract or the service will fail to start.

nodes.label: QueryServiceConfig and Unquoted Binary Path Vulnerability
nodes.description: QueryServiceConfigA returns a QUERY_SERVICE_CONFIGA structure containing the service binary path (lpBinaryPathName). When a service path contains spaces and is unquoted (e.g., C:\Program Files\My Service\svc.exe), Windows attempts to execute progressively-qualified intermediates (C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\My.exe) before the actual binary. A writable directory in that path prefix becomes a privilege escalation vector by placing a malicious binary at the unquoted intermediate location. SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS access is required on the handle.

nodes.label: ChangeServiceConfig Binary Path Modification
nodes.description: ChangeServiceConfigA accepts an optional lpBinaryPathName parameter that, when supplied, replaces the configured executable for an existing service. This is a persistence-by-modification primitive: rather than registering a new service (which generates a service-install event), the operator re-points an existing, already-authorized service at a malicious binary. The companion ChangeServiceConfig2 manages service triggers, enabling trigger-based activation rather than auto-start, reducing persistence footprint. Both APIs return BOOL.

nodes.label: StartServiceCtrlDispatcher and SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY
nodes.description: StartServiceCtrlDispatcher receives a SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY array mapping service names to their ServiceMain functions (LPSERVICE_MAIN_FUNCTION). The dispatcher connects the service process to the SCM and routes incoming start requests to the matching ServiceMain. For a single-service binary the table has one entry plus a {NULL, NULL} terminator; multi-service shared-process binaries register multiple entries. Failure to call StartServiceCtrlDispatcher at process start causes the SCM to mark the service as failed-to-start.

nodes.label: ServiceMain and RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx
nodes.description: ServiceMain (called by the dispatcher when the service starts) is responsible for registering a control handler via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerExA, initializing SERVICE_STATUS global state (dwServiceType=SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS, dwWaitHint, dwServiceSpecificExitCode), and beginning service work. The handler is the callback invoked by SCM for control requests (STOP, PAUSE, INTERROGATE). Mismanagement of SERVICE_STATUS transitions is a common reason malicious services fail or trigger SCM alerts.

nodes.label: SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS Isolation
nodes.description: Specifying SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS as the service type indicates the service runs in its own dedicated process rather than sharing a host (svchost, services). Shared-process services crash when a co-resident service crashes — a reliability problem for malicious services. OWN_PROCESS isolation plus a configured failure action (restart on failure) produces a self-healing service that survives crashes and restarts without operator intervention, which is desirable for resilience but increases per-service process-count telemetry.

nodes.label: CreateService API as Persistence Primitive
nodes.description: CreateService() is the underlying API invoked by both sc.exe and the PowerShell service cmdlets (New-Service, Install-Service). It accepts SCManager handle, service name, display name, service type, start type, error control, binary path, load order group, dependencies, account, password. The name passed must match the name registered via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx in the binary. Using CreateService directly (rather than sc.exe) avoids spawning a child process under the implant's parent, reducing process-tree telemetry.

nodes.label: Anonymous Pipes IPC
nodes.description: Anonymous pipes are unnamed IPC primitives restricted to parent-child process relationships, are local-only (cannot traverse the network), and are one-way (a single end cannot both read and write). They have lower overhead than named pipes and are commonly used for stdin/stdout redirection of spawned child processes. Their parent-child binding makes them useful for staged loader→implant handoff but unsuitable for arbitrary interprocess or cross-host communication.

nodes.label: Named Pipes: Duplex and Network Capable
nodes.description: Named pipes are named IPC primitives that can be used between unrelated processes, support duplex (bidirectional) communication on a single pipe end, and — when the Server service (LanmanServer) is running — become accessible over the network to remote systems. This makes named pipes a transport substrate for both local IPC and remote C2 channels. The Server-service dependency is a deployment-environment consideration: hosts with the service disabled cannot receive remote pipe connections.

nodes.label: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue Registry Watchdog
nodes.description: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue signals a caller when registry changes occur matching a filter mask (REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_NAME for subkey create/delete, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_ATTRIBUTES, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_LAST_SET for value create/modify/delete, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_SECURITY). The REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC flag (Windows 8+) decouples the notification from the calling thread, so the wait does not need to be drained by the originating thread. The hKey handle must have REG_NOTIFY access. Excessive polling is discouraged in favor of event-triggered notification.

nodes.label: Primary and Impersonation Token Distinction
nodes.description: A primary token is assigned to a process and represents the process's security context for object access checks; an impersonation token is temporarily attached to a thread to act in another security context. Token theft operations (e.g., TokenThief pattern) duplicate a primary token from a higher-privilege process and either assign it to a new spawned process (CreateProcessWithTokenW) or attach it as impersonation to the calling thread (ImpersonateLoggedOnUser). The distinction governs which token APIs are valid for the operation.

nodes.label: Windows Named Pipe Duplex IPC
nodes.description: Named pipes in Windows are duplex, can be used between unrelated processes, and are accessible over the network when the server service is running. A pipe server creates instances via CreateNamedPipe; pipe clients connect via CreateFile or CallNamedPipe using the \\.\pipe\<name> convention. Anonymous pipes by contrast are unidirectional and cannot operate over the network.

nodes.label: Fileless Memory-Resident Reboot Constraint
nodes.description: Memory-resident payloads do not survive system reboot because RAM is flushed. Source A identifies this as the primary disadvantage of fileless malware: machines reboot for updates, power failure, or user action, and the implant loses initial access. This makes some form of disk-dropped or registry-stored persistence practically unavoidable for long-term presence.

nodes.label: PE-sieve Memory Scanner (Hasherzade)
nodes.description: PE-sieve is a user-mode memory scanning tool by Hasherzade that scans a process and can dump implants, detecting 'all kinds of injection methods' per Source A. It works by comparing in-memory module layouts against on-disk PE files and flagging discrepancies such as modified.text sections, unbacked executable regions, and hollowed modules.

nodes.label: Moneta Memory Scanner (forrest-orr)
nodes.description: Moneta is a user-mode Windows memory analysis tool by forrest-orr, similar in purpose to PE-sieve. Source A lists it alongside PE-sieve and Volatility as a memory forensics tool that can identify in-memory implants even when on-disk AV does not catch them.

nodes.label: Volatility Memory Forensics Framework
nodes.description: Volatility, from the Volatility Foundation, ingests full memory dumps and provides numerous plugins for analyzing process memory, loaded modules, and injected code. Source A notes that almost everything an implant does on a Windows system can be logged by something and that motivated memory analysts remain a detection risk even when on-disk scanning is bypassed.

nodes.label: Registry Run Key Autostart Persistence
nodes.description: The Run key under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run is the most-used persistence mechanism by APTs including APT28 and Emotet per Source A. HKLM requires admin privileges; HKCU does not. The method is trivially detected by SysInternals AutoRuns but is favored for simplicity.

nodes.label: Registry RunOnce / RunOnceEx Persistence
nodes.description: RunOnce and RunOnceEx registry keys execute a process once and then delete the registry entry, minimizing persistence artifacts. Source A frames this as good for short-term operational goals and bad for long-term presence. HKLM version runs as admin; HKCU version is recommended as an initial downloader until a more reliable persistence method is established.

nodes.label: AppInit_DLLs Registry-Driven DLL Loading
nodes.description: When the registry value LoadAppInit_DLLs (REG_DWORD) is enabled under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows, every newly created user-mode process linked against user32.dll loads the DLLs listed in AppInit_DLLs (REG_SZ, comma-separated). Source A cites APT39, CherryPicker, and T9000 as users. Requires admin privileges to modify HKLM.

nodes.label: AppCert DLLs Process-Creation Hook
nodes.description: AppCert DLLs is a registry-driven mechanism where Windows checks the registry for DLLs that must be loaded into a process when certain Create* API calls are invoked, including CreateProcess and WinExec. Like AppInit_DLLs it requires HKLM modification (admin). Source A lists it as a MITRE ATT&CK autostart location detectable by SysInternals AutoRuns.

nodes.label: Disk Artifact Placement Tradecraft
nodes.description: When an implant must drop to disk for persistence, Source A recommends placing the binary in user-trafficked folders (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Temp, App Data, Program Files, SysWow64, System32, OneDrive) to blend in. Operators should avoid being the first or last file in a directory listing because that position attracts analyst attention during folder review.

nodes.label: Service Control Manager (SCM) Failure Determination
nodes.description: The Service Control Manager is the authority for service lifecycle. SCM considers a service failed when the service terminates without reporting SERVICE_STOPPED, or when the Win32ExitCode member of the SERVICE_STATUS structure does not indicate ERROR_SUCCESS. SCM then consults the service's configured SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS to determine the response. Services that do not answer to SCM are promptly terminated.

nodes.label: SERVICE_STATUS Structure and Win32ExitCode
nodes.description: The SERVICE_STATUS structure is reported by a service to SCM and includes the dwCurrentState (e.g., SERVICE_STOPPED) and dwWin32ExitCode members. SCM uses these to determine whether the service has failed: a non-SERVICE_STOPPED state on termination or a non-ERROR_SUCCESS Win32ExitCode triggers the configured failure actions.

nodes.label: Service Security Descriptor and SDDL Concealment
nodes.description: Each service has a security descriptor stored by SCM, viewable via sc.exe sdshow <service> and writable via sc.exe sdset <service> <SDDL>. The SDDL string defines DACL and SACL ACEs that determine which SIDs can enumerate, query, or control the service. By stripping standard users (IU, SU) and interactive (BA) query permissions from the DACL, the service disappears from Get-Service output and sc.exe query enumeration without requiring a kernel driver or API hook. Joshua Wright's SDDL pattern applies to several SIDs simultaneously.

nodes.label: Service ImagePath, binPath, and FailureCommand Values
nodes.description: ImagePath is a Registry value holding the absolute path to the service binary on disk and any arguments passed to it. binPath is the SCM-facing property that typically matches ImagePath. FailureCommand (set via SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS.lpCommand) is executed by SCM when the service is determined failed. All three can be modified via sc.exe config or the ChangeServiceConfig2 API to redirect service execution to an attacker-controlled binary or to trigger execution on service failure.

nodes.label: WMI Event Subscriptions for Persistence
nodes.description: WMI permanent event subscriptions combine an event filter (e.g., system startup, user logon) with an event consumer (CommandLineEventConsumer, ActiveScriptEventConsumer) to execute arbitrary commands on event trigger. Source A lists WMI Event Subscriptions as a persistence module alongside services, IFEO, and Registry keys. The vault does not currently document WMI-based persistence.

nodes.label: Run / RunOnce / RunTwice Registry Persistence Keys
nodes.description: The Run and RunOnce Registry keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run execute specified programs at user logon or system startup. Source A identifies Run as the most commonly used key for persistence (over RunOnce and RunTwice). Modifying HKLM-hosted Run keys requires Administrator privileges. The vault's T-017 card does not list Run-key persistence as a discrete layer.

nodes.label: ChangeServiceConfig2 API and SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS
nodes.description: ChangeServiceConfig2 modifies service configuration parameters beyond what ChangeServiceConfig covers. Called with SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS, it accepts a SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONSA structure to set the dwResetPeriod, lpRebootMsg, lpCommand, and lpsaActions for a service. Source A's implementation pattern zeros the struct with SecureZeroMemory, sets dwResetPeriod=INFINITE, lpCommand to the attacker payload (e.g., 'ping C2'), cActions=0, lpsaActions=NULL.

nodes.label: HKLM Hive Modification Privilege Requirement
nodes.description: Modifying Registry keys in the HKLM hive requires Administrator privileges. Source A review material explicitly contrasts User, Admin, and Guest roles and identifies Admin as the requirement for HKLM key modification. This constrains HKLM-hosted persistence vectors (Run keys, service ImagePath, IFEO, AppInit) to post-privilege-escalation operational stages.

nodes.label: Image File Execution Options Debugger Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence via the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<ProcessName> registry key with a Debugger value. When the target process is launched, Windows redirects execution to the debugger path specified in the value, launching the implant instead of or alongside the original executable. Source A notes this method is primarily effective for EXE files rather than DLLs and recommends targeting boot-early processes such as userinit.exe to guarantee execution on system startup.

nodes.label: Gflags.exe and GlobalFlag Registry Value
nodes.description: Gflags.exe is a Windows SDK tool located at C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64 that enables advanced debugging features by setting the GlobalFlag registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<ProcessName>. Setting GlobalFlag to decimal 512 enables the Silent Process Exit monitoring feature. Source A notes the SDK must be installed to use gflags.exe, though the same registry value can be set programmatically via RegSetValueEx.

nodes.label: WMI Event Subscription Persistence
nodes.description: Persistence achieved by creating WMI event filters (queries that detect system events), event consumers (actions to take when a filter matches), and filter-to-consumer bindings. Source A introduces WMI event filters and subscriptions as triggers for specified actions, describing them as a persistence mechanism where a consumer executes an implant when a monitored event occurs. The architecture involves providers generating events, infrastructure routing them, and consumers acting on them.

nodes.label: HKLM Registry Key ACL Requirements
nodes.description: Registry keys under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, including the IFEO key path and Print\Monitors key path, are protected by ACLs that deny write access to basic users. Source A states that Admin or SYSTEM privileges are required to modify these keys for IFEO persistence, and local administrator is required for port monitor persistence. The SYSTEM account has broad access to HKLM keys. This permission requirement is a limiting factor for both persistence methods.

nodes.label: Boot-Early Process Target Selection
nodes.description: Operational tradecraft for IFEO persistence involving selection of a target process that executes early in the boot process or is frequently invoked by the user. Source A specifically names userinit.exe as a good candidate because it kicks off when the system is starting up, ensuring the IFEO-configured implant executes automatically on boot without requiring user interaction.

nodes.label: Win32 Registry API Set for Persistence
nodes.description: The Win32 registry API functions RegOpenKeyExA, RegCreateKeyExA, and RegSetValueEx provide programmatic access to create and modify registry values for persistence. Source A describes these as an alternative to the reg.exe command-line utility for implementing IFEO persistence, enabling the implant to set the Debugger, GlobalFlag, ReportingMode, and MonitorProcess values directly without spawning a child process.

nodes.label: Kernel-Mode EDR Monitoring
nodes.description: EDR products may implement kernel-mode monitoring components that continue to observe process behavior even when userland ntdll hooks have been removed. Source A states that unhooking does not truly blind a security product because a kernel module may still be watching. This means NTDLL unhooking only addresses the userland introspection layer; kernel-mode components remain active and detect injection, memory protection changes, and other suspicious operations regardless of userland hook status.

nodes.label: Userland NTDLL Hooks
nodes.description: EDR products install inline hooks in ntdll.dll's.text section to intercept NT API calls before they transition to the kernel. Source A describes these hooks as providing introspection into process behavior. Unhooking restores the original ntdll.text bytes, removing this userland monitoring layer. The material explicitly notes that this only blinds userland introspection, not kernel-mode monitoring.

nodes.label: C2 Check-in and Beaconing Pattern
nodes.description: The operational cycle structuring implant-to-C2 communication described across Source A units 25-34. An initial call-home signals the implant's existence and provides system information. Periodic check-ins at randomized intervals with jitter report status and receive tasking. Missed check-ins may indicate compromise or failure. The C2 LP issues tasks during check-in responses. The implant parses JSON responses, assigns unique task IDs via UuidCreateSequential, executes tasks, stores results in memory or encrypted files, formats them as JSON with encryption and encoding, and returns them via HTTP POST either during the next check-in or immediately.

nodes.label: WMI Intrinsic and Extrinsic Events
nodes.description: WMI events are categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic. Intrinsic events fire on changes to the standard WMI model, such as __InstanceCreationEvent when a new WMI object instance is created. Extrinsic events are not tied to WMI model changes and include RegistryKeyChangeEvent for registry modifications. Event filters use WQL (WMI Query Language) to specify trigger conditions, such as filtering for specific process names like notepad.exe.

nodes.label: Service Hiding from SCM
nodes.description: A technique to conceal a malicious Windows service from system view after installation. Source A Lab 4.4 instructs developing code to hide a service after it has been installed, using Win32 APIs. The material notes there are multiple approaches but identifies the most straightforward as using proper Win32 APIs to manipulate service visibility.

nodes.label: Leaked Handle Exploitation for Injection
nodes.description: Windows handles are leaked when an application fails to close them after use.
