The Windows object manager exposes typed kernel objects including Process, Thread, Section, Token, Mutex, Key, Desktop, Event, and File. Each object has a standardized header with type-specific sub-headers; generic services (CloseHandle, DuplicateHandle, WaitForSingleObject, query/set security) operate uniformly across types while create/open/query services are type-specific. The WinObj utility enumerates all live object types and instances.
contents.concept:executive-file-object-and-handle:
# Executive File Object and Handle Table Model

CreateFile transitions through Kernelbase.dll into the NtCreateFile system call, which constructs an executive file object in kernel space and returns a process-relative handle. The handle table maps small integer handles to kernel object pointers, enabling cross-process handle duplication and the object-centric access control model that injection and handle-blocking techniques operate against.
contents.concept:eprocess-kprocess-structure:
# EPROCESS and KPROCESS Process Objects

CreateProcess triggers kernel-side creation of process objects in system space, represented by EPROCESS (executive process) wrapping KPROCESS (kernel process) structures. The kernel maintains all process objects on a doubly-linked list, which is the same list queried by WTSEnumerateProcessesEx, EnumProcesses, and the kernel's PsActiveProcessHead walker used by rootkits and detection tools.
contents.concept:cross-session-process-injection:
# Cross-Session Process Injection via WTSEnumerateProcessesEx

WTSEnumerateProcessesEx returns per-process WTS_PROCESS_INFO structures including SessionId, PID, and process image name. Unlike EnumProcesses which yields only PIDs, this API lets an implant enumerate processes across terminal-service sessions and select targets outside its own session, enabling cross-session injection paths that bypass session-scoped defensive controls.
contents.concept:com-wua-update-session:
# COM-Based Windows Update Agent API Pattern

The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API is entirely COM-based. Threads must call CoInitialize before instantiating COM objects; the IUpdateSession interface is obtained via CoCreateInstance against the CLSID and supports search/download/install/uninstall operations. This pattern exemplifies how COM classes are registered, instantiated, and dispatched via the registry-resolved class store — the same mechanism COM hijack persistence abuses by re-registering CLSID to a malicious in-proc server.
contents.concept:win32-error-handling-model:
# Windows API Error Return Value Taxonomy

Win32 API functions signal failure through inconsistent return types: BOOL returns FALSE, LSTATUS returns non-zero (ERROR_SUCCESS is 0), HRESULT encodes severity/facility/code in a 32-bit bitfield checked via SUCCEEDED/FAILED macros, and HANDLE returns NULL or INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE. GetLastError retrieves the per-thread last-error code and must be captured immediately before any intervening call overwrites it. FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM resolves numeric codes to human-readable strings.
contents.concept:findfirstfile-recursive-walk:
# FindFirstFile/FindNextFile Recursive Directory Walk

Directory enumeration begins with FindFirstFileA returning a search HANDLE and populating a WIN32_FIND_DATA structure; FindNextFile continues enumeration and FindClose releases the handle. lpFileName supports wildcards (* and ?) for pattern matching. Recursive directory walks combine FindFirstFile with depth-first traversal using. and.. filter exclusion, enabling an implant to enumerate filesystems for files of interest such as credentials, documents, or staged payloads.
contents.concept:hresult-bitfield-layout:
# HRESULT 32-bit Severity/Facility/Code Layout

HRESULT is a 32-bit value laid out as S|R|C|N|r|Facility|Code, where bit 31 (S) is severity (0=success, 1=failure), R/C/N/r are reserved facility-code bits including an NT-mapped-status indicator, the Facility field identifies the originating subsystem (FACILITY_NULL, FACILITY_RPC, FACILITY_DISPATCH, FACILITY_WIN32, etc.), and the Code field holds the actual error number. SUCCEEDED(hr) tests (hr >= 0); FAILED(hr) tests (hr < 0).
contents.concept:pe-file-format-architecture-agno:
# PE Format as Architecture-Agnostic Container

The Portable Executable format, defined in winnt.h, is architecture-agnostic: the same container layout (DOS header → NT headers → section table → sections) describes both PE32 (32-bit, Magic 0x10B) and PE32+ (64-bit, Magic 0x20B) images. The format covers executable images (EXE, DLL) and object files (COFF). The internal structure is complex, with multiple layered structures a parser must traverse in order.
contents.concept:image-file-header:
# IMAGE_FILE_HEADER Structure

The IMAGE_FILE_HEADER sits inside the NT headers and contains Machine, NumberOfSections, TimeDateStamp, PointerToSymbolTable, NumberOfSymbols, SizeOfOptionalHeader, and Characteristics. NumberOfSections drives the loop that walks the section table, and SizeOfOptionalHeader tells the parser how far to skip to reach the section table. These two fields are essential for any custom PE parser or loader.
contents.concept:image-optional-header64:
# IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 (PE32+)

The 64-bit optional header begins with Magic (0x20B for PE32+), followed by linker version, SizeOfCode/InitializedData/UninitializedData, AddressOfEntryPoint, ImageBase, SectionAlignment, FileAlignment, DllCharacteristics (CFG, ASLR, DEP flags), SizeOfStackReserve/Commit, SizeOfHeapReserve/Commit, and a DataDirectory array of IMAGE_NUMBEROF_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES entries. The DataDirectory entries for IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT and IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT are the bridge to resolving named exports and imports.
contents.concept:image-export-directory:
# IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY and RVA-Based Export Resolution

The IMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY (40 bytes) contains NumberOfFunctions, NumberOfNames, AddressOfFunctions (RVA to function pointer array), AddressOfNames (RVA to name pointer array), and AddressOfNameOrdinals (RVA to ordinal array). NumberOfFunctions may exceed NumberOfNames because some functions are exported only by ordinal. To resolve a named export: binary search AddressOfNames for the target name, use the index into AddressOfNameOrdinals to get an ordinal, then use that ordinal as the index into AddressOfFunctions to get the function RVA. This is the mechanism a manual GetProcAddress implementation replicates.
contents.concept:manual-getprocaddress-flow:
# Manual GetProcAddress via Export Directory Walk

Instead of calling GetProcAddress — which is itself hooked by EDRs and leaves static call traces — an operator parses the export directory of an already-resolved module (typically ntdll, kernel32, kernelbase) and walks AddressOfNames → AddressOfNameOrdinals → AddressOfFunctions to locate the target function's RVA. This produces a function pointer without invoking the loader's API surface and is the basis for PEB-walker-style dynamic API resolution used to bootstrap syscall stubs and NT API bindings.
contents.concept:windows-file-enumeration-pattern:
# Filesystem Enumeration Triplet (FindFirstFile/FindNextFile/FindClose)

Directory enumeration on Windows uses three Find* APIs: FindFirstFileW opens a search handle and returns the first match, FindNextFileW iterates subsequent matches in a do/while loop checking its BOOL return, and FindClose releases the search handle. The WIN32_FIND_DATAW structure returned per entry contains file attributes, timestamps, size, and long/short names. This pattern is the primitive for host-survey file discovery, exfil targeting, and persistence-target location.
contents.concept:windows-registry-enumeration-pat:
# Registry Access API Pattern

Registry operations follow a fixed sequence: RegOpenKeyExW returns an HKEY with KEY_READ/KEY_WRITE/KEY_SET_VALUE access (returns LSTATUS, errors resolved via FormatMessage with FORMAT_MESSAGE_FROM_SYSTEM), RegQueryInfoKey retrieves subkey count and max-name sizes for buffer allocation, RegEnumKeyEx iterates subkeys (loop ends on ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS), RegQueryValueExW queries named values using a two-call pattern (size query then value read), and RegCloseKey releases the handle. This pattern is the primitive for registry-based persistence target discovery and host-fingerprint collection.
contents.concept:iphlpapi-network-statistics:
# IPHLPAPI Network Reconnaissance Primitives

GetIpStatistics fills a MIB_IPSTATS structure with dwDefaultTTL, dwInReceives, dwInHdrErrors, dwInAddrErrors, dwForwDatagrams, dwOutRequests, dwOutDiscards, dwOutNoRoutes, and routing/fragment counters — the data netstat surfaces. GetAdaptersAddresses accepts Family (AF_INET/AF_INET6/AF_UNSPEC), Flags, Reserved, AdapterAddresses, and SizePointer, returning an IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES linked list covering both IPv4 and IPv6. These IPHLPAPI calls are the documented primitives for replicating ipconfig/arp/netstat without spawning those binaries.
contents.concept:language-diversity-signature-avo:
# Language Diversity for Signature Avoidance

The material explicitly recommends varying implementation language (C, C++, Rust, C#, Go) and even compiler choices across a toolset to produce diverse static signatures, reducing the value of static signature coverage against any single toolchain. Rust is called out as increasingly used for offensive tools and shellcode. The operational principle: a toolset built entirely in one language/compiler produces a coherent signature surface that one detection rule can collapse.
contents.concept:pe-data-directory-array:
# PE DataDirectory Array

The IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER64 contains a 16-entry DataDirectory array. Each entry is an IMAGE_DATA_DIRECTORY with VirtualAddress (DWORD RVA) and Size (DWORD) fields. Index 1 is the Import Directory. The RVAs are relative to the image base and must be added to the loaded module base to yield an absolute virtual address at runtime. WinDbg's dx command can dump the entire array and individual entries for inspection.
contents.concept:image-import-descriptor:
# IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR Structure

Each imported DLL is described by an IMAGE_IMPORT_DESCRIPTOR with OriginalFirstThunk (RVA to Import Lookup Table / INT), TimeDateStamp (0 = not bound, -1 = bound), ForwarderChain (-1 = no forwarders), Name (RVA to DLL name string), and FirstThunk (RVA to Import Address Table / IAT). The loader walks this structure during process initialization to resolve and patch imported function addresses into the IAT, which is the same structure a PEB walker parses to locate function pointers in a loaded module.
contents.concept:thread-context-struct:
# CONTEXT Structure and Context Switching

Each thread has a CONTEXT structure holding its saved register state — including R11 through R15, Rip, and the LastExceptionToRip/LastExceptionFromRip fields — captured when its quantum ends or it is preempted by a higher-priority thread. The processor swaps these contexts to schedule threads. CR3 (page-table base) governs per-process address space and swaps as part of the broader scheduling state. GetThreadContext and SetThreadContext expose CONTEXT to user mode and are the primitives used to suspend a thread, modify Rip to redirect execution to shellcode, and resume — the material frames this as the malicious use of thread context.
contents.concept:windows-scm-service-model:
# Windows Service Control Manager Programming Model

A Windows service binary must implement a service entry point, a ServiceMain function, and a ServiceControlHandler. The process connects to the SCM via StartServiceControlDispatcher, registers its handler via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx, and reports state transitions through SetServiceStatus using a SERVICE_STATUS struct (dwServiceType, dwServiceSpecificExitCode, dwWaitHint). SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS indicates the service runs in its own address space rather than sharing a host (svchost). The handler must respond to SCM control requests. This contract is the surface an implant binary implements to masquerade as a legitimate service and receive SCM-launched execution at boot.
contents.concept:createservice-parameters:
# CreateService Parameter Semantics

CreateService parameters control the service's runtime identity: lpBinaryPathName is the full executable path and may include trailing command-line arguments; lpLoadOrderGroup is optional (NULL acceptable); lpdwTagId is only meaningful for kernel driver services; lpDependencies is an optional list of dependent service names; lpServiceStartName is the logon account under which the service executes; lpPassword is the account password. These parameters determine how the SCM loads and authenticates the service at boot, which determines the privilege context and persistence characteristics of an implant deployed as a service.
contents.concept:anonymous-pipes-ipc:
# Anonymous Pipes (CreatePipe) for IPC

Anonymous pipes are created with CreatePipe, which returns separate read and write handles, each access-restricted to its respective operation. They are local-only (cannot traverse the network), one-way (cannot read and write at the same end), and restricted to related processes (parent/child). Handle inheritance or DuplicateHandle propagates pipe ends to child processes, typically via stdin/stdout redirection. They carry lower overhead than named pipes, which is the tradeoff for the restricted flexibility.
contents.concept:named-pipes-ipc:
# Named Pipes for IPC

Named pipes support duplex (bidirectional) communication and can traverse the network, unlike anonymous pipes. They are accessible to unrelated processes — not just parent/child — and are created with CreateNamedPipe. The additional flexibility carries higher overhead than anonymous pipes, which is the tradeoff operators evaluate when choosing between the two IPC mechanisms for staged payload communication or implant-to-host channels.
contents.concept:appinit-dlls-registry:
# AppInit_DLLs Registry Key

The HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs registry value causes specified DLLs to be loaded into any process that loads user32.dll. Unit 1 (InitToWinit bootcamp challenge) frames AppInit_DLLs as a DLL execution foothold. Modern Windows restricts loading based on the RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs flag and architecture matching, but the mechanism remains a documented persistence and injection vector distinct from the techniques in T-017.
contents.concept:addmonitor-port-monitor-api:
# AddMonitor Port Monitor API

The AddMonitor API (winspool.drv) installs a port monitor under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors. Unit 35 explicitly distinguishes AddMonitor from plausible-but-wrong candidate names (CreateNewMonitor, AddNewMonitor) as the correct API for installing a new port monitor. Port monitor DLLs load into the spoolsv.exe service context at service startup and survive reboot, making this a recognized persistence vector not present in the vault's T-017.
contents.concept:silentprocessexit-registry-monit:
# SilentProcessExit Registry Key

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit can be configured to trigger actions when a process exits, including attaching a debugger or launching a monitoring process. Unit 36 lists SilentProcessExit and Debugger as registry keys usable to watch for process termination. Defenders use the key for forensic monitoring; attackers abuse the same key as a persistence trigger that fires when a sacrificial process exits.
contents.concept:pe-sieve-defensive-scanner:
# PE-sieve Memory Scanner

PE-sieve is a defensive scanning tool that inspects running processes for malware artifacts and injection indicators. Unit 29 (Lab 1.1) positions PE-sieve as a 'hackerverse' GitHub project that catches injection methods. The scanner is used during payload development to verify which injection techniques leave detectable artifacts in process memory (unbacked executable regions, modified.text sections, replaced PE images).
contents.concept:ms-dos-header-byte-layout:
# MS-DOS Header Byte Layout

Unit 30 frames the byte following the MS-DOS header as 0x00 (the correct answer among 0x00, 0x90, 0x5A). This byte is the start of the MS-DOS stub program that follows the IMAGE_DOS_HEADER in a PE file. The stub is a minimal DOS program that typically prints 'This program cannot be run in DOS mode' and exits; its first byte is part of the stub's instruction sequence. The unit reinforces that PE parsing begins with recognizing the DOS header and stub before the e_lfanew pointer transitions to the NT headers.
contents.concept:itaskscheduler-com-interface:
# ITaskScheduler COM Enumeration Interface

Unit 11 frames ITaskScheduler as the COM interface used to create enumeration objects for scheduled tasks (vs. IUnknown or 'IBelieve'). ITaskScheduler is the legacy COM interface exposed by the Windows Task Scheduler service; modern code uses ITaskService, but ITaskScheduler remains the documented interface for task enumeration on legacy Windows and is referenced in T-017's schtask persistence work.
contents.concept:process-creation-hook-states:
# Process Creation Pre-LdrInitializeThunk Window

Unit 22 frames a review question about process-creation states (Suspended, Terminated, Running) and the stage at which hooks are not yet implemented. In a CREATE_SUSPENDED process, the loader (LdrInitializeThunk) has not yet executed, so userland EDR hook DLLs have not been injected into the new process. This pre-LdrInitializeThunk window is the basis for T-012 Early Cascade APC injection and informs T-014 NtCreateUserProcess and T-015 PPID Spoofing tradecraft.
contents.concept:sal-source-annotation-language:
# SAL Source Annotation Language

Unit 8 frames SAL as standing for 'Source-code annotation language' (vs. 'Structured annotation language' or 'Silent analysis language'). Unit 24 (Lab 1.5: Safer with SAL) notes that SAL annotations make code more understandable. SAL is Microsoft's annotation syntax for expressing buffer sizes, pointer validity, and call contracts on Windows API functions, used in headers like winnt.h to communicate contract expectations between callers and callees.
contents.concept:ms-dos-pe-stub:
# MS-DOS Header and DOS Stub

The MS-DOS header (MZ) at the start of every PE file is followed by the DOS stub. The unit review quiz identifies the byte following the MS-DOS header as 0x90, which corresponds to the first instruction of the DOS stub program that typically prints 'This program cannot be run in DOS mode.'
contents.concept:thread-scheduling-quantum:
# Thread Scheduling Quantum

The default thread scheduling quantum on Windows Server editions is the subject of an Source A/Source A unit review question with options of 2, 8, and 12 clock cycles. The quantum governs how long a thread runs before the scheduler preempts it, which is relevant to APC draining behavior, thread-hijack timing windows, and sleep-obfuscation frame windows.
contents.concept:token-theft-lab:
# Token Theft / Impersonation Lab

Source A Lab 3.5 'TokenThief' covers stealing and reusing Windows access tokens for privilege escalation and lateral movement. The vault currently has no dedicated technique card for token impersonation, theft, or MakeToken-equivalent tradecraft despite its central role in red team operations.
contents.concept:windows-object-manager-handle-mo:
# Windows Object Manager Handle/Object Model

Windows represents system resources (files, processes, threads, registry keys, sections, tokens, mutexes, desktops) as data structures in system address space. The kernel creates the object at the request of a user application and returns a handle to the caller; user space never touches the object directly. The Source A material notes over 4,000 executive object types, many not reachable through documented Win32 APIs. This separation is why cross-process operations require handle duplication and why object types such as Process and Section gate injection primitives.
contents.concept:executive-object-types:
# Executive Object Types (Process, Thread, Section, Token, Mutex, Key, Desktop)

The Windows executive implements object types that gate operations relevant to offensive tradecraft: Process objects own a virtual address space controlling one or more Thread objects; Section objects back shared memory and file mappings used by mapping injection and module loaders; Token objects hold the security profile that governs what a thread/process can access; Mutex objects serialize access; Key objects reference registry data; Desktop objects bound window-station-scoped UI operations. The full type list is visible via the WinObj utility from Sysinternals.
contents.concept:createfile-to-ntcreatefile-flow:
# CreateFile to NtCreateFile to Executive Object Flow

A Win32 API call such as CreateFile transitions to NtCreateFile, which causes the object manager to allocate an executive File object in system space and return a handle to the user-mode caller. The same flow applies to CreateThread, CreateEvent, CreateToolhelp32Snapshot, and the broader Create* family (nearly 100 functions). The transition crosses the user/system boundary via the NT syscall dispatcher, which is the layer EDRs hook and the layer indirect-syscall techniques (T-001, T-002, T-003) bypass.
contents.concept:dll-search-order:
# Windows DLL Search Order

When a process resolves a DLL by name without a full path, Windows searches in a documented order: (1) the directory containing the configuration file, (2) the current directory of the process, (3) the system directory returned by GetSystemDirectory, (4) the Windows directory returned by GetWindowsDirectory, and (5) directories listed in %PATH%. The current-directory slot (2) is the basis for DLL search-order hijacking and is constrained by SafeDLLSearchMode and the DllCharacteristics IMAGE_DLLCHARACTERISTICS_DYNAMIC_BASE-equivalent flags. This order governs where a proxy or hijacked DLL must be placed to load in preference to the legitimate module.
contents.concept:findfirstfile-directory-walk:
# FindFirstFile/FindNextFile Directory Enumeration

FindFirstFileA/W initializes a directory walk by returning a search handle and populating a WIN32_FIND_DATA structure with the first matching entry. The wildcard-capable lpFileName parameter accepts patterns such as C:\Windows\System32\*.dll. Subsequent FindNextFile calls drain the search until no more matches exist, at which point the handle must be closed with FindFindClose to avoid handle leaks. The ANSI variant should be avoided for non-English paths because it cannot represent characters outside the system code page.
contents.concept:hinstance-hmodule-interchangeabi:
# HINSTANCE and HMODULE Handle Equivalence

In the Win32 API, HINSTANCE and HMODULE are interchangeable handle types that both reference a loaded module's base address. The equivalence exists for historical 16-bit Windows compatibility, where an instance handle and a module handle were distinct concepts. Modern 32-bit and 64-bit Windows treats GetModuleHandle and GetInstanceHandle results as the same value, which matters for PEB-walking code that resolves module bases via either API.
contents.concept:securable-object-acl:
# Securable Object ACL and Security Descriptor

Objects exposed to user mode are protected by access control lists (ACLs) and security descriptors. The Object Manager acts as a gatekeeper, checking ACLs before granting access to querying or manipulating processes. Kernel-internal objects not exposed to user mode do not require the same ACL protection. Process Explorer can enumerate and display handles to securable objects, making handle-based tradecraft visible to defenders who inspect open handles and their associated access masks.
contents.concept:eprocess-kprocess:
# _EPROCESS and _KPROCESS Structures

Process creation via CreateProcess triggers the kernel to construct a process object in system space. The _EPROCESS is the executive process object containing the PEB pointer, image filename, and security context. The _KPROCESS is the kernel process object (embedded within _EPROCESS) containing scheduler-related fields such as thread list and quantum. The kernel tracks all processes by linking _EPROCESS objects in a doubly-linked list, which is the mechanism underlying process enumeration and PEB-based module walking.
contents.concept:ntquerysysteminformation-enum:
# NtQuerySystemInformation with SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION

NtQuerySystemInformation is the NT-level API for enumerating system information. When called with the SystemProcessInformation class, it returns an NTSTATUS and populates a buffer of SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structures, each describing a process's image name, PID, thread count, handle count, and CPU time. This API underlies tools that perform process enumeration without relying on the Win32 Toolhelp API (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot) or WTS session enumeration (WTSEnumerateProcesses).
contents.concept:windows-service-pack:
# Windows Service Packs and Hotfix Bundling

Service packs bundle groups of hotfixes so that a user can apply all prior fixes in a single update without installing each one sequentially. Different service pack levels change the set of patched vulnerabilities on a target, which affects exploit compatibility — implant developers and LPE technique authors must account for the target OS version and service pack when selecting or adjusting exploits, including those sourced from frameworks like Metasploit.
contents.concept:wua-patch-enumeration:
# Windows Update Agent (WUA) APIs for Patch Enumeration

The Windows Update Agent APIs provide a programmatic interface for querying installed patches and hotfixes. Red team tools can use WUA APIs to retrieve patch information during reconnaissance, determining which vulnerabilities remain unpatched on a target system and therefore which exploits or LPE techniques are viable.
contents.concept:windows-thread-scheduling:
# Windows Dispatcher Thread Scheduling

Windows uses a preemptive, priority-based dispatcher. Threads are selected for execution but may never actually run because a higher-priority thread preempts them. Each thread runs for a quantum measured in clock cycles. When a high-priority thread leaves its waiting state and becomes ready, it preempts any currently-running lower-priority thread in its quantum. Server and endpoint configurations use different default quantum values.
contents.concept:apc-alertable-wait:
# APC Alertable Wait State

An Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) is a mechanism that allows an I/O operation to complete later, providing asynchronous execution. APC objects are placed into a thread's queue and execute only when the thread enters an alertable waiting state. A thread that never enters an alertable wait will not drain its user-mode APC queue, causing queued APCs (including injection payloads) to remain pending without error.
contents.concept:svchost-service-hosting:
# svchost.exe Shared vs Isolated Service Hosting

Windows services are special processes with no GUI and no direct user interaction. A shared service hosts multiple services sharing address space within a single svchost.exe process; if one crashes, they all crash. An isolated service is hosted in svchost.exe without sharing its address space with other services. The hosting model determines blast radius and affects which services can be safely targeted for process injection.
contents.concept:ntfs-directory-entry-table:
# NTFS Directory Entry Table

NTFS tracks directories and child directories in a directory tree. Each directory has a table holding entries with the names of files contained in that directory. The directory entry table, combined with hard links, forms the structural basis for NTFS file system navigation. APIs include CreateDirectory, CreateDirectoryEx, and CreateDirectoryTransacted.
contents.concept:regqueryinfokey-enumeration:
# RegQueryInfoKey Registry Enumeration API

RegQueryInfoKey (declared in Winreg.h, returns LSTATUS) retrieves detailed information about a registry key: class string, number of subkeys (lpcSubKeys), number of values (lpcValues), max subkey name length (lpcbMaxSubKeyLen), max value name length (lpcbMaxValueNameLen), and max value data size (lpcbMaxValueLen). Used to enumerate registry structure before walking subkeys and values.
contents.concept:regnotifychangekeyvalue-watchdog:
# RegNotifyChangeKeyValue Registry Watchdog

RegNotifyChangeKeyValue (declared in Winreg.h, returns LSTATUS) is used to be notified when specific changes happen to a registry key. Parameters include hKey (must have REG_NOTIFY access mask), bWatchSubtree (Boolean for recursive watch), dwNotifyFilter (which change types trigger notification), hEvent (optional event handle), and fAsynchronous (Boolean for async vs sync notification). Functions as a sentry for registry persistence writes.
contents.concept:thread-entrypoint-initial:
# Process Initial Thread and AddressOfEntryPoint

A thread is an entity within a process that can be scheduled for execution — the smallest unit of execution tied to a process. Every process has at least one initial thread that kicks off image code execution at the image's AddressOfEntryPoint. This initial thread and its entry point form the foundation of process startup that injection techniques such as Early Cascade (T-012) intercept before LdrInitializeThunk.
contents.concept:securable-objects-security-attri:
# Securable Objects and SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES

Windows securable objects — files, processes, threads, registry keys — carry a security descriptor that the SRM checks on every access request. The Create* Win32 API family (CreateProcess, CreateThread, CreateFile) accepts a SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure pointer to attach a descriptor at object creation. OpenProcess and similar handle-acquisition APIs trigger an access check against this descriptor, returning ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED when the caller lacks the requested access rights in the DACL.
contents.concept:sddl-security-descriptor-string-:
# Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL)

SDDL is a string format consumed by ConvertSecurityDescriptorToStringSecurityDescriptor and ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptor. The string encodes Owner (O:), Primary Group (G:), DACL (D:), and SACL (S:) sections, each with control flags. ACE strings follow the form (AceType;;AccessMask;;;Sid) — e.g. (A;;RPWPCCDCLCSWRCWDWOGA;;;S-1-0-0) is an ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE_TYPE granting READ_CONTROL|WRITE_DAC|WRITE_OWNER|GENERIC_ALL to the NULL SID.
contents.concept:port-monitors-print-spooler-brid:
# Windows Port Monitors (spoolsv.exe to Kernel Bridge)

Windows print monitors come in two types: language monitors and port monitors. A port monitor bridges user-mode spoolsv.exe (the Windows Print Spooler service) to a kernel-mode port driver. Port monitors are implemented as DLLs loaded by spoolsv.exe and registered through the Win32 AddPrinter API. Because spoolsv.exe loads these DLLs at service start, registering a malicious port monitor DLL achieves persistence with SYSTEM-equivalent privileges in the spooler process.
contents.concept:cim-wmi-schema-model:
# Common Information Model (CIM) and WMI Schemas

CIM is an industry-standard object-oriented model WMI uses to represent systems, processes, devices, and applications. CIM defines three class levels: Core (general managed objects), Common (system, application, network extensions), and Extended (technology-specific). Classes are grouped into schemas: the CIM Schema contains classes prefixed CIM_ (Core and Common definitions), and the Win32 Schema contains classes prefixed Win32_ (Extended CIM specific to the Win32 environment). Developers can author custom classes in either schema.
contents.concept:ntdll-vs-win32k-syscall-division:
# NTDLL Native vs WIN32K.SYS GUI Syscall Split

Windows exposes two syscall surfaces. NTDLL.DLL provides native syscalls (NtOpenProcess, NtCreateProcess) that enter the kernel and executive directly. WIN32.DLL (user32/gdi32) provides GUI syscalls (NtUserOpenClipboard, NtUserCloseClipboard) that route into WIN32K.SYS, a separate kernel-mode subsystem. A console/native thread makes only NTDLL syscalls; a GUI thread additionally issues WIN32K syscalls. Syscall dispatch techniques operating on ntdll gadgets do not cover the WIN32K syscall surface.
contents.concept:dll-loadlibrary-getprocaddress-r:
# Win32 DLL Loading APIs (LoadLibrary / GetProcAddress)

Windows provides LoadLibrary/FreeLibrary for explicit DLL load and unload, and GetProcAddress for symbol address resolution. These are the Win32 parallels to Linux dlopen/dlclose/dlsym. Both PE (Windows) and ELF (Linux) export symbols that the loader resolves at runtime. Manual resolution techniques (PEB walking, export table parsing) reimplement GetProcAddress behavior without invoking the API directly, avoiding IAT-based detection of which functions a module imports.
contents.concept:windows-object-header-body:
# Object Header and Object Body Schema

Every executive object has a standardized header containing type, name, directory, security descriptor, handle count and list, and optional subheaders; the object body is unique to the object type. This separation is what lets the Object Manager service any object with generic operations. The handle count and list in the header track every process handle table entry that currently references the object — relevant when a process object's handle count is inspected by EDR or when an injector relies on the handle list for duplication.
contents.concept:windows-handle-mechanics:
# Handle Value Mechanics

Handle values are always a multiple of 4, never zero, with the first valid handle being 4. A handle is a per-process table index (scaled by 4 on use) into the process handle table, which is itself managed by the Object Manager. Source A notes handle values are 32-bit or 64-bit depending on architecture. The 'multiple of 4' property encodes the table slot index in the low bits and historically left room for inherit/protect/audit attributes in the low two bits — relevant when an operator inspects or forges handle values.
contents.concept:securable-objects-acl-sd:
# Securable Objects, ACLs, and Security Descriptors

Objects exposed to user mode must be protected. Each securable object carries its own access control list (ACL) and security descriptor that dictates what actions a querying process may perform. The system acts as gatekeeper, performing access checks on every Open*/NtOpen* call. Source A notes that internal kernel objects not exposed to user mode may not carry the same protections — a distinction operators rely on when reasoning about which objects an EDR's kernel callback can observe.
contents.concept:generic-vs-specific-object-servi:
# Generic vs. Type-Specific Object Services

All objects regardless of type support generic services (Close, Duplicate, Query/Set Security, WaitForSingleObject); each object type additionally exposes type-specific services (Create, Open, Query). CloseHandle works on file, process, thread, event, and key handles alike because the generic dispatch path reads the object header to find the type-specific close routine. This is why a single NtClose syscall retires any handle and why handle-blocking techniques must intercept at the generic layer to be effective.
contents.concept:windows-data-types-handle:
# HANDLE/HMODULE/HINSTANCE Typedef Lineage

Per WinNt.h, HANDLE is a typedef of PVOID (void*). Derived handle types (HKEY, HMODULE, HINSTANCE, HRSRC, LPHANDLE) are all built on this HANDLE base and are technically interchangeable — Source A demonstrates casting HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE directly to PVOID with no functional issue. The convention exists for code clarity, not type safety. HMODULE and HINSTANCE are explicitly interchangeable; this matters when an operator inspects a loader-returned HMODULE in PEB-walking code (T-004) and treats it as a raw pointer for arithmetic.
contents.concept:windows-system-dll-hierarchy:
# System DLL Hierarchy: Ntdll, Kernel32, Kernelbase, User32

Several system DLLs are mapped into nearly every process. Ntdll is the only one strictly required and is mapped by the OS. Ntdll exports functions acting as the gateway to kernel land. Kernel32 re-exports a large number of ntdll functions, with some exports consisting of nothing but jumps or forwarders to ntdll. User32 holds GUI component functions. The material notes that user-mode hooks placed in these DLLs can be bypassed by unloading the system DLLs.
contents.concept:thread-states-windows:
# Windows Thread States: Ready, Running, Waiting

Windows tracks threads in three primary states: Ready (eligible to run but not currently dispatched), Running (currently executing on a logical processor), and Waiting (blocked on a dispatcher object such as an event, semaphore, or alertable wait). Thread-state-dependent injection techniques select threads in Waiting state because their context is stable and their resume semantics are predictable.
contents.concept:thread-scheduling-preemptive-pri:
# Preemptive Priority-Based Thread Scheduling

The Windows dispatcher selects threads for execution under a preemptive, priority-based scheduling model. Higher-priority threads preempt lower-priority ones. This affects injection timing because a hijacked or APC-targeted thread's quantum arrival depends on its priority and the dispatcher's selection, not on a deterministic call from the implant.
contents.concept:thread-creation-internals:
# Thread Creation Internal Flow: NtCreateThreadEx → PspCreateThread

Thread creation converts parameters into flags, adds the client ID and TEB address to an attribute list, determines whether the thread is local or remote, then calls NtCreateThreadEx which initializes user-mode thread context and invokes PspCreateThread. The thread is created initially suspended and later resumed so the dispatcher can schedule it. This suspended initial state is the window during which APC injection payloads are queued before the thread runs.
contents.concept:apc-queue-thread-execution:
# APC Queue as Routine Dispatch Mechanism

Threads process routines queued to their APC queue when they enter their quantum. The APC queue is the mechanism that allows kernel and user-mode code to schedule routine execution on a target thread without direct invocation. APC injection techniques exploit this by queuing payload-bearing APCs to threads that will drain the queue during an upcoming quantum or alertable wait.
contents.concept:securable-objects-security-descr:
# Securable Objects and SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES

Securable objects in Windows carry a corresponding security descriptor. The Create* family of Win32 APIs (CreateProcess, CreateThread, CreateFile, CreateRegistryKey, etc.) accept a pointer to a SECURITY_ATTRIBUTES structure that controls access. Handles returned from these APIs are gated by the security descriptor and the handle table. Process injection and handle-blocking evasion techniques interact with this model when opening remote process handles or denying external handle access.
contents.concept:anonymous-vs-named-pipes-ipc:
# Anonymous and Named Pipes for IPC

Pipes are one of several interprocess communication methods on Windows. Anonymous pipes are local only, one-way, and have less overhead than named pipes. Named pipes support bidirectional and cross-host communication. Implant tradecraft uses pipes for C2 channel multiplexing, localhost relay between staged components, and impersonation token theft via named pipe security descriptors.
contents.concept:cim-class-hierarchy:
# Common Information Model (CIM) Class Hierarchy

WMI uses the industry-standard Common Information Model to represent managed objects in an object-oriented schema. CIM defines three tiers: Core (universal, technology-agnostic primitives), Common (commonly applicable system, process, and device abstractions like Win32_Process), and Extended (vendor- or technology-specific extensions). Understanding the tier hierarchy clarifies which WMI classes are guaranteed across Windows versions and which are vendor-specific.
contents.concept:wql-query-types:
# WQL Data, Event, and Schema Queries

Windows Query Language supports three query classes. Data queries (e.g., SELECT * FROM Win32_NTLogEvent WHERE logfile='System' AND EventCode='4625') retrieve instances. Event queries subscribe to instance lifecycle changes via __InstanceCreationEvent / __InstanceDeletionEvent with a WITHIN polling interval. Schema queries (SELECT * FROM meta_class WHERE __this ISA 'Win32_Process') enumerate class definitions rather than instances. Intrinsic events require explicit polling intervals while extrinsic events fire from provider callbacks.
contents.concept:wmi-intrinsic-vs-extrinsic-event:
# WMI Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Event Model

Intrinsic WMI events are synthesized by the WMI infrastructure from instance changes (creation, modification, deletion) in a CIM repository and must be polled at a defined WITHIN interval — the consumer does not receive them unless it actively queries. Extrinsic events are raised by event providers directly (e.g., Win32_ProcessStartTrace), require no polling interval, and deliver near-real-time. Persistence consumers using intrinsic events incur polling overhead and a maximum delay equal to the WITHIN interval.
contents.concept:wmi-event-subscription-persisten:
# WMI Event Subscription Persistence

WMI permanent event subscriptions achieve persistence by binding an __EventFilter (a WQL trigger condition) to an __EventConsumer (typically CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer) via a __FilterToConsumerBinding instance. All three are stored in the CIM repository and survive reboots. The subscription fires asynchronously whenever the filter condition is satisfied, executing the consumer payload without an attacker-controlled process needing to remain resident.
contents.concept:ifeo-image-file-execution-option:
# Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Persistence

IFEO registry entries under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>.exe allow an attacker to register a Debugger value that is invoked in place of (or in addition to) the target executable. When the system launches the target binary, the debugger path is executed instead, providing a fileless, reboot-surviving persistence trigger tied to legitimate binary launches.
contents.concept:sddl-null-sid-ace:
# SDDL ACE Granting to NULL SID (S-1-0-0)

The SDDL string 'O:AOG:DAD:(A;;RPWPCCDCLCSWRCWDWOGA;;;S-1-0-0)' encodes a DACL with a single ACCESS_ALLOWED_ACE_TYPE entry granting READ_CONTROL | WRITE_DAC | WRITE_OWNER | GENERIC_ALL to the NULL well-known SID (S-1-0-0). Granting rights to NULL SID effectively permits access to subjects with no authenticated identity — a known technique for loosening security descriptors on services, named pipes, or kernel objects to permit anonymous or low-privilege access.
contents.concept:wua-hotfix-enumeration:
# Windows Update Agent (WUA) Hotfix Enumeration

The Windows Update Agent API family is the documented method for querying installed hotfixes, also known as Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) updates. Source A identifies WUA as the correct API family for hotfix enumeration (vs. LUA or FUA), used by offensive operators to enumerate patch level and identify missing security updates for vulnerability selection.
contents.concept:process-enumeration-api-triad:
# Process Enumeration API Triad

Three Win32/NT APIs provide process information from a PID: OpenProcess() returns a handle used for subsequent queries; WTSEnumerateProcessesEx() enumerates all processes in a session with extended info in a single call; NtQuerySystemInformation() with SystemProcessInformation returns a flat buffer of all EPROCESS-linked process records from the kernel. The trade-offs are handle-based access vs. snapshot enumeration vs. native NT buffer walk.
contents.concept:windows-hotfix-qfe:
# Windows Hotfix / Quick Fix Engineering Updates

Windows Hotfixes, also referred to as Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) updates, are Microsoft's mechanism for applying critical fixes to deployed software. They are enumerated via the WUA API family and appear in WMI as Win32_QuickFixEngineering instances. Operators enumerate QFE state to identify missing patches and select viable privilege-escalation or LPE primitives.
contents.concept:thread-quantum-running-state:
# Thread Quantum Slice and Running State

A thread executing during its allocated quantum slice is in the Running state, distinct from Waiting (blocked on a dispatcher object) and Ready (eligible to run but not currently scheduled). The quantum is the time allowance the scheduler grants before preempting the thread for another Ready thread of equal priority. This state distinction matters for injection techniques that target suspended or waiting threads, because a thread in Running state has an actively executing context that cannot be safely modified without synchronization.
contents.concept:anonymous-pipes-windows-ipc:
# Anonymous Pipes (Windows IPC)

Anonymous pipes are a one-way, local-only interprocess communication mechanism with lower overhead than named pipes. Because they cannot span process boundaries on remote machines and lack the kernel namespace registration of named pipes, they are less observable via Sysmon Event ID 17/18 (PipeEvent) and are sometimes used for parent-child implant communication where stealth is preferred over flexibility. They require an inheritable handle to be passed to the child at creation time.
contents.concept:ifeo-persistence:
# Image File Execution Options Persistence

Image File Execution Options is a registry-based persistence mechanism under HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target.exe> where setting the Debugger value to an attacker-controlled path causes any launch of target.exe to invoke the attacker binary instead with the original command line appended. Source A lists IFEO alongside registry keys, services, port monitors, and WMI Event Subscriptions as a Section 4 persistence topic. The technique is detectable via registry monitoring on the IFEO key tree and is privilege-gated to HKLM write access.
contents.concept:extrinsic-vs-intrinsic-events:
# Extrinsic vs Intrinsic Event Polling

Extrinsic events are externally triggered and require the implant to poll at some interval to detect them — examples include file drops, registry changes, or external process creation. Intrinsic events are driven by the implant's own execution state and can be handled synchronously. Source A poses both as event classes that must be polled at some interval, which frames the operational trade-off: tighter polling improves responsiveness but increases the implant's CPU footprint and detection surface; looser polling reduces footprint but risks missing transient signals like short-lived child processes or rapidly deleted staging files.
contents.concept:windows-dispatcher-quantum:
# Windows Dispatcher and Thread Quantum

The Windows dispatcher is a preemptive, priority-based scheduler. Threads are assigned priorities and run for a fixed number of clock cycles called a quantum. A higher-priority thread leaving its waiting state and becoming ready preempts any lower-priority thread currently in its quantum. Thread state transitions between Running, Ready, and Waiting govern when user-mode APCs can be delivered, since APCs require the target thread to enter an alertable wait state.
contents.concept:ethread-kernel-object-residency:
# Thread Object Residency in System (Kernel) Space

Newly created thread objects reside in system (kernel) space, not user space or the process handle table. The ETHREAD/KTHREAD structures are kernel objects managed by the executive. User-mode code interacts with them only through opaque handles returned by NtCreateThreadEx. This residency underpins why thread hijacking, APC queuing, and thread-context manipulation all require NT syscalls and cannot be performed via Win32 userland APIs alone.
contents.concept:concept-pe-sieve:
# PE-sieve Memory Scanner

PE-sieve is an open-source memory scanner that detects injected implants by walking process memory and comparing in-memory module contents against their on-disk counterparts. It flags modified.text sections, unbacked executable regions, and replaced module content. The tool operates from user mode by default and is therefore subject to the same handle-access constraints as EDR userland scanners.
contents.concept:concept-wmi-event-subscription:
# WMI Event Subscription Persistence

WMI Event Subscriptions are a persistence mechanism that combines an EventFilter (a query describing the triggering condition), an EventConsumer (an action to take — typically CommandLineEventConsumer or ActiveScriptEventConsumer), and a FilterToConsumerBinding linking them. The subscription executes asynchronously when the filter condition is met, with no requirement for an interactive logon. Source A lists this as a Section 4 persistence lab.
contents.concept:concept-ifeo-persistence:
# Image File Execution Options Persistence

Image File Execution Options (IFEO) is a registry subtree under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options that supports a Debugger value. When a process matching the IFEO subkey name is launched, the debugger value is executed instead, allowing an attacker to redirect execution to a malicious payload on every invocation of the targeted binary. Source A documents this as Lab 4.3 'IFEOPersist'.
contents.concept:concept-port-monitor-persistence:
# Port Monitor Persistence

Port Monitors are print spooler components registered under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors. A malicious DLL registered as a Port Monitor is loaded by the print spooler service (spoolsv.exe), which runs as SYSTEM, on service start. The technique persists across reboots and runs in a privileged context. Source A lists Port Monitors as a Section 4 persistence topic.
contents.concept:concept-ntdll-unhooking:
# NTDLL Unhooking (Source A framing)

Source A's Section 5 lab 'UnhookTheHook' frames NTDLL unhooking as restoring the ntdll.dll.text section to a clean state to defeat userland API hooks placed by AV/EDR. The course positions this as a prerequisite evasion step before additional AV/EDR bypass techniques are layered on.
contents.concept:concept-amsi-bypass:
# AMSI Bypass (Source A framing)

Source A's Section 5 lab 'AMSI No More' covers bypassing the Anti-Malware Scan Interface. AMSI is a Windows service interface that allows registered AV products to scan script content from PowerShell, VBA, and similar script engines. Bypass approaches typically target amsi.dll in the script host process.
contents.concept:concept-custom-loader:
# Custom Loader Development

Source A's Section 5 opens with custom loader development (Lab 5.1: The Loader) as the foundation for staging shellcode, applying evasion, and establishing C2. The loader is positioned as the host component that integrates subsequent evasion modules (unhooking, AMSI bypass) before the implant calls home.
contents.concept:concept-wtsenum-proctoolhelp-rec:
# WTSEnumProcesses and CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Recon

WTSEnumProcesses enumerates processes on a WTS session (including other sessions on the same host) and returns per-process SID information. CreateToolhelp32Snapshot takes a snapshot of process, thread, heap, and module state. Source A Section 2 covers both as primary recon primitives for implant situational awareness — enumerating processes to identify targets for injection, defense-relevant processes, and adversary tooling already in the environment.
contents.concept:concept-windows-update-agent-rec:
# Windows Update Agent API for Patch Recon

The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API exposes interfaces (notably IWindowsUpdateAgent) that can enumerate installed hotfixes and service packs. Source A identifies WUA as the API family used to query hotfixes, used by implants to determine patch level and infer whether specific privilege-escalation or kernel-exploit paths are viable on a target.
contents.concept:concept-appinit-dlls:
# AppInit_DLLs Registry Persistence

When LoadAppInit_DLLs (REG_DWORD) is set to 1 under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows, every newly created user-mode process linked against User32.dll loads the comma-separated DLLs listed in AppInit_DLLs (REG_SZ). Requires administrative privileges. Documented as used by APT39, CherryPicker, and T9000. Operator must avoid infinite loops where the injected DLL spawns a process that re-triggers AppInit loading.
contents.concept:concept-silent-process-exit:
# Silent Process Exit via GlobalFlag

Configured via Gflags.exe (Windows SDK, located at C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64) or directly via the GlobalFlag registry key. The 'Silent Process Exit' feature monitors an exiting process (the 'Image') and invokes a configured 'Monitor' process. Used as a persistence trigger fired on process termination rather than on system boot or process launch. GflagsX by Pavel Yosifovich provides a modern GUI for managing these flags.
contents.concept:concept-service-imagepath-modifi:
# Service ImagePath/binPath/FailureCommand Persistence

Existing or newly created Windows services can be modified for persistence by altering ImagePath (registry key holding the absolute path to the service binary), binPath (the command-line passed to the service binary), or FailureCommand (executed when the service fails to start or terminates unexpectedly). Modifications performed via sc.exe or the CreateService API. Service modification produces reboot-survivable execution via SCM.
contents.concept:concept-classic-dll-injection:
# Classic CreateRemoteThread DLL Injection

The legacy four-step DLL injection flow documented in Source A: (1) obtain a handle to the target process, (2) allocate memory in the target via VirtualAllocEx, (3) write the DLL path string to the allocated region via WriteProcessMemory, (4) spawn a remote thread via CreateRemoteThread with start address pointing to LoadLibraryA/W. Requires the target process to expose LoadLibrary in its export table.
contents.concept:concept-apc-queue-thread-quantum:
# APC Queue and Thread Quantum Scheduling

Per the Source A review question, the APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when entering their quantum. User-mode APCs drain during alertable waits; kernel APCs drain at IRQL drop. Thread quantum entry provides a scheduling window where queued APCs dispatch — the same window Early Cascade (T-012) targets with pre-LdrInitializeThunk APCs.
contents.concept:concept-win32-find-data:
# WIN32_FIND_DATA Structure

User-mode structure that holds the attributes of a file returned by FindFirstFile/FindNextFile. Distinguished from KUSER_SHARED_DATA (shared user/kernel page containing system time and tick count) and FILE_OBJECT (the kernel-mode structure representing an open file instance). The Source A review answer identifies WIN32_FIND_DATA as the user-mode file-attribute structure.
contents.concept:concept-ms-dos-pe-header:
# MS-DOS / PE Header Layout

PE files begin with an MS-DOS stub. The Source A review question asks what byte typically follows the MS-DOS header — establishing that the operator must recognize the MS-DOS header boundary to navigate to the PE header (e_lfanew field at offset 0x3C points to 'PE\0\0'). Required knowledge for manual PE parsing in injection and module-stomping techniques.
contents.concept:concept-sddl-security-descriptor:
# SDDL Security Descriptor Definition Language

Security Descriptor Definition Language is the language used to describe the security of a Windows object descriptor. The Source A review question confirms SDDL (not ACL or DACL, which are components within a security descriptor) is the descriptive language. sc.exe is the command-line utility for viewing an object's security descriptor.
contents.concept:concept-itask-scheduler-com:
# ITaskScheduler COM Interface

COM interface used to create enumeration objects for scheduled tasks. Source A review question identifies ITaskScheduler (not IUnknown) as the interface called to create a task enumeration object. Relevant to scheduled-task persistence enumeration and creation via COM rather than the schtasks.exe command-line.
contents.concept:concept-kuser-shared-data:
# KUSER_SHARED_DATA

User-readable shared page (fixed virtual address 0x7FFE0000 on x86, 0x7FFE0000 on x64) mapped read-only into every process. Contains system time, tick count, CPU information, and other low-overhead globally-shared values. Distinguished from WIN32_FIND_DATA and FILE_OBJECT in the Source A review question. Useful for system-time queries without syscalls.
contents.concept:concept-thread-object-residency:
# Thread Object Residency in System Space

Per the Source A review question, when a new thread is created the thread object resides in system (kernel) space, not user space and not the process handle table. Thread objects are kernel structures (ETHREAD/KTHREAD) accessible from user mode only through handles. Establishes why thread manipulation requires object-handle access patterns.
contents.concept:apc-queue-thread-quantum:
# APC Queue and Thread Quantum Dispatch

APC queues allow routines to be queued for execution when a thread enters its quantum or alertable wait. Source A identifies the APC queue as the mechanism that lets threads process routines during quantum entry. User-mode APCs require an alertable wait to drain; kernel APCs are not subject to that constraint. This is the scheduling primitive that Early Bird, Early Cascade, and other APC-based injection techniques depend on.
contents.concept:registry-run-keys:
# Registry Run / RunOnce / RunOnceEx Autostart Keys

Run, RunOnce, and RunOnceEx under HKCU and HKLM Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion are the most-used persistence keys across APTs (Source A cites APT28 and Emotet as examples). HKCU keys require no elevation; HKLM keys require Administrator. HKLM variants execute as the receiving context (e.g., SYSTEM for machine-wide Run, Admin for user-targeted HKLM Run). The method is not novel but remains effective because of implementation simplicity and visibility fatigue.
contents.concept:ifeo-debugger-value:
# Image File Execution Options Debugger Value

IFEO is a registry key under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options intended for tracing or debugging a process at startup. Setting the Debugger value on a target subkey causes the specified debugger path to launch instead of the original executable. Source A recommends targeting early-boot processes such as userinit.exe for reliable trigger frequency. The mechanism persists across reboots without modifying the original binary.
contents.concept:scm-service-hiding-sddl:
# SDDL-Based Service Hiding

Services can be hidden from detection by manipulating the Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL) on the service object to deny read or enumerate access to non-privileged queries. Source A documents manual service hiding via SDDL as the closing lab of its services-persistence module, preventing listing tools from surfacing the malicious service entry.
contents.concept:wmi-permanent-subscription:
# WMI Permanent Event Subscription Persistence

WMI permanent subscriptions combine an event filter (__EventFilter), a consumer (typically ActiveScriptEventConsumer or CommandLineEventConsumer), and a binding (__FilterToConsumerBinding) stored in the CIM repository. They survive reboots and execute on configured triggers such as system uptime thresholds, process creation, or failed logon. Source A Lab 4.6 OhMyWMI builds a subscription keyed on system uptime to launch a persistence tool. The configuration persists in the WMI repository rather than on disk as a script file.
contents.concept:create-toolhelp32snapshot-enum:
# CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration

CreateToolhelp32Snapshot with TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS produces a snapshot handle; Process32First and Process32Next iterate PROCESSENTRY32 records exposing process name, PID, parent PID, and thread count. Source A's example passes NULL as the third argument to capture all processes rather than a single one. The handle is checked against INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE on failure. This is the canonical user-mode recon primitive for selecting injection or token-theft targets.
contents.concept:openprocesstoken-handle:
# OpenProcessToken for Token Handle Acquisition

OpenProcessToken takes an OpenProcess handle and a desired access mask, returning a token handle used by subsequent token-manipulation APIs such as DuplicateTokenEx and SetThreadToken. Source A identifies OpenProcessToken() as the API for obtaining a process token handle, distinct from OpenProcess() (process handle) and the non-existent OpenToken().
contents.concept:windows-sockets-callback:
# Windows Sockets for C2 Callback

Source A explicitly names Windows Sockets (Winsock) as the transport for implant callbacks to a C2 listening post, checking in for pending tasks and returning results on subsequent connections. The callback module frames socket selection as one of multiple callback methods the operator chooses among rather than the only option.
contents.concept:p2p-listener-chain:
# Peer-to-Peer Listener Chaining (SMB/TCP)

Source B documents Cobalt Strike peer-to-peer listeners as a method for chaining Beacon communications over SMB or TCP when a compromised host cannot reach the Team Server over HTTP. Each Beacon becomes a relay, extending reach into network-segmented hosts. The listener name persists across lateral-movement Beacon commands, so descriptive naming is operationally important.
contents.concept:hklm-sam-bcd-hives:
# HKLM SAM and BCD Registry Hives

The HKLM hive contains the SAM subkey holding account password hashes and the BCD subkey holding boot configuration entries. Source A surfaces both as high-value registry targets during post-exploitation. SAM extraction requires either SYSTEM access or offline hive parsing; BCD modification can enable boot-time persistence.
contents.concept:in-memory-execution-fileless:
# In-Memory Execution and Fileless Malware

Source A's module summary defines in-memory execution as loading and running payload without touching disk, citing WannaCry and EternalBlue as high-profile examples. Advantages include reduced on-disk artifact footprint; disadvantages include volatility across reboots and exposure to memory-forensics techniques that scan for unbacked executable regions. Memory forensics is identified as the primary defensive counter.
contents.concept:scm-service-attributes:
# Service Control Manager Attributes (Start Type, Service Type, Error Level)

Each Windows service carries Start Type (auto-start, on-demand, disabled), Service Type (own process vs shared svchost grouping), and Error Level (severity and recovery action on failure). Source A emphasizes SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS for malicious services because shared-process hosting causes cascading crashes if a sibling service faults; failure actions can be configured to auto-restart.
contents.concept:service-scm-housekeeping:
# SCM Five-Step Service Startup

When SCM starts a service it executes five housekeeping steps including image load, process creation, ServiceMain dispatch via StartServiceCtrlDispatcher, RegisterServiceCtrlHandler registration, and SetServiceStatus reporting. A service binary must implement ServiceMain, the control handler, and status reporting or SCM will treat the service as failed.
contents.concept:createservice-api:
# CreateService / ChangeServiceConfig API Surface

CreateService is the underlying API for service installation used by sc.exe and PowerShell service cmdlets. ChangeServiceConfig and ChangeServiceConfig2 modify existing services, including lpBinaryPathName and trigger configuration. SERVICE_NO_CHANGE preserves a parameter during partial config edits. Unquoted binary paths in lpBinaryPathName are an explicit privilege escalation vector.
contents.concept:anonymous-vs-named-pipes:
# Anonymous vs Named Pipe IPC Distinction

Anonymous pipes are local-only, one-way, and restricted to parent-child process pairs. Named pipes support duplex communication, can be accessed between unrelated processes, and — with the Server service running — become accessible over the network via \\ComputerName\pipe\PipeName. Named pipes are created with CreateNamedPipe and connected via CreateFile or CallNamedPipe.
contents.concept:thread-state-machine:
# Windows Thread State Machine (Ready/Running/Waiting)

Windows tracks at least nine thread states; Source A focuses on Ready (scheduled, awaiting quantum), Running (executing on a CPU during its quantum), and Waiting (blocked on a synchronization event). Only Ready threads are picked up by the dispatcher. Thread state must be modified during thread hijacking operations.
contents.concept:apc-alertable-wait-quantum:
# APC Queue Dispatch at Quantum Entry

The APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when entering their quantum. User-mode APCs require the target thread to be in an alertable wait state to drain; the dispatcher drains the APC queue as the thread transitions back to Running. This dispatch path is what APC injection techniques queue into.
contents.concept:access-token-primary-impersonati:
# Primary vs Impersonation Access Token

After successful logon, each process receives a primary token containing SID, Logon SID, default DACL, privileges, and a primary/impersonation flag. The security descriptor of the token is checked on access to securable objects. Impersonation tokens are tied to a thread for client-impersonation scenarios. TOKEN_PRIVILEGES (winnt.h) enumerates enabled/disabled privilege state.
contents.concept:medium-il-privilege-auto-enablem:
# Medium-IL Privilege Auto-Enablement Without Elevation

Source A demonstrates that SeTimeZonePrivilege transitions from Disabled to Enabled when SystemSettings.exe changes the time zone, with no UAC prompt — SystemSettings.exe runs at Medium-IL. This illustrates that privilege enablement is distinct from privilege presence; a token may hold a privilege without it being enabled, and Medium-IL processes can enable certain privileges autonomously.
contents.concept:wmi-architecture:
# WMI Architecture (Providers, Infrastructure, Consumers)

WMI is structured into Providers and Objects (data sources, e.g. the Win32 provider enumerating processes), WMI Infrastructure (the WMI Repository and WMI Query Language — WQL), and WMI Consumers (C++, PowerShell, or COM-based clients that query or subscribe to events). Data flows from providers into the repository and onward to consumers.
contents.concept:wmi-intrinsic-extrinsic-events:
# WMI Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Events

Intrinsic WMI events fire on changes to the standard WMI model — e.g. __InstanceCreationEvent when an object is added to the repository. Extrinsic events fire on external conditions not directly tied to model changes — e.g. RegistryKeyChangeEvent. Both event classes are subscribable via WQL filters.
contents.concept:scm-handles:
# SCM Handle Types (SCManager, Service, Database Lock)

Interacting with the SCM requires distinct handle types: SCManager handles for top-level database access, Service handles for per-service operations, and Database lock handles for serialized modification. Handles are required to query (QueryServiceStatusEx, QueryServiceConfig), modify (ChangeServiceConfig), delete, or create (CreateService) service objects.
contents.concept:wmi-permanent-event-subscription:
# WMI Permanent Event Subscription (FilterToConsumerBinding)

WMI permanent subscriptions combine three classes: __EventFilter (the trigger query, e.g. filtering for notepad.exe process creation or system uptime thresholds), __EventConsumer (the action — typically CommandLineEventConsumer for executing a binary), and the FilterToConsumerBinding class that links the two. Permanent subscriptions survive reboot because they are stored in the WMI repository rather than running only in the WMI provider host process.
contents.concept:appcert-dlls-registry:
# AppCert DLLs Registry Loading Mechanism

The AppCert registry key is queried when CreateProcess, CreateProcessAsUser, CreateProcessWithLogon, CreateProcessWithToken, or WinExec is called. Windows examines the key for a list of DLLs that must be loaded into the newly created process. Requires administrative privileges and a system reboot to take effect, and is easily enumerated by Sysinternals AutoRuns.
contents.concept:run-runonce-registry-keys:
# Run / RunOnce / RunOnceEx Registry Keys

The Run key is identified by Source A as 'the most used key for persistence by several APTs' under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM\...\Run. RunOnce and RunOnceEx execute the process once and delete the registry entry, useful for artifact minimization but inadequate for long-term persistence. HKLM variants require Administrator privileges and execute as SYSTEM; HKCU variants are usable by standard users as an initial downloader stage.
contents.concept:service-control-manager-failure-:
# Service Control Manager Failure Contract

The SCM considers a service to have failed when the service terminates without reporting SERVICE_STOPPED status to the SCM, or when the Win32ExitCode member of SERVICE_STATUS does not indicate ERROR_SUCCESS. Services must answer to the SCM and are promptly terminated if they do not. This contract defines the trigger surface for SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS-based persistence.
contents.concept:service-failure-actions-structur:
# SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS Structure

SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONSA defines what takes place after a service failure as determined by SCM. Members include dwResetPeriod (failure count reset window), lpRebootMsg, lpCommand (command executed on failure), cActions, and lpsaActions (array of SC_ACTION structures specifying actions like SC_ACTION_RESTART with delays). Set via ChangeServiceConfig2, this structure can be abused to execute a persistence binary when an attacker-controlled service 'fails' on demand.
contents.concept:memory-forensics-scanners:
# Memory Forensics Scanner Suite (Volatility, PE-sieve, Moneta)

Three memory forensics tools are identified by Source A as the detection surface for in-memory fileless implants: Volatility (full-process memory analysis framework), PE-sieve (scans for PE modules in memory that do not match on-disk images — detects hollowed, injected, and unmapped PE payloads), and Moneta (scans for unbacked executable memory and anomalies). These tools specifically target the memory-resident techniques the dark_crystal framework relies on for execution without disk artifacts.
contents.concept:on-disk-patching-system-dlls:
# On-Disk Patching of System Binaries

Patching binaries on the file system rather than their memory-mapped images enables survival across reboots but introduces cascading risks. Source A flags that patching system files like Ntdll.dll could render the system unstable, that changes are harder to undo than in-memory patches, and that on-disk modifications are detected faster by file integrity monitoring. The technique has a legitimate use case of patching signature-scanning binaries to disable AV capability persistently.
contents.concept:disk-placement-tradecraft:
# Strategic Disk Placement Tradecraft

When a memory-resident implant must drop to disk to survive reboot, placement follows blending rules: candidate directories include Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Temp, AppData, Program Files, SysWOW64, System32, and OneDrive. Operational rules specify not being the first or last file in a folder (which attracts analyst attention), choosing less-browsed directories, and using a limited-feature binary for the disk-resident component to minimize exposure if the binary is captured and reverse-engineered.
contents.concept:sysinternals-autoruns-detection:
# Sysinternals AutoRuns Enumeration Surface

AutoRuns enumerates the Run/RunOnce/RunOnceEx keys, AppInit_DLLs, AppCert DLLs, scheduled tasks, services, and dozens of other autostart extensibility points (ASEPs) in a single consolidated view. Source A explicitly notes that all registry-based persistence methods discussed — Run, RunOnce, AppInit, AppCert — 'should be easily detected using SysInternals AutoRuns,' flagging it as the canonical hunter tool for these vectors.
contents.concept:fileless-reboot-flush-limitation:
# Fileless Reboot Flush Limitation

Memory-resident implants are flushed from RAM on system reboot (power loss, Windows update restart, scheduled maintenance). The limitation is framed by Source A as 'arguably the biggest disadvantage when it comes to fileless malware' — the operational consequence is that pure in-memory execution cannot maintain access across reboots, forcing operators to maintain multiple persistence methods to regain initial access after a power cycle.
contents.concept:implant-drm-protection:
# Implant DRM for Capture Resistance

Source A references the PoC Skrull as an example of 'DRMing' an implant to protect it from analysis if captured on disk. The technique applies creative anti-analysis measures to the dropped binary itself so that even if the disk artifact is captured by defenders, reverse engineering the implant is hindered. This complements but is distinct from the operational goal of avoiding detection in the first place.
contents.concept:windows-service-persistence:
# Custom Windows Service Persistence

Persistence via OpenSCManager + CreateService to install a malicious service that runs under SYSTEM via the Service Control Manager. Source A frames this as the 'perfect action' once admin or SYSTEM privileges are obtained, because services execute at boot under SYSTEM authority and survive reboots.
contents.concept:security-descriptor-definition-l:
# Security Descriptor Definition Language (SDDL)

Microsoft's string format for security descriptors consumed by ConvertStringSecurityDescriptorToSecurityDescriptor and ConvertSecurityDescriptorToStringSecurityDescriptor. SDDL encodes Owner (O:), Group (G:), DACL (D:), and SACL (S:) with control flags (SDDL_PROTECTED, SDDL_AUTO_INHERITED). ACE strings include ace_type (A/D/OA/OD/AU/AL), ace_flags (CI/OI/NP/IO/ID), and rights tokens (GA/GR/GW/GX, RC/SD/WD/WO, KA/KR/KW, etc.).
contents.concept:spoolsv-print-spooler-service:
# spoolsv.exe (Print Spooler Service)

User-mode Windows service (Spooler) that bridges user-mode printer queue management to kernel-mode port drivers. Source A identifies spoolsv.exe as the host process for port monitors — abusing port monitor registration causes spoolsv.exe to load attacker-controlled DLLs at service startup.
contents.concept:ifeo-silentprocessexit-persisten:
# IFEO and SilentProcessExit Registry Persistence

Persistence via HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options. The Debugger value substitutes a target executable's launch with an attacker payload; SilentProcessExit uses GlobalFlag=512 (FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT) plus SilentProcessExit\ReportingMode=1 and MonitorProcess pointing to the attacker payload, triggering execution on target process exit. Source A explicitly notes Admin or SYSTEM is required.
contents.concept:image-file-execution-options-key:
# Image File Execution Options Registry Key

Registry path HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options contains per-executable subkeys. Originally designed for debug/trace hooks (Debugger value swaps the executable launch path), IFEO is also abused for persistence and process redirection. SilentProcessExit subkey triggers process-exit monitoring via the Windows Error Reporting (WER) subsystem.
contents.concept:silent-process-exit-mechanism:
# Silent Process Exit Monitoring Mechanism

Windows mechanism that triggers user-configured actions when a process exits after IFEO GlobalFlag is set. Configured under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit with ReportingMode (1 = launch monitor process, 2 = notify, 4 = dump) and MonitorProcess (path to executable). Implementation routes through RtlReportSilentProcessExit and the Windows Error Reporting service.
contents.concept:globalflag-registry-value:
# GlobalFlag Registry Value (FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT)

The GlobalFlag DWORD value under IFEO\<ProcessName> configures system-wide debug/trace flags for a process. Flag 0x200 (512, FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT) enables the Silent Process Exit monitoring hook — when the target process exits, Windows Error Reporting invokes the configured MonitorProcess. Source A instructs setting GlobalFlag=512 as the IFEO persistence precursor.
contents.concept:security-descriptor-control-apis:
# Security Descriptor Control APIs

Windows APIs in securitybaseapi.h and aclapi.h that programmatically manipulate service/object security descriptors: SetSecurityDescriptorControl, SetNamedSecurityInfo, SetServiceObjectSecurity. Source A contrasts these with manual sc.exe sdset SDDL string authoring, framing the API path as more reliable for automated service-hiding workflows.
contents.concept:admin-system-privilege-gate:
# Admin / SYSTEM Privilege Gate

Access control boundary that prevents non-admin users from writing HKLM\...\Image File Execution Options, HKLM\...\SilentProcessExit, the Services SCM namespace, and the Print Monitors registry path. Source A explicitly lists Admin and SYSTEM as the only effective privilege levels for IFEO persistence — basic users receive ACCESS_DENIED.
contents.concept:ifeo-debugger-key:
# Image File Execution Options Debugger Key

The Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry key (under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options) allows associating a debugger with a target executable. Source A identifies IFEO as a registry key used to watch for process creation — when the target executable is launched, the configured debugger process is invoked instead, enabling both persistence and process creation monitoring.
contents.concept:nt-query-system-information-enum:
# NtQuerySystemInformation for Process Enumeration

Source A identifies NtQuerySystemInformation as an undocumented API that can be used to enumerate processes. When called with the SystemProcessInformation class, it returns an array of SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION structures describing every process on the system. Unlike the documented Win32 enumeration APIs, this NT-level function bypasses userland wrappers and provides direct kernel-level process data.
contents.concept:create-toolhelp-snapshot:
# CreateToolhelp32Snapshot and Its Snapshot Timing Limitation

Source A describes CreateToolhelp32Snapshot as a popular method for enumerating processes, threads, and modules. It takes a snapshot of the system state at a point in time. The material explicitly identifies the major downside: newly created processes after the snapshot is taken will be missed. This timing gap is a fundamental limitation of snapshot-based enumeration compared to continuous monitoring approaches.
contents.concept:windows-update-agent-api:
# Windows Update Agent (WUA) API

Source A identifies WUA (Windows Update Agent) as the update family of APIs used to query hotfixes. The UpdateSearcher object is used to find updates on a system, and UpdateSession creates the search context. This API family provides programmatic access to installed hotfix and patch information, which is useful for vulnerability assessment and recon. The PowerShell cmdlet Get-HotFix queries the Quick Fix Engineering (QFE) class as a higher-level wrapper around the same data.
