contents.concept:native-application-entry:
# Native Application Entry Point: NtProcessStartup

Source A identifies NTSTATUS NtProcessStartup(PPEB peb) as the function signature for a native Windows application. Native applications bypass the Win32 subsystem and receive a pointer to the Process Environment Block (PEB) directly. This entry point convention is relevant to direct NT process creation and minimal-footprint implants that avoid the Win32 initialization path.
contents.concept:reflective-dll-loading:
# Reflective DLL Loading from Memory

Source A identifies reflective loading as the preferred method for loading a DLL received over a socket — keeping the DLL in memory and loading it reflectively rather than writing it to disk and calling LoadLibrary. This avoids disk-based artifacts (file creation events, on-disk AV scans) and enables in-memory only execution. The technique requires a reflective loader stub that performs the work of LoadLibrary manually: mapping sections, resolving imports, fixing relocations, and calling DllMain.
contents.concept:c2-checkin-loop:
# C2 Check-In Loop with Jittered Sleep

Source A describes the C2 check-in loop as a while(alive) loop that performs a check-in to the C2 listening post, parses the response for tasks via JSON parsing, executes any tasked commands, stores results, and sleeps for a jittered interval before the next check-in. The check-in serves dual purposes: reporting implant liveness and retrieving pending tasks. Failure to check in at expected times signals compromise or failure. Results can be sent during check-in or independently, and a thread pool may handle encryption and encoding of results before HTTP POST transmission.
contents.concept:unhooking-kernel-residual:
# Userland Unhooking and Kernel Residual Monitoring

Source A establishes that unhooking userland hooks does not truly blind a security product because a kernel module may still be watching. This means that NTDLL unhooking removes userland introspection (ntdll hook-based detection) but does not affect kernel-level EDR components such as kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks), ETW-TI, or minifilter drivers. The residual kernel monitoring layer continues to receive telemetry regardless of userland hook state.
contents.concept:windows-service-types:
# Windows Service Process Types (SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS)

SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS indicates a service that does not share its address space with other processes — each instance runs in its own process. The alternative, SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS, places multiple services in a single host process (svchost). OWN_PROCESS is selected when an operator needs the service binary to occupy a dedicated address space, which is required for in-memory execution or self-contained payload staging within the service host.
contents.concept:createservice-scm:
# CreateService SCM Registration

CreateServiceA accepts hSCManager, lpServiceName, lpDisplayName, dwDesiredAccess, dwServiceType, dwStartType, dwErrorControl, lpBinaryPathName, and dependencies. It returns an SC_HANDLE to a newly registered service object added to the SCM database. An operator uses OpenSCManager first to obtain the hSCManager handle, then CreateService to register a binary, then StartService to launch it. dwStartType controls boot trigger (SERVICE_DEMAND_START, SERVICE_AUTO_START).
contents.concept:windows-registry-hives:
# Windows Registry Five-Hive Structure

The Windows Registry is a collection of five hives (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, HKEY_CURRENT_USER, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, HKEY_USERS, HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG), each exposing configuration data. The registry API family (RegOpenKeyEx, RegSetValueEx, RegQueryValueEx) is the canonical interface. HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run is the most commonly used persistence key per Source A, autoloaded at user logon.
contents.concept:registry-run-key:
# Registry Run Key Persistence

The HKCU or HKLM Run key (SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) is the most commonly used registry key for persistence per Source A. Values written under this key are interpreted as executable paths and launched automatically by explorer.exe (HKCU) or winlogon.exe (HKLM) at logon. RunOnce executes once then deletes the value. The technique is noisy — registry modification telemetry and Sysmon E13 capture it directly.
contents.concept:thread-states-ready-running-wait:
# Thread Dispatch States (Ready/Running/Waiting)

Windows threads occupy at least nine states; the three operational ones are Ready (queued for dispatch, not on a CPU), Running (executing instructions during its quantum slice), and Waiting (blocked on an event or object signal). Only Ready threads are dispatched by the scheduler. A thread is in the Running state specifically during its quantum slice. The Waiting state is the prerequisite for alertable APC delivery — a thread must transition through a Wait with ALERTABLE set before user-mode APCs drain from its queue.
contents.concept:kernel-thread-object:
# Kernel-Resident Thread Object

When a new thread is created, the thread object resides in system (kernel) space, not user space or the process handle table. The ETHREAD/KTHREAD structures are kernel objects. User-mode code receives a handle to this kernel object via the process handle table, but cannot directly dereference the object — all access goes through NT syscalls. This placement constrains user-mode thread-context manipulation to the NtGetContextThread/NtSetContextThread syscall interface and prevents direct memory patching of thread state.
contents.concept:apc-queue-dispatch:
# APC Queue In-Quantum Routine Dispatch

The APC queue is the mechanism that allows threads to process routines when the thread enters its quantum. User-mode APCs are delivered when the thread transitions to an alertable wait (SleepEx with ALERTABLE, WaitForSingleObjectEx, etc.). Kernel APCs are delivered regardless of alertable state. Early Bird injection queues an APC before the thread begins executing its real entry point, causing the APC routine to run first. Context and Event objects do not provide this dispatch path.
contents.concept:thread-context-concept:
# Thread Context (Legitimate vs Malicious)

Thread context is the saved CPU register state (RIP, RSP, general-purpose registers, segment registers, FPU/XMM state) for a thread, accessed via GetThreadContext/SetThreadContext or the NT equivalents. Legitimate use includes debuggers suspending and inspecting threads, and fibers saving/restoring state across cooperative switches. Malicious use includes thread hijack injection: suspend target thread, overwrite RIP with payload address, resume — the thread begins executing injected code in its original process context with its original token.
contents.concept:process-integrity-levels:
# Process Integrity Levels (System/High/Medium/Low)

Each process token carries a mandatory integrity level (System, High, Medium, Low, AppContainer). Process Explorer displays these levels: wm10gon.exe runs at System (kernel-equivalent trust), explorer.exe at Medium (standard user), procexp64.exe at High (elevated admin). Processes cannot write to higher-integrity objects. UAC splits Medium (filtered admin) from High (full admin) — the boundary UAC bypass techniques cross. Token theft (TokenThief) often targets a System-integrity token from a process like winlogon or lsass.
contents.concept:access-token:
# Windows Access Token Structure

An access token describes the security context of a process or thread — user SID, group SIDs, privileges (SeDebugPrivilege, SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege), integrity level, and logon session. Primary tokens are assignable to new processes; impersonation tokens can be attached to threads. Token theft duplicates a victim's token (via DuplicateTokenEx) and applies it with CreateProcessAsUser or SetThreadToken. SeDebugPrivilege permits opening any process for token extraction, including lsass and winlogon.
contents.concept:process-monitor-procmon:
# Process Monitor (ProcMon) Defensive Telemetry

Process Monitor captures real-time file, registry, process, thread, and network I/O activity with call stacks for every operation. Source A uses ProcMon in Lab 1.2 to demonstrate how defenders observe application behavior — the same telemetry defenders use to detect registry writes (persistence), file drops (dropper artifacts), and process spawns (service launch). ProcMon's filter highlights registry Run key writes, SCM service install calls, and suspicious file opens during token theft — the operations T-017 and T-021 techniques perform.
contents.concept:fileless-in-memory-execution:
# Fileless / In-Memory Execution

In-memory execution is code execution not backed by a file on disk — the payload resides entirely in process memory as MEM_PRIVATE or MEM_IMAGE-mapped shellcode or a reflective PE. Source A frames this as the operational counter to on-disk AV scanning. The trade-off is memory-resident detection: scanners like Moneta and PE-sieve specifically hunt for code regions that lack on-disk backing. Dropping to disk brings filesystem telemetry risk; staying in memory brings memory-scan risk.
contents.concept:process-suspended-no-hooks:
# Suspended Process Creation State Without Hooks

A process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED enters the suspended state before its initial thread executes, before ntdll's LdrInitializeThunk runs, and before any user-mode hooking layer (ntdll inline hooks installed by EDR) has been applied to the new process address space. Source A identifies this suspended stage as the window in which no hooks are implemented. Techniques that queue an APC for execution during the suspended state (Early Bird, Early Cascade) operate before EDR hooks land in the new process.
contents.concept:dropping-capability-to-disk-risk:
# Risk of Dropping Capability to Disk

Source A frames dropping a capability (DLL, EXE, shellcode) to disk on a target with an unknown security product as risking both detection (AV signature scan) and loss of capability (quarantine/deletion). The 'all of the above' framing in the review answer indicates both outcomes are operationally equivalent failures. This risk drives the entire class of file-less execution techniques that keep payloads in memory or use delete-pending/section-mapped execution paths.
contents.concept:ifeo-debugger-persistence:
# IFEO Debugger Key Persistence

Persistence via the Image File Execution Options registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target>.exe with a Debugger value naming an attacker executable. When the target executable is launched, the OS transparently launches the attacker executable instead, passing the target's original command line as an argument. Source A Lab 4.3 (IFEOPersisto) covers this variant, distinct from the SilentProcessExit variant.
contents.concept:silent-process-exit-persistence:
# SilentProcessExit Monitoring Persistence

Persistence and process-monitoring via the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\<process>.exe registry key with ReportingMode and MonitorProcess values. When the monitored process exits, WerFault.exe launches the configured MonitorProcess executable. Source A identifies SilentProcessExit as a registry key that can watch for process termination and process creation, functioning as an event-driven persistence trigger activated by the exit of a specific process rather than a fixed schedule.
contents.concept:wmi-extrinsic-vs-intrinsic-event:
# WMI Extrinsic vs Intrinsic Events

Intrinsic WMI events fire immediately when an instance of a WMI class is created, modified, or deleted (e.g., __InstanceCreationEvent). Extrinsic events are produced by an event provider on a specific occurrence (e.g., Win32_ProcessStartTrace) and must be polled at some interval because the provider raises them asynchronously. Source A review questions ask which event types must be polled, with extrinsic being the canonical answer; intrinsic events do not require polling because the CIM repository raises them in real time.
contents.concept:egress-vs-p2p-listener:
# Egress vs Peer-to-Peer C2 Listeners

Source B distinguishes egress listeners (beacon reaches the team server across a network boundary, typically HTTP/S to the internet) from peer-to-peer listeners (beacon chains through another compromised host, e.g., SMB or TCP peer-to-peer). The HTTP egress listener is described as the majority-of-the-time listener, with peer-to-peer used for pivoting through segmented networks or when direct egress is blocked. Exposing port 50050 directly to the internet is identified as an OPSEC failure; VPN or SSH tunnel access is recommended for remote operators.
contents.concept:security-descriptor-viewing:
# Security Descriptor Viewing via sc.exe

Source A review questions identify sc.exe as the command-line utility for viewing an object's security descriptor (via sc sdshow). A security descriptor encodes the owner SID, group SID, DACL (discretionary access control list), and SACL (system access control list) for a securable Windows object — service, file, registry key, etc. cmd.exe and tasklist.exe do not expose security descriptor content; sc.exe's sdshow/sdset subcommands are the canonical service-security-descriptor tool.
contents.concept:hidden-service-scm:
# Service Control Manager Hidden Service

A Windows service can be hidden from typical enumeration by manipulating Service Control Manager database entries so that standard listing APIs do not return the record. Techniques include deleting the service registry entry while keeping the binary loaded, or modifying DisplayName, ImagePath, and Description to mimic legitimate services, evading sc query and Get-Service enumeration.
contents.concept:suspended-process-hook-window:
# Suspended Process Pre-Initialization Window

A process created with CREATE_SUSPENDED begins life before its main thread has executed LdrInitializeThunk, before ntdll.dll has been hooked by EDR products, and before any DLLs in the IAT have been loaded. This pre-initialization window is the rationale for techniques such as process hollowing and Early Bird APC injection that queue work to the suspended thread so the payload runs before userland EDR hooks are in place.
contents.concept:capability-staging-opsec:
# Capability Staging Operational Security

Operational principle that capability DLLs and tools should not be written to disk on systems where the deployed security product is unknown. Dropping a capability to disk risks both losing the capability via quarantine or deletion and detection by static signature or behavioral monitoring. Reflective in-memory loading is the preferred alternative when transporting capability DLLs over sockets.
contents.concept:eprocess-structure:
# _EPROCESS Kernel Process Object

The _EPROCESS structure is the kernel object representing a process. Microsoft treats it as opaque to user mode. Notable members shown in the Source A WinDbg dump include Pcb (the embedded _KPROCESS at offset 0x0), ProcessLock at 0x438, UniqueProcessId at 0x440, ActiveProcessLinks (a LIST_ENTRY at 0x448), and RundownProtect at 0x458. The structure is approximately 0xa40 bytes on the build shown. Enumeration APIs and tools such as Get-Process and tasklist walk the ActiveProcessLinks list rather than querying a fixed table.
contents.concept:activeprocesslinks-dkom:
# ActiveProcessLinks DKOM Process Hiding

Direct Kernel Object Manipulation (DKOM) attacks unlink a target _EPROCESS from the doubly-linked ActiveProcessLinks list maintained by the kernel. Once unlinked, the process disappears from standard enumeration tools (Get-Process, tasklist, EnumProcesses, CreateToolhelp32Snapshot) because those tools walk the list rather than scanning kernel memory directly. The attack requires kernel-mode write access. The Source A material treats this as the canonical kernel-level counterpart to user-mode process hiding such as PEB unlink.
contents.concept:process-handle-access-rights:
# Process and Thread Access Rights

Process and thread handles carry access masks that gate what operations can be performed on the underlying object. The rights relevant to offensive tradecraft per the Source A material include PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (all possible process rights), THREAD_ALL_ACCESS (all possible thread rights), PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS (create a child process from this process), PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD (create a thread in the process — required for CreateRemoteThread), and PROCESS_DUP_HANDLE (duplicate a handle out of the process). GetCurrentProcess and GetCurrentThread return pseudo-handles for the calling process and thread, respectively.
contents.concept:leaked-handle-abuse:
# Leaked Handle Exploitation

Handles are considered leaked when an application fails to close them after use. Source A shows that handles leaked to high-privilege objects such as a SYSTEM process with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS can be enumerated by an attacker using Process Explorer or Sysinternals handle.exe and then abused for shellcode injection via VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread against the leaked handle. The pattern is a privilege-escalation primitive that bypasses the need to call OpenProcess with the desired access.
contents.concept:programmatically-hidden-service:
# Programmatic Service Hiding via DACL

Windows services can be hidden from standard service enumeration by modifying the discretionary access control list (DACL) on the service object so that the Service Control Manager and standard enumerators are denied read access. Source A contrasts a manual approach against a programmatic approach using Windows security APIs to alter the service object's permissions, hiding the service while retaining its ability to start and persist across reboots.
contents.concept:enumprocesses-api:
# EnumProcesses Process Enumeration API

EnumProcesses is a documented Psapi function that returns an array of process identifiers on the system. The function signature takes an output DWORD buffer, a buffer size, and a pointer that receives the number of bytes returned. It is the simplest of the documented enumeration APIs but returns only PIDs — no process name, session, parent, or other metadata. Additional information must be obtained by opening a handle to each PID via OpenProcess and querying attributes individually.
contents.concept:createtoolhelp32snapshot-api:
# CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Enumeration API

CreateToolhelp32Snapshot produces a snapshot of processes, threads, heaps, and modules. The process enumeration variant is commonly used in malware because it returns more detailed information than EnumProcesses (PID, parent PID, process name, module list) in a single iteration via Process32First and Process32Next. Source A identifies it as 'perhaps one of the more common APIs used in malwarez for process enumeration.'
contents.concept:wtse-numerate-processesex:
# WTSEnumerateProcessesEx Cross-Session Enumeration

WTSEnumerateProcessesEx queries process information from the Terminal Services subsystem and returns a count plus detailed per-process information including the session identifier associated with each process. Unlike EnumProcesses, it can query remote systems and enumerate processes across multiple local sessions. The session field enables the operator to select injection targets in a different logon session, which Source A calls cross-session process injection.
contents.concept:wua-updatesearcher:
# Windows Update Agent UpdateSearcher Object

The Windows Update Agent (WUA) API exposes COM objects for querying installed patches and available updates. UpdateSession creates an UpdateSearcher, whose Search method returns a SearchResult containing the matching updates. The Source A material identifies UpdateSearcher as the WUA object used to find updates on a system, and Get-HotFix as the PowerShell cmdlet that queries the Win32_QuickFixEngineering WMI class for installed hotfixes. Together these support patch-gap analysis during post-exploitation reconnaissance.
contents.concept:host-survey-tool:
# Host Survey Tool Pattern

Source A frames the host survey tool as the developer's primary post-exploitation deliverable after initial access: a tool that gathers OS, process, patch, and security-product information to decide whether to continue operations. The pattern is the operational precursor to selection of injection targets, persistence placement, and C2 staging. The host survey output drives go/no-go decisions based on observed defensive controls.
contents.concept:netuserenum-api:
# NetUserEnum API and USER_INFO Levels

NetUserEnum (Netapi32.dll) retrieves information about all user accounts on a local or remote system. The level parameter selects the USER_INFO structure returned: level 0 returns account names only, level 10 returns name/comment/auth flags, level 20 returns extended info including last logon. The returned buffer must be freed with NetApiBufferFree. The function accepts a remote servername parameter enabling domain-wide enumeration.
contents.concept:getusername-api:
# GetUserNameA and Impersonation Token Behavior

GetUserNameA returns the username of the current thread or process token. When called from a thread impersonating a client, the function returns the impersonated user's name rather than the process owner. The lpBuffer and pcbBuffer parameters follow the standard pattern where the caller provides a buffer and a pointer to its size; if the buffer is too small the function fails and returns the required size in pcbBuffer.
contents.concept:windows-service-archetypes:
# Windows Service Process Archetypes

Windows defines three service hosting models: special process (no GUI, runs in background), shared service (multiple services share address space in a single svchost.exe — if one service crashes they all crash), and isolated service (hosted in its own svchost.exe without sharing address space). The SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS flag indicates a service that does not share its address space with other services; SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS indicates shared svchost hosting.
contents.concept:task-scheduler-com-interfaces:
# Task Scheduler COM Enumeration Interfaces

Scheduled task enumeration on legacy Task Scheduler v1.0 uses COM via CoInitialize followed by CoCreateInstance of the TaskScheduler CLSID. The ITaskScheduler::Enum method returns an IEnumWorkItems enumerator; IEnumWorkItems::Next then retrieves task name strings in batches. This COM path avoids spawning schtasks.exe or at.exe, leaving no process-creation telemetry for the enumeration step.
contents.concept:hklm-registry-hive:
# HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE Subkey Hierarchy

HKLM is the root key holding systemwide configuration. Major subkeys: BCD00000000 (boot entries), COMPONENTS (Component-Based Servicing state), HARDWARE (enumerated hardware description), SAM (account password database — restricted access requiring SYSTEM), SECURITY (security policy and LSA secrets — restricted), SOFTWARE (non-boot-critical systemwide configuration and third-party app settings), SYSTEM (boot-critical configuration with a maintenance copy of the last known good control set).
contents.concept:sam-registry-subkey:
# HKLM\SAM Subkey (Security Accounts Manager)

The SAM subkey under HKLM stores the local account password database as hashed credentials. Direct access is restricted to the SYSTEM principal; even Administrators cannot read it in-flight without impersonating SYSTEM or extracting the hive offline. The material identifies this as the credential store targeted by tools that dump SAM via registry save or in-memory hash extraction.
contents.concept:hkey-performance-data:
# HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA (HKPD) Programmatic-Only Access

HKPD is unique among registry root keys because it cannot be viewed via regedit.exe — it must be accessed programmatically via RegQueryValueEx. Performance counters from system components or server applications appear here, but the data is not actually stored in the registry; it is provided on demand by external perfmon providers. The material notes Pdh.dll functions are a preferred alternative for retrieving performance data.
contents.concept:registry-value-types:
# Registry Value Types (REG_DWORD, REG_BINARY, REG_SZ)

Registry values can be one of 12 types but three dominate: REG_DWORD (32-bit number or boolean), REG_BINARY (raw data — used for values exceeding 32-bit or encrypted material), and REG_SZ (Unicode or ANSI string used for names, paths, file names, type identifiers). The type determines how the byte payload is interpreted when the value is read back via RegQueryValueEx or enumerated via RegEnumValue.
contents.concept:regnotifychangekey-watchdog:
# RegNotifyChangeKey Registry Watchdog

RegNotifyChangeKey signals a caller when a registry key or its values change. The material notes it only signals that a change occurred — it does not report what changed, requiring the caller to re-read the key to identify the delta. Implants use it as a watchdog to detect post-installation events such as antivirus product installation or tampering with the implant's own persistence keys. The material cautions against polling too frequently.
contents.concept:regenumvalue-iteration:
# RegEnumValue Iteration Pattern

RegEnumValue retrieves one value under an open registry key per call, indexed by dwIndex. The standard pattern initializes dwIndex to 0, calls the function, increments, and repeats until ERROR_NO_MORE_ITEMS is returned. The lpValueName buffer receives the value name; lpcchValueName receives the character count on return. The function is declared in WinReg.h and returns LSTATUS.
contents.concept:last-known-good-control-set:
# HKLM\SYSTEM Last Known Good Control Set

The SYSTEM subkey under HKLM holds boot-critical configuration. Modifying it can render the system unbootable, so Windows maintains a maintenance copy known as the Last Known Good control set, selectable at boot. This allows administrators to revert to a working configuration if a change breaks the boot sequence. The control set structure is what persistence mechanisms that target boot-time drivers or services must respect.
contents.concept:findfirstfile-findnextfile-walk:
# FindFirstFile / FindNextFile Directory Walk

Directory enumeration in Win32 uses FindFirstFile to open a find handle against a path spec (typically with a wildcard) and FindNextFile to iterate subsequent matches. A recursive walk from the system root visits every file and directory reachable to the caller's permissions, yielding software inventory, document inventory, and operator-tooling discovery. The material notes a recursive walk from the root can take a while but can yield significant survey information.
contents.concept:registry-virtualization-wow64:
# Registry Virtualization (WoW64 Redirect)

32-bit applications running under WoW64 on a 64-bit Windows system are transparently redirected from HKLM\Software to HKLM\Software\WOW6432Node for many writes. This redirection enables legacy 32-bit installers to persist settings without modification while the native 64-bit view remains clean. The material notes this affects registry survey tooling because a 32-bit survey tool sees a different registry view than a 64-bit tool querying the same logical paths.
contents.concept:apc-queue-thread-dispatch:
# APC Queue and Thread Quantum Processing

The APC queue is the mechanism Windows uses to schedule routines for execution when a thread enters its quantum. User-mode APCs require the target thread to be in an alertable wait state to drain; kernel APCs bypass this constraint. This is the dispatch primitive Early Bird, Early Cascade, and threadless APC injection variants all rely on — the difference is the timing and mechanism of queue insertion.
contents.concept:thread-object-kernel-space-resid:
# Thread Object Kernel-Space Residency

When a new thread is created, the thread object (ETHREAD/KTHREAD) resides in system (kernel) space — not user space, not the process handle table. The handle table holds references to kernel objects but the object body itself is in the kernel's paged/nonpaged pools. This means user-mode scanners cannot directly enumerate thread internals without handle-mediated access, which affects how injection techniques must locate thread state and APC delivery targets.
contents.concept:integrity-levels-high-il-uac:
# Integrity Levels and UAC Gating

Windows Mandatory Integrity Control assigns processes Low, Medium, or High integrity levels. Standard user processes run at Medium-IL with only SeChangeNotify enabled by default; an elevated process (right-click → Run as Administrator, consent via UAC prompt) runs at High-IL with a substantially larger disabled-but-present privilege set (SeDebug, SeImpersonate, SeTcb, etc.) that can be enabled on demand via AdjustTokenPrivileges. Process Explorer exposes integrity level per-process. The UAC prompt is the gate separating Medium from High-IL — bypassing it (T-021) is the prerequisite for accessing High-IL privilege sets.
contents.concept:openprocess-token-handle:
# OpenProcessToken API

OpenProcessToken takes a ProcessHandle, DesiredAccess mask, and outputs a TokenHandle. The desired access mask (TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, TOKEN_QUERY, TOKEN_DUPLICATE, TOKEN_ALL_ACCESS) determines what subsequent operations are permitted — AdjustTokenPrivileges requires TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, DuplicateTokenEx requires TOKEN_DUPLICATE. Has a BOOL return type; failure modes are silent unless GetLastError is consulted. This is the entry point for every token theft and privilege adjustment workflow.
contents.concept:scm-service-housekeeping:
# SCM Service Startup Housekeeping

When the Service Control Manager starts a service, it performs five housekeeping steps: (1) check the service account information against LSASS, (2) load the user profile for the service account, (3) create the service process in suspended state (effectively a process-hollowing-like start), (4) map the service binary, (5) resume execution from the suspended state. This suspended-start sequencing is what allows service-based persistence to inject and aligns with how legitimate services bootstrap — operators creating malicious services must conform to this contract or the service will fail to start.
contents.concept:query-service-config-unquoted-pa:
# QueryServiceConfig and Unquoted Binary Path Vulnerability

QueryServiceConfigA returns a QUERY_SERVICE_CONFIGA structure containing the service binary path (lpBinaryPathName). When a service path contains spaces and is unquoted (e.g., C:\Program Files\My Service\svc.exe), Windows attempts to execute progressively-qualified intermediates (C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\My.exe) before the actual binary. A writable directory in that path prefix becomes a privilege escalation vector by placing a malicious binary at the unquoted intermediate location. SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS access is required on the handle.
contents.concept:change-service-config-binary-mod:
# ChangeServiceConfig Binary Path Modification

ChangeServiceConfigA accepts an optional lpBinaryPathName parameter that, when supplied, replaces the configured executable for an existing service. This is a persistence-by-modification primitive: rather than registering a new service (which generates a service-install event), the operator re-points an existing, already-authorized service at a malicious binary. The companion ChangeServiceConfig2 manages service triggers, enabling trigger-based activation rather than auto-start, reducing persistence footprint. Both APIs return BOOL.
contents.concept:startservicectrldispatcher-servi:
# StartServiceCtrlDispatcher and SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY

StartServiceCtrlDispatcher receives a SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY array mapping service names to their ServiceMain functions (LPSERVICE_MAIN_FUNCTION). The dispatcher connects the service process to the SCM and routes incoming start requests to the matching ServiceMain. For a single-service binary the table has one entry plus a {NULL, NULL} terminator; multi-service shared-process binaries register multiple entries. Failure to call StartServiceCtrlDispatcher at process start causes the SCM to mark the service as failed-to-start.
contents.concept:servicemain-register-service-ctr:
# ServiceMain and RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx

ServiceMain (called by the dispatcher when the service starts) is responsible for registering a control handler via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerExA, initializing SERVICE_STATUS global state (dwServiceType=SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS, dwWaitHint, dwServiceSpecificExitCode), and beginning service work. The handler is the callback invoked by SCM for control requests (STOP, PAUSE, INTERROGATE). Mismanagement of SERVICE_STATUS transitions is a common reason malicious services fail or trigger SCM alerts.
contents.concept:service-win32-own-process-isolat:
# SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS Isolation

Specifying SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS as the service type indicates the service runs in its own dedicated process rather than sharing a host (svchost, services). Shared-process services crash when a co-resident service crashes — a reliability problem for malicious services. OWN_PROCESS isolation plus a configured failure action (restart on failure) produces a self-healing service that survives crashes and restarts without operator intervention, which is desirable for resilience but increases per-service process-count telemetry.
contents.concept:createservice-api-persistence:
# CreateService API as Persistence Primitive

CreateService() is the underlying API invoked by both sc.exe and the PowerShell service cmdlets (New-Service, Install-Service). It accepts SCManager handle, service name, display name, service type, start type, error control, binary path, load order group, dependencies, account, password. The name passed must match the name registered via RegisterServiceCtrlHandlerEx in the binary. Using CreateService directly (rather than sc.exe) avoids spawning a child process under the implant's parent, reducing process-tree telemetry.
contents.concept:anonymous-pipes-parent-child-ipc:
# Anonymous Pipes IPC

Anonymous pipes are unnamed IPC primitives restricted to parent-child process relationships, are local-only (cannot traverse the network), and are one-way (a single end cannot both read and write). They have lower overhead than named pipes and are commonly used for stdin/stdout redirection of spawned child processes. Their parent-child binding makes them useful for staged loader→implant handoff but unsuitable for arbitrary interprocess or cross-host communication.
contents.concept:named-pipes-duplex-network:
# Named Pipes: Duplex and Network Capable

Named pipes are named IPC primitives that can be used between unrelated processes, support duplex (bidirectional) communication on a single pipe end, and — when the Server service (LanmanServer) is running — become accessible over the network to remote systems. This makes named pipes a transport substrate for both local IPC and remote C2 channels. The Server-service dependency is a deployment-environment consideration: hosts with the service disabled cannot receive remote pipe connections.
contents.concept:regnotifychangekeyvalue-watch:
# RegNotifyChangeKeyValue Registry Watchdog

RegNotifyChangeKeyValue signals a caller when registry changes occur matching a filter mask (REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_NAME for subkey create/delete, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_ATTRIBUTES, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_LAST_SET for value create/modify/delete, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_SECURITY). The REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC flag (Windows 8+) decouples the notification from the calling thread, so the wait does not need to be drained by the originating thread. The hKey handle must have REG_NOTIFY access. Excessive polling is discouraged in favor of event-triggered notification.
contents.concept:primary-vs-impersonation-token-c:
# Primary and Impersonation Token Distinction

A primary token is assigned to a process and represents the process's security context for object access checks; an impersonation token is temporarily attached to a thread to act in another security context. Token theft operations (e.g., TokenThief pattern) duplicate a primary token from a higher-privilege process and either assign it to a new spawned process (CreateProcessWithTokenW) or attach it as impersonation to the calling thread (ImpersonateLoggedOnUser). The distinction governs which token APIs are valid for the operation.
contents.concept:named-pipe-duplex-ipc:
# Windows Named Pipe Duplex IPC

Named pipes in Windows are duplex, can be used between unrelated processes, and are accessible over the network when the server service is running. A pipe server creates instances via CreateNamedPipe; pipe clients connect via CreateFile or CallNamedPipe using the \\.\pipe\<name> convention. Anonymous pipes by contrast are unidirectional and cannot operate over the network.
contents.concept:fileless-reboot-volatility:
# Fileless Memory-Resident Reboot Constraint

Memory-resident payloads do not survive system reboot because RAM is flushed. Source A identifies this as the primary disadvantage of fileless malware: machines reboot for updates, power failure, or user action, and the implant loses initial access. This makes some form of disk-dropped or registry-stored persistence practically unavoidable for long-term presence.
contents.concept:memory-forensics-pe-sieve:
# PE-sieve Memory Scanner (Hasherzade)

PE-sieve is a user-mode memory scanning tool by Hasherzade that scans a process and can dump implants, detecting 'all kinds of injection methods' per Source A. It works by comparing in-memory module layouts against on-disk PE files and flagging discrepancies such as modified.text sections, unbacked executable regions, and hollowed modules.
contents.concept:memory-forensics-moneta:
# Moneta Memory Scanner (forrest-orr)

Moneta is a user-mode Windows memory analysis tool by forrest-orr, similar in purpose to PE-sieve. Source A lists it alongside PE-sieve and Volatility as a memory forensics tool that can identify in-memory implants even when on-disk AV does not catch them.
contents.concept:memory-forensics-volatility:
# Volatility Memory Forensics Framework

Volatility, from the Volatility Foundation, ingests full memory dumps and provides numerous plugins for analyzing process memory, loaded modules, and injected code. Source A notes that almost everything an implant does on a Windows system can be logged by something and that motivated memory analysts remain a detection risk even when on-disk scanning is bypassed.
contents.concept:registry-run-key-persistence:
# Registry Run Key Autostart Persistence

The Run key under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run and HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run is the most-used persistence mechanism by APTs including APT28 and Emotet per Source A. HKLM requires admin privileges; HKCU does not. The method is trivially detected by SysInternals AutoRuns but is favored for simplicity.
contents.concept:registry-runonce-key-persistence:
# Registry RunOnce / RunOnceEx Persistence

RunOnce and RunOnceEx registry keys execute a process once and then delete the registry entry, minimizing persistence artifacts. Source A frames this as good for short-term operational goals and bad for long-term presence. HKLM version runs as admin; HKCU version is recommended as an initial downloader until a more reliable persistence method is established.
contents.concept:appinit-dlls-mechanism:
# AppInit_DLLs Registry-Driven DLL Loading

When the registry value LoadAppInit_DLLs (REG_DWORD) is enabled under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows, every newly created user-mode process linked against user32.dll loads the DLLs listed in AppInit_DLLs (REG_SZ, comma-separated). Source A cites APT39, CherryPicker, and T9000 as users. Requires admin privileges to modify HKLM.
contents.concept:appcert-dlls-mechanism:
# AppCert DLLs Process-Creation Hook

AppCert DLLs is a registry-driven mechanism where Windows checks the registry for DLLs that must be loaded into a process when certain Create* API calls are invoked, including CreateProcess and WinExec. Like AppInit_DLLs it requires HKLM modification (admin). Source A lists it as a MITRE ATT&CK autostart location detectable by SysInternals AutoRuns.
contents.concept:disk-artifact-blending:
# Disk Artifact Placement Tradecraft

When an implant must drop to disk for persistence, Source A recommends placing the binary in user-trafficked folders (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Pictures, Temp, App Data, Program Files, SysWow64, System32, OneDrive) to blend in. Operators should avoid being the first or last file in a directory listing because that position attracts analyst attention during folder review.
contents.concept:service-control-manager-scm:
# Service Control Manager (SCM) Failure Determination

The Service Control Manager is the authority for service lifecycle. SCM considers a service failed when the service terminates without reporting SERVICE_STOPPED, or when the Win32ExitCode member of the SERVICE_STATUS structure does not indicate ERROR_SUCCESS. SCM then consults the service's configured SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS to determine the response. Services that do not answer to SCM are promptly terminated.
contents.concept:service-status-structure:
# SERVICE_STATUS Structure and Win32ExitCode

The SERVICE_STATUS structure is reported by a service to SCM and includes the dwCurrentState (e.g., SERVICE_STOPPED) and dwWin32ExitCode members. SCM uses these to determine whether the service has failed: a non-SERVICE_STOPPED state on termination or a non-ERROR_SUCCESS Win32ExitCode triggers the configured failure actions.
contents.concept:service-security-descriptor-sddl:
# Service Security Descriptor and SDDL Concealment

Each service has a security descriptor stored by SCM, viewable via sc.exe sdshow <service> and writable via sc.exe sdset <service> <SDDL>. The SDDL string defines DACL and SACL ACEs that determine which SIDs can enumerate, query, or control the service. By stripping standard users (IU, SU) and interactive (BA) query permissions from the DACL, the service disappears from Get-Service output and sc.exe query enumeration without requiring a kernel driver or API hook. Joshua Wright's SDDL pattern applies to several SIDs simultaneously.
contents.concept:service-imagepath-binpath-failur:
# Service ImagePath, binPath, and FailureCommand Values

ImagePath is a Registry value holding the absolute path to the service binary on disk and any arguments passed to it. binPath is the SCM-facing property that typically matches ImagePath. FailureCommand (set via SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONS.lpCommand) is executed by SCM when the service is determined failed. All three can be modified via sc.exe config or the ChangeServiceConfig2 API to redirect service execution to an attacker-controlled binary or to trigger execution on service failure.
contents.concept:wmi-event-subscriptions-persiste:
# WMI Event Subscriptions for Persistence

WMI permanent event subscriptions combine an event filter (e.g., system startup, user logon) with an event consumer (CommandLineEventConsumer, ActiveScriptEventConsumer) to execute arbitrary commands on event trigger. Source A lists WMI Event Subscriptions as a persistence module alongside services, IFEO, and Registry keys. The vault does not currently document WMI-based persistence.
contents.concept:run-runonce-runtwice-registry-ke:
# Run / RunOnce / RunTwice Registry Persistence Keys

The Run and RunOnce Registry keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run execute specified programs at user logon or system startup. Source A identifies Run as the most commonly used key for persistence (over RunOnce and RunTwice). Modifying HKLM-hosted Run keys requires Administrator privileges. The vault's T-017 card does not list Run-key persistence as a discrete layer.
contents.concept:change-service-config2-api:
# ChangeServiceConfig2 API and SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS

ChangeServiceConfig2 modifies service configuration parameters beyond what ChangeServiceConfig covers. Called with SERVICE_CONFIG_FAILURE_ACTIONS, it accepts a SERVICE_FAILURE_ACTIONSA structure to set the dwResetPeriod, lpRebootMsg, lpCommand, and lpsaActions for a service. Source A's implementation pattern zeros the struct with SecureZeroMemory, sets dwResetPeriod=INFINITE, lpCommand to the attacker payload (e.g., 'ping C2'), cActions=0, lpsaActions=NULL.
contents.concept:hklm-hive-permissions:
# HKLM Hive Modification Privilege Requirement

Modifying Registry keys in the HKLM hive requires Administrator privileges. Source A review material explicitly contrasts User, Admin, and Guest roles and identifies Admin as the requirement for HKLM key modification. This constrains HKLM-hosted persistence vectors (Run keys, service ImagePath, IFEO, AppInit) to post-privilege-escalation operational stages.
contents.concept:ifeo-debugger:
# Image File Execution Options Debugger Persistence

Persistence via the HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<ProcessName> registry key with a Debugger value. When the target process is launched, Windows redirects execution to the debugger path specified in the value, launching the implant instead of or alongside the original executable. Source A notes this method is primarily effective for EXE files rather than DLLs and recommends targeting boot-early processes such as userinit.exe to guarantee execution on system startup.
contents.concept:gflags-globalflag:
# Gflags.exe and GlobalFlag Registry Value

Gflags.exe is a Windows SDK tool located at C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Debuggers\x64 that enables advanced debugging features by setting the GlobalFlag registry value under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<ProcessName>. Setting GlobalFlag to decimal 512 enables the Silent Process Exit monitoring feature. Source A notes the SDK must be installed to use gflags.exe, though the same registry value can be set programmatically via RegSetValueEx.
contents.concept:wmi-event-subscription:
# WMI Event Subscription Persistence

Persistence achieved by creating WMI event filters (queries that detect system events), event consumers (actions to take when a filter matches), and filter-to-consumer bindings. Source A introduces WMI event filters and subscriptions as triggers for specified actions, describing them as a persistence mechanism where a consumer executes an implant when a monitored event occurs. The architecture involves providers generating events, infrastructure routing them, and consumers acting on them.
contents.concept:hklm-admin-system-acl:
# HKLM Registry Key ACL Requirements

Registry keys under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, including the IFEO key path and Print\Monitors key path, are protected by ACLs that deny write access to basic users. Source A states that Admin or SYSTEM privileges are required to modify these keys for IFEO persistence, and local administrator is required for port monitor persistence. The SYSTEM account has broad access to HKLM keys. This permission requirement is a limiting factor for both persistence methods.
contents.concept:userinit-boot-target:
# Boot-Early Process Target Selection

Operational tradecraft for IFEO persistence involving selection of a target process that executes early in the boot process or is frequently invoked by the user. Source A specifically names userinit.exe as a good candidate because it kicks off when the system is starting up, ensuring the IFEO-configured implant executes automatically on boot without requiring user interaction.
contents.concept:registry-win32-api-set:
# Win32 Registry API Set for Persistence

The Win32 registry API functions RegOpenKeyExA, RegCreateKeyExA, and RegSetValueEx provide programmatic access to create and modify registry values for persistence. Source A describes these as an alternative to the reg.exe command-line utility for implementing IFEO persistence, enabling the implant to set the Debugger, GlobalFlag, ReportingMode, and MonitorProcess values directly without spawning a child process.
contents.concept:kernel-edr-monitoring:
# Kernel-Mode EDR Monitoring

EDR products may implement kernel-mode monitoring components that continue to observe process behavior even when userland ntdll hooks have been removed. Source A states that unhooking does not truly blind a security product because a kernel module may still be watching. This means NTDLL unhooking only addresses the userland introspection layer; kernel-mode components remain active and detect injection, memory protection changes, and other suspicious operations regardless of userland hook status.
contents.concept:userland-ntdll-hooks:
# Userland NTDLL Hooks

EDR products install inline hooks in ntdll.dll's.text section to intercept NT API calls before they transition to the kernel. Source A describes these hooks as providing introspection into process behavior. Unhooking restores the original ntdll.text bytes, removing this userland monitoring layer. The material explicitly notes that this only blinds userland introspection, not kernel-mode monitoring.
contents.concept:c2-beaconing-pattern:
# C2 Check-in and Beaconing Pattern

The operational cycle structuring implant-to-C2 communication described across Source A units 25-34. An initial call-home signals the implant's existence and provides system information. Periodic check-ins at randomized intervals with jitter report status and receive tasking. Missed check-ins may indicate compromise or failure. The C2 LP issues tasks during check-in responses. The implant parses JSON responses, assigns unique task IDs via UuidCreateSequential, executes tasks, stores results in memory or encrypted files, formats them as JSON with encryption and encoding, and returns them via HTTP POST either during the next check-in or immediately.
contents.concept:wmi-event-types:
# WMI Intrinsic and Extrinsic Events

WMI events are categorized as intrinsic or extrinsic. Intrinsic events fire on changes to the standard WMI model, such as __InstanceCreationEvent when a new WMI object instance is created. Extrinsic events are not tied to WMI model changes and include RegistryKeyChangeEvent for registry modifications. Event filters use WQL (WMI Query Language) to specify trigger conditions, such as filtering for specific process names like notepad.exe.
contents.concept:service-hiding-technique:
# Service Hiding from SCM

A technique to conceal a malicious Windows service from system view after installation. Source A Lab 4.4 instructs developing code to hide a service after it has been installed, using Win32 APIs. The material notes there are multiple approaches but identifies the most straightforward as using proper Win32 APIs to manipulate service visibility.
contents.concept:leaked-handle-exploitation:
# Leaked Handle Exploitation for Injection

Windows handles are leaked when an application fails to close them after use. A handle leaked with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS rights permits an attacker to call VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread on the target process without invoking OpenProcess — the API EDRs most heavily instrument. Source A identifies Process Explorer and SysInternals handle.exe as the diagnostic tools used to enumerate leaked handles in a running process.
contents.concept:dpapi-master-key-hierarchy:
# DPAPI Master Key and Blob Decryption

The Data Protection API (DPAPI) is a Windows component that encrypts and decrypts data blobs using cryptographic keys derived from the user's logon password. Windows Credential Manager uses DPAPI to protect saved secrets such as RDP credentials, and Google Chrome uses DPAPI to protect web credentials stored in the AppData Login Data database. Master keys are stored under the user profile and must be accessed to decrypt blobs offline.
contents.concept:regnotify-change-key-watchdog:
# RegNotifyChangeKey Registry Watch Dog

RegNotifyChangeKey allows an implant to register for asynchronous notification of registry changes without polling. REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_NAME signals subkey create/delete, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_ATTRIBUTES signals attribute changes, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_LAST_SET signals value create/delete/modify, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_SECURITY signals security descriptor changes, and REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC makes the notification persist across threads. The API only signals that a change occurred, not what changed — the caller must re-read the key to determine the delta.
contents.concept:wts-enumerate-processes-cross-se:
# WTSEnumerateProcessesEx and Cross-Session Injection

WTSEnumerateProcessesEx queries local processes and returns per-process session ID. Unlike EnumProcesses, it returns a count and detailed per-process metadata. The session ID field enables an operator to identify processes in other users' sessions, supporting cross-session process injection — injecting into a process running under a different user's logon session.
contents.concept:getipstatistics-netstat-replicat:
# GetIpStatistics for Native netstat Replication

GetIpStatistics is exported by IPHLPAPI and fills a PMIB_IPSTATS struct with system IP statistics, returning ULONG. An implant can call this API to gather network statistics equivalent to the netstat command without spawning netstat.exe, eliminating command-line and process-creation telemetry that would surface in Sysmon EID 1.
contents.concept:registry-software-vs-system-subk:
# HKLM SOFTWARE vs SYSTEM Subkey Semantics

The HKLM\SOFTWARE subkey holds systemwide configuration that is not critical for booting — third-party applications store settings here. The HKLM\SYSTEM subkey holds critical boot configuration; modification can render the system unbootable. SYSTEM maintains a last known good control set as a maintenance copy, allowing administrators to revert to a known-working configuration if a change bricks the boot path. Persistence configuration placed in SOFTWARE is operationally safer than SYSTEM for this reason.
contents.concept:startup-folder-lnk-persistence:
# Startup Folder.LNK Persistence

Persistence is established by creating a.LNK shortcut file in the user's Startup folder (%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup) that points to the implant binary. The link executes on user logon. The method is userland, requires no administrative privilege, and is visible via Startup folder enumeration and autoruns scanners — Source A documents the User_EnvSetup.lnk pattern with a hidden PowerShell launcher.
contents.concept:windows-tasks-hijack-vs-create:
# Windows Tasks: Hijack vs Create

Windows Tasks (scheduled tasks) can be created new for persistence, but doing so increases the attacker's profile by adding a new task object that defenders can enumerate. Hijacking an existing task — replacing its action while preserving its trigger and metadata — reduces telemetry footprint. Source A frames this as a noise-vs-stealth tradeoff in persistence selection.
contents.concept:getuserprofile-directory-api:
# GetUserProfileDirectoryA API

GetUserProfileDirectoryA (USERENVAPI) takes a token handle and returns the root directory of the corresponding user's profile. The recommended pattern is to call once with a NULL buffer and 0 size to retrieve the required buffer length, allocate, then call again to fill the buffer. Useful for constructing user-specific paths such as the Chrome User Data directory without relying on environment variable expansion.
contents.concept:cross-platform-injection-opsec:
# Cross-Platform Injection OPSEC Constraint

Performing process injection across architectures — for example an x64 implant injecting shellcode into an x86 (WoW64) process — is operationally unsound. The architecture mismatch causes shellcode execution to fail or crash the target. Source B explicitly flags this as an OPSEC consideration: the operator must verify target process architecture matches the implant and shellcode architecture before injection.
contents.concept:domain-cached-credentials-mscash:
# Domain Cached Credentials (DCC2 / mscash2)

Windows caches domain logon credentials locally so users can authenticate when the domain controller is unreachable. These cached verifiers (DCC2, also called mscash2) are stored in the registry and use a PBKDF2-based derivation that is offline-crackable with tools such as hashcat. The Source B material surfaces the boomercig mssql::msaad_cache output format with local name, domain FQDN, hash_key, and hash_value fields.
contents.concept:process-enumeration-opsec-dual-r:
# Process Enumeration Dual Role: Target Selection and Security Product Detection

Process enumeration serves two operational purposes simultaneously: identifying candidate processes for shellcode injection (long-running, low-privilege, appropriate architecture) and detecting security products (AV/EDR) whose presence may halt further operations or trigger alerts. Source A states the result of process enumeration can determine whether an operation proceeds or stops.
contents.concept:windows-integrity-levels:
# Windows Integrity Levels (IL)

Windows uses six integrity levels for privilege separation: Untrusted (S-1-16-0x0), Low (S-1-16-0x40), Medium (S-1-16-0x80), High (S-1-16-0x120), System (S-1-16-0x1000), and Protected (S-1-16-0x4000). Anonymous-group and AppContainer processes run at Untrusted; standard UAC user processes at Medium; UAC-elevated processes at High; wininit/winlogon/lsass at System; Protected is settable only by kernel-mode callers. The IL is queried via GetTokenInformation with TokenIntegrityLevel and mediates the no-write-up rule — lower-IL processes cannot write to higher-IL securable objects.
contents.concept:se-backup-restore-privileges:
# SeBackupPrivilege and SeRestorePrivilege — ACL Bypass

Two privileges that bypass the standard file ACL check entirely: SeBackupPrivilege grants complete read access (FILE_GENERIC_READ equivalent) regardless of the file's DACL, and SeRestorePrivilege grants complete write access (FILE_GENERIC_WRITE equivalent). Unlike most privileges which still require a subsequent privilege check, these two skip the ACL evaluation step. Documented in winnt.h as SE_BACKUP_NAME and SE_RESTORE_NAME, typically granted to Backup Operators and Administrators.
contents.concept:se-debug-privilege:
# SeDebugPrivilege — Cross-Process Handle Acquisition

SeDebugPrivilege (SE_DEBUG_NAME) grants the right to open any process handle with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS regardless of the process's security descriptor. Without it, OpenProcess on wininit/winlogon/lsass or other PPL-adjacent system processes fails with access denied. Standard user tokens do not have this privilege present; High-IL admin tokens have it present but disabled by default and enable it on demand via AdjustTokenPrivileges. It is the privilege-level enabler for token theft, process hollowing into system processes, and LSASS access for credential dumping.
contents.concept:se-load-driver-privilege:
# SeLoadDriverPrivilege — User-Mode Driver Loading

SeLoadDriverPrivilege (SE_LOAD_DRIVER_NAME) authorizes loading and unloading device drivers via NtLoadDriver/NtUnloadDriver from user mode. Standard users lack it; administrators have it present-disabled. Source A explicitly identifies this privilege as the user-mode entry point for driver loading operations, making it the prerequisite for BYOVD chains and kernel-attack surfaces that load a vulnerable signed driver as a stepping stone.
contents.concept:admin-to-system-privilege-set:
# Admin-to-SYSTEM Privilege Escalation Set

Source A identifies five privileges that enable escalation from Administrator to SYSTEM: SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege (take ownership of any securable object), SeTcbPrivilege (act as part of the Trusted Computing Base), SeCreateTokenPrivilege (create tokens), SeLoadDriverPrivilege (load kernel drivers), and SeDebugPrivilege (open any process). These are not present on standard user tokens — only on admin/elevated tokens. Any one of them, when enabled, provides a distinct path from High-IL admin to System-IL.
contents.concept:token-privilege-manipulation-api:
# Token Privilege Manipulation API Sequence

The canonical three-API sequence for enabling a privilege on a token: OpenProcessToken(handle, TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, &tokenHandle) obtains the token handle; LookupPrivilegeValue(NULL, SE_*_NAME, &luid) resolves the privilege name to its LUID; AdjustTokenPrivileges(tokenHandle, FALSE, &newState,...) flips the SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED attribute on that LUID entry inside the TOKEN_PRIVILEGES structure. The Boolean return of AdjustTokenPrivileges does not indicate success — GetLastError must be checked for ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED when the privilege is not present in the token.
contents.concept:token-privileges-luid-structure:
# TOKEN_PRIVILEGES and LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES Structures

TOKEN_PRIVILEGES contains a count and an array of LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES entries. Each LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES pairs a LUID (locally unique identifier, a 64-bit value split into LowPart DWORD and HighPart LONG) that names the privilege with a DWORD of attribute flags: SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED, SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT, SE_PRIVILEGE_REMOVED, SE_PRIVILEGE_USED_FOR_ACCESS. Privileges are not tied to specific objects — they gate system-wide operations like shutdown, driver loading, and debug access.
contents.concept:uac-fusion-autoelevate-manifest:
# UAC Fusion Manifest and autoElevate Element

During CreateProcess, Windows consults the Fusion database to read an application's XML manifest embedded as a resource. The manifest contains elements including requestedExecutionLevel, uiAccess, heapType, and autoElevate. When autoElevate is set to true on a signed, Windows-located binary, the binary is launched at High-IL without a UAC consent prompt — this is the auto-elevation mechanism UAC bypass research targets. Source A Lab 3.7 (UACBypass-Research) uses Process Monitor to find system binaries with autoElevate=true and weaponizes their IPC or registry interactions to coerce them into performing privileged actions on the attacker's behalf.
contents.concept:uac-elevation-prompt-color-codin:
# UAC Consent Prompt Color Coding

UAC consent prompts use title-bar color to signal trust level: blue indicates a Microsoft-signed and Windows-trusted binary; yellow indicates a signed but non-Microsoft publisher; red indicates an unsigned binary. The color is a visual heuristic to alert the user to elevation risk — blue prompts auto-approve more readily than red. The prompt color is determined by signature verification and publisher reputation, not by the requested privilege level itself.
contents.concept:port-monitor-registry-persistenc:
# Port Monitor Registry Persistence / LPE

Abuse of HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors — adding a subkey whose Driver value points to a malicious DLL in System32\ causes the spooler to load that DLL as a port monitor at service startup or reboot. Requires local admin to write the key and survives reboot. The loaded DLL runs in the spooler service context, which is LocalSystem, yielding SYSTEM-level code execution. Source A identifies this as both a persistence and LPE primitive — same key modification achieves both.
contents.concept:token-stealing-lpe:
# Token Stealing (TokenThief) LPE Pattern

Privilege escalation by duplicating another process's primary token and applying it to a new process. Source A Lab 3.5 (TokenThief): with SeDebugPrivilege enabled, open winlogon.exe or another System-IL process, call OpenProcessToken, DuplicateTokenEx to produce a primary token, then CreateProcessWithTokenW to spawn a child under that token. The spawned process inherits the source's IL and group membership — yielding a System-IL process from a High-IL admin context. This is the conceptual basis of Meterpreter's getsystem technique 1 (named pipe impersonation) and technique 3 (token duplication).
contents.concept:explicit-access-structure:
# EXPLICIT_ACCESS_A Structure for ACL Modification

EXPLICIT_ACCESS_A describes one access-control entry for a trustee, pairing grfAccessPermissions (DWORD of access rights), grfAccessMode (ACCESS_MODE enum: GRANT_ACCESS, DENY_ACCESS, SET_AUDIT_SUCCESS, etc.), grfInheritance (DWORD inheritance flags), and TRUSTEE_A (the user/group/program to apply against). Used by SetEntriesInAcl to build a new ACL programmatically. Source A references it as the primary structure for modifying ACLs on securable objects from custom tools.
contents.concept:access-token-luid:
# LUID-Indexed Access Token Privileges

Windows privileges present in a process access token are referenced by a Locally Unique Identifier (LUID) rather than by name. LookupPrivilegeValue translates a privilege constant (e.g., SeDebugPrivilege) into its LUID on the local system; the LUID is then embedded in a TOKEN_PRIVILEGES structure passed to AdjustTokenPrivileges to enable or disable the privilege on a token handle obtained via OpenProcessToken. Privileges must be *present* in the token to be enabled; absent privileges cannot be inserted programmatically by an unprivileged caller.
contents.concept:sedebugprivilege-enablement:
# SeDebugPrivilege Enablement Sequence

Three-API sequence (LookupPrivilegeValue → OpenProcessToken with TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES → AdjustTokenPrivileges) that transitions SeDebugPrivilege from disabled to enabled in the calling process's token. Once enabled, the holder can open any process (including LSASS, Winlogon, and PPL-excluded system processes) with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, regardless of the target's DACL. Source A frames this as the canonical prerequisite step for token stealing and credential access operations.
contents.concept:scm-service-database:
# Service Control Manager Database and OpenSCManager

The SCM maintains a database of installed services under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services, with the SCManager object acting as a container for individual service objects. OpenSCManager returns a handle to this container; that handle is required before any operation (enumerate, modify, delete, create) on a service object. Services can start at boot and run without an interactive logon (e.g., BITS, EventLog, schedule, iphlpsvc), making them a privilege-escalation and persistence surface available in session 0.
contents.concept:unquoted-service-path-lpe:
# Unquoted Service Path Local Privilege Escalation

When a service's ImagePath contains spaces and is not quoted (e.g., C:\Program Files\My Service\svc.exe), Windows' CreateProcess resolution attempts to execute progressively shorter prefixes (C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\My.exe,...). If a non-administrative user can write to any prefix path, dropping a malicious binary at that path causes the service to execute attacker code in the context of the service (often LocalSystem). EnumServicesStatus and QueryServiceStatus enumerate ImagePath values to discover vulnerable services.
contents.concept:autoelevate-manifest-attribute:
# Application Manifest autoElevate Attribute

Windows applications carry an XML manifest parsed by the Fusion subsystem during CreateProcess. The autoElevate element, when set to TRUE, signals that the binary should silently elevate to High-IL when launched by an administrator in an elevated split-token session — without displaying a UAC consent prompt. Binaries with autoElevate=TRUE are the targets of UAC bypass techniques: an attacker injects into or hijacks such a binary to inherit its silent elevation.
contents.concept:uacme-fusion-scanning:
# UACMe Project Fusion Scan Workflow

The UACMe GitHub project ships fusion.c and fusion.h, which implement three functions — FusionScanDirectory, FusionScanFiles, FusionCheckFile — for enumerating on-disk binaries and parsing their embedded manifests to identify those declaring autoElevate=TRUE. This scan workflow is the discovery phase that surfaces candidate binaries for UAC bypass weaponization; bypass methods in the same project then exploit specific behaviors of the discovered binaries (e.g., DLL hijack, COM interface abuse) to gain High-IL.
contents.concept:sddl-ace-string-layout:
# SDDL ACE String Syntax

Security Descriptor Definition Language encodes ACEs as compact strings: ace_type (A=allow, D=deny, OA=object-allow, OD=object-deny, AU=audit, AL=alarm), ace_flags (CI=container-inherit, OI=object-inherit, NP=no-propagate, IO=inherit-only, ID=inherited, SA=audit-success), and rights constants partitioned by object type (generic: GA/GR/GW/GX; standard: RC/SD/WD/WO; directory: RP/WP/CC/DC/LC/SW; registry: KA/KR/KW/KX; file: FA/FR/FW/FX). SID constants abbreviate well-known accounts (BA=Builtin Administrators, IU=Interactive User, SU=Service User, SY=Local System). sc.exe sdshow emits service security descriptors in this format.
contents.concept:uac-non-security-boundary:
# UAC as Non-Security Boundary

Source A explicitly characterizes UAC as a convenience feature rather than a security boundary: a High-IL admin in a split-token session runs un elevated processes at Medium-IL by default, but autoElevate binaries transition to High-IL silently without consent. Because the boundary is administrative rather than enforced, bypass techniques that route through autoElevate binaries are not treated by Microsoft as security vulnerabilities — they are within the supported elevation contract, which is why UAC bypass remains a durable tradecraft primitive rather than a patched attack surface.
contents.concept:token-stealing-primitive:
# Token Stealing for Privilege Escalation

Privilege-escalation pattern in which a process with SeDebugPrivilege opens a higher-privilege target (typically winlogon.exe or lsass.exe), retrieves its access token via OpenProcessToken, and assigns it to the calling thread via ImpersonateLoggedOnUser or SetThreadToken. The stolen token carries the target's privileges and integrity level, elevating the caller without spawning a new process or modifying service configuration. Source A frames this as the conceptual payload enabled by the SeDebugPrivilege enablement sequence.
contents.concept:adjust-token-privileges:
# AdjustTokenPrivileges and PTOKEN_PRIVILEGES

AdjustTokenPrivileges enables or disables privileges on an access token using a PTOKEN_PRIVILEGES structure containing NewState, BufferLength, and PreviousState parameters. The function returns BOOL and does not throw — callers must check the return value and GetLastError, since partial success (privilege present but not all attributes set) is possible. Source A identifies this as the final step in privilege escalation after the token handle is opened.
contents.concept:luid-and-attributes:
# LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES Structure

LUID_AND_ATTRIBUTES pairs a Locally Unique Identifier (LUID) for a privilege with an attributes DWORD describing its state. Source A enumerates four SE_PRIVILEGE_* attribute flags: ENABLED (privilege is set and active), ENABLED_BY_DEFAULT (enabled at token creation), REMOVED (used to strip privileges from a token), and USED_FOR_ACCESS (the privilege was checked during an object open). These attributes are what AdjustTokenPrivileges modifies.
contents.concept:windows-service-control-manager:
# Service Control Manager (SCM)

SCM is the Windows subsystem managing services — processes that start at boot and run without a logged-on user. Source A identifies schedule, EventLog, BITS, gupdate, and iphlpsvc as services running in the background. OpenSCManager returns a handle to the SCManager object container, which holds individual service objects, a database lock, and supports operations EnumServicesStatus and QueryServiceStatus used by LPE scanners to find unquoted service paths and weak binary permissions.
contents.concept:uac-security-context:
# UAC as Non-Security Boundary

Source A explicitly states UAC is not a security boundary — it is a convenience feature. UAC prompts present three title bar colors: blue (Microsoft-signed, trusted), yellow (known publisher, unverified), red (unsigned or unknown publisher). Standard users run at Medium-IL; admin users with UAC enabled also run at Medium-IL until a consent prompt elevates them to High-IL. autoElevate in an application manifest allows a Microsoft-signed binary to silently elevate without a prompt, which is the substrate UAC bypass techniques exploit.
contents.concept:uac-autoelevate-manifest:
# Application Manifests and autoElevate

Application manifests are XML files embedded in PE binaries describing security context, including supportedOS, heapType (e.g., SegmentHeap), and the autoElevate element. When CreateProcess invokes the Fusion database, it reads the manifest; if autoElevate is TRUE and the binary is signed by Microsoft, the process is silently elevated to High-IL without a UAC consent prompt. Source A identifies this as the target surface for UAC bypass research — find an autoElevate binary with a logic flaw and weaponize it.
contents.concept:uacme-project:
# UACMe Project

UACMe is a GitHub repository hosting a collection of UAC bypass methods. Source A describes its Fusion parsing utilities — fusion.c and fusion.h with three key functions: FusionScanDirectory (walk a directory for PE binaries), FusionScanFiles (filter to candidates with embedded manifests), and FusionCheckFile (extract and read the autoElevate element value). The project serves as both a bypass catalog and a research tool for discovering new autoElevate binaries.
contents.concept:image-file-execution-options-per:
# Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Persistence

IFEO persistence uses HKLM Registry keys under the Image File Execution Options subtree to redirect execution of a target binary to an attacker payload. Source A requires Admin or SYSTEM privileges — standard users are denied access to HKLM. The technique appears in Lab 4.2 (Sauron IFEO) and Lab 4.3 (IFEOPersisto). The course recommends building an uninstall command to revert registry modifications and avoid leaving traces.
contents.concept:token-stealing-privesc:
# Token Stealing Privilege Escalation

Token stealing is the pattern of opening a higher-privileged process (typically SYSTEM via SeDebugPrivilege), extracting its primary token, and applying it to the attacker's process or thread via SetThreadToken or NtSetInformationProcess. Source A Book 3 includes a dedicated lab on the steps and APIs involved, framing it as the canonical LPE technique when an admin token is already present but SYSTEM is required.
contents.concept:explicit-access-a-acl-modificati:
# EXPLICIT_ACCESS_A and ACL Modification

EXPLICIT_ACCESS_A structures describe access control entries for a trustee, containing grfAccessPerms (permission mask), grfAccessMode (GRANT_ACCESS, DENY_ACCESS, SET_ACCESS, REVOKE_ACCESS), grfInheritance, and a TRUSTEE_A identifying the user/group/program. Source A identifies this as the primary structure used with SetNamedSecurityInfoA to apply changes to an object's security descriptor, including DACL and SACL modifications.
contents.concept:applocker-whitelisting:
# AppLocker Application Whitelisting

AppLocker is Microsoft's application whitelisting technology. Source B states that when an AppLocker category is enforced, everything in that category is blocked by default, and specific deny rules override allow rules. The default-deny posture means an operator must identify an allow rule that covers a usable LOLBin or staging path, or target the rule set itself for modification.
contents.concept:gpo-abuse-privesc:
# GPO Abuse for Privilege Escalation

SharpGPOabuse is a tool for weaponizing write access to Group Policy Objects to push arbitrary settings — including scheduled tasks, immediate tasks, and PowerShell one-liners — that execute as SYSTEM on every machine in the GPO's scope. Source B frames this as a domain-tier privesc/lateral movement vector: compromise a principal with GPO write access, push code, and harvest execution on multiple hosts simultaneously.
contents.concept:getnativesysteminfo:
# GetNativeSystemInfo and SYSTEM_INFO

Kernel32 export that populates a SYSTEM_INFO structure with page size, min/max application address, active processor mask, processor count, and architecture (wProcessorArchitecture). Source A contrasts it with GetSystemInfo for WoW64 correctness — a 32-bit process calling GetSystemInfo receives the 32-bit subsystem view, while GetNativeSystemInfo returns the host architecture, which is the value needed for architecture-aware payload selection.
contents.concept:wmi-quickfix-engineering:
# Win32_QuickFixEngineering WMI Class

A WMI class exposed by the CIM repository that returns installed hotfix records (HotFixID, InstalledOn, Description). Source A documents that both the Get-HotFix PowerShell cmdlet and the wmic qfe list command ultimately query this class, meaning they return the same data set and may not show every update applied by modern servicing stacks — a limitation operators should account for when assessing patch coverage.
contents.concept:wua-com-api:
# Windows Update Agent (WUA) COM APIs

A COM-based API surface (Wuapi.h, Wuaueng.lib) introduced with Windows XP for programmatically querying installed and available updates via UpdateSession -> CreateUpdateSearcher -> Search(criteria) -> ISearchResult -> IUpdateCollection. Source A presents this as a more thorough alternative to Win32_QuickFixEngineering when enumerating patch status, at the cost of additional COM instantiation telemetry.
contents.concept:createtoolhelp32-snapshot:
# CreateToolhelp32Snapshot Process Enumeration

Kernel32 export that captures a snapshot of running processes, threads, heaps, and modules for enumeration via Process32First/Process32Next. Source A describes it as one of the more common malware APIs because it returns detailed per-process records (PID, PPID, name, module list) in a single snapshot, making it suitable for injection-target and AV/EDR-process identification.
contents.concept:enum-processes:
# EnumProcesses (Psapi)

A minimal Psapi export that returns an array of process IDs with no associated metadata. Source A describes it as the easiest enumeration API but notes the lack of detail (no name, no PID-to-path resolution) makes it unsuitable for AV/EDR identification without a follow-up call such as GetModuleBaseName per PID, which increases the API-call surface.
contents.concept:ip-helper-api:
# IP Helper API (IPHLPAPI)

A user-mode DLL exposing network configuration and statistics queries. Source A specifically references GetIpStatistics (MIB_IPSTATS — IP datagram counts) and GetAdaptersAddresses (IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES — per-NIC addresses, gateway, DNS, adapter type) for NIC inventory. The same surface is exposed to defenders via Get-NetAdapter and netstat -e, so query patterns are well-baselined.
contents.concept:hkcr-registry-root:
# HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT Merged View

A virtual registry root formed by merging HKCU\SOFTWARE\Classes over HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes. Source A documents that HKCR holds file-extension associations, COM class registrations, and the virtualized registry root used by UAC file/registry virtualization. Per-user class registrations in HKCU\SOFTWARE\Classes take precedence over HKLM, which is the mechanism COM hijack persistence relies on.
contents.concept:host-survey-script:
# Host Survey Script

An operational pattern documented by Source A in which an implant or operator-collected script enumerates OS version, service pack, hotfixes, installed software, running processes, services, tasks, NIC configuration, and registry state before any further action.
